rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb:
Rio de Janeiro, on Brazil's Atlantic coast, may have the most dramatic setting of any great city. Bald granite peaks shoot up from a blue tropical bay, forest spills down their flanks, and long white beaches curl around their feet. The mountains that make it beautiful also shape its dangers.

Its name is a famous mistake, by the traditional account. A Portuguese fleet steered through a narrow, cliff-lined gap on the first day of January 1502, and the sailors mistook the wide bay beyond for the mouth of a great river. They called the place the River of January, Rio de Janeiro, but no river flows there: the city curls around a bay, Guanabara Bay.

High above it all stands Christ the Redeemer, 30 metres of concrete faced in pale soapstone, its arms spread 28 metres wide on top of the granite peak called Corcovado. It was finished in 1931, and a worldwide vote in 2007 put it on the list of New Seven Wonders.

Rio's two most famous mountains carry nicknames. In the old sugar trade, sugar was boiled down and set in moulds as a tall cone called a sugarloaf, and Portuguese traders thought the bare granite dome at the bay's mouth looked just like one. So they named it Pao de Acucar, Sugarloaf Mountain. Corcovado's name is a blunter joke: it is Portuguese for hunchback, after the bent, humped outline of the peak.

Sugarloaf got its own ride very early: the Bondinho, a cable car designed by the engineer Augusto Ferreira Ramos, opened in 1912 and rises in two stages to the 396-metre summit. It was reportedly only the third passenger cableway built anywhere in the world.

Guanabara Bay is itself a drowned valley. Its waters reach some 31 kilometres inland around more than 130 islands, yet they meet the ocean through a gap only a kilometre and a half across, with Sugarloaf standing guard. Long ago it was a dry river valley; when melting ice-age glaciers raised the sea, the ocean poured in and filled it, making what geographers call a ria.

Sugarloaf and Corcovado are leftovers: cores of especially tough granite once buried in softer rock that weathered away over the ages, leaving the hard domes bald and alone. Geologists call such a lone, exhumed dome a bornhardt, a kind of inselberg, or island mountain, named for Wilhelm Bornhardt, who described the rock islands of the African plains in 1900.

The dark-green forest on Rio's inner mountains looks like wild jungle, but people made it. In the 1800s coffee plantations stripped those slopes bare, and the springs that supplied the city began to dry up. So from 1861 Emperor Pedro II had the Tijuca Forest planted again by hand, one tree at a time, under Major Manuel Gomes Archer.

Rio also gave the world samba. It took shape a little after 1900 in the Afro-Brazilian streets by the docks, an area called Little Africa, and much of it was nurtured in the house of Tia Ciata, a matriarch from Bahia. The first samba ever put on record, Pelo Telefone, registered by the musician Donga, became the great hit of the 1917 Carnival.

The Tijuca replanting has a startling footnote. More than 100,000 trees went into the bare slopes between 1861 and 1887. Records credit most of that work to just six enslaved workers: Eleuterio, Constantino, Manuel, Mateus, Leopoldo and Maria.

Christ the Redeemer pays for its lofty perch: standing alone on an exposed summit with its arms flung wide, it is struck by lightning again and again. A strike in February 2008 chipped its head, eyebrows and fingers, and another in 2014 snapped off a fingertip.

The granite is dangerous in another way. Many favelas cling to the steep slopes, and in a downpour their shallow soil fills with water and can let go all at once. In January 2011 landslides in the mountains north of the city killed more than 900 people. Rio answered by putting up rainfall warning sirens in its most exposed hillside favelas, which sound when the rain reaches dangerous levels.

river-deltas-where-a-river-drops-its-loa.context_blurb:
Where a big river meets the sea, it slows down, and the mud it has carried for thousands of kilometres settles out. Year after year that mud builds new land, a fan of rich soil laced with channels. These deltas feed some of the most crowded places on Earth, and they keep growing only as long as the river keeps them supplied.

The landform's name comes from Egypt. Just before the Nile reaches the Mediterranean it splits into branches that spread across a broad green fan of farmland. Greek visitors saw that the fan matched their triangle-shaped capital letter Delta, and the land took the letter's name. For thousands of years its black soil kept the pharaohs' Egypt fed. Egyptians called it Lower Egypt, even though it lies at the north end of the country, because the Nile flows north and the delta is the downstream, low end of the river.

In pharaonic times the Nile met the sea through seven mouths, and Greek writers named every one, from the Pelusiac in the east to the Canopic in the west. Over some two thousand years, silt and modern flood control closed the others, and only two still flow: the Rosetta and the Damietta, the delta's two great arms.

The Mississippi builds a very different shape. It unloads sediment faster than the Gulf of Mexico's feeble waves and tides can sweep it off, so it pushes long, narrow lobes of land, called passes, far out to sea. From the air the delta looks like a bird's foot, its toes spread across the water.

Geographers sort deltas by which of three forces wins: the river, the waves or the tide. A strong river builds fingers like the Mississippi's, and strong waves press the mud into a smooth arc, as along the Nile's coast. Where the tide rules, its daily rise and fall combs the mud into long, parallel sandbars and islands threaded by channels.

The tide is master where the Ganges and the Brahmaputra, joined by the Meghna, meet the sea. Together they carry so much Himalayan sediment that they have built the Bengal delta, the largest on Earth, spread over more than 105,000 square kilometres of Bangladesh and India's West Bengal. It is home to over 250 million people. On its seaward edge grows the Sundarbans, the largest tidal mangrove forest in the world, where salt-tolerant trees stand in brackish water and their roots knot through countless tidal creeks. Its name comes from the sundri tree that fills it.

Far up in Siberia, the Lena River ends its 2,700-mile run by spreading across the tundra of Yakutia into the Laptev Sea, building the largest delta in the Arctic, about 400 kilometres wide. For about seven months a year it lies frozen hard as tundra; then the summer thaw floods across its islands, and the whole fan bursts into a lush green wetland for a few short months.

Not every delta reaches the sea. The Okavango River flows down from the highlands of Angola into Botswana, where it drops into a sunken trough in the earth. There, in the middle of the Kalahari Desert, it splits into countless channels, lagoons and islands; each flood triples the area under water, and then the water soaks into the sand and dries away. It is one of the world's great inland deltas, and almost none of its water ever touches an ocean.

A delta lives only while its river feeds it. Dams upstream now catch nearly half the Mississippi's sediment, and levees stop the river from spilling into its marshes, so the hungry delta is subsiding and the sea is reclaiming it. Coastal Louisiana lost about 2,000 square miles of land between 1932 and 2016. At the worst of it, the state was losing one football field of wetland every 34 minutes.

rome-the-eternal-citys-engineering.context_blurb:
Rome, on the River Tiber in central Italy, ruled an empire for some five hundred years, and its engineers built so well that their work still stands, still drains and still carries traffic. Walk its streets today and you pass a temple roof nearly two thousand years old, a stadium designed for crowd control and a sewer older than the empire itself.

Start in the Pantheon, a temple whose great concrete dome has stood for about 1,900 years. Its only daylight falls through one round opening at the crown, some 9 metres across and open to the sky: the oculus, Latin for eye. As the sun moves, the shaft of light sweeps around the marble walls like a slow spotlight. When it storms, rain pours through the oculus onto the floor, yet the temple never floods, because the floor bulges very slightly in the middle and 22 small drain holes, almost invisible, carry the water into a channel underground.

At the Colosseum, which held some 50,000 spectators, each of the 80 arched entrances had a number carved above it, from I to LXXX. A ticket sent each fan to the right arch and from there straight to a seat, the same crowd control a modern stadium uses.

The dome spans 43.3 metres, and the height from its floor to the oculus matches it exactly. That means a perfect sphere 43.3 metres across would fit snugly inside the round hall. It is still the largest dome of concrete without steel reinforcement in the world. So much concrete might have split under its own load, so the builders lightened the concrete as it rose: heavy travertine at the base, then terracotta, then light volcanic tufa. Near the crown they used pumice, a volcanic rock so full of air pockets that it floats on water. The shell also thins from 6.4 metres at the bottom to 1.2 at the top.

On hot days a vast cloth awning, the velarium, was stretched over the Colosseum's spectators from 240 wooden masts. Handling it was skilled and dangerous work high above the stands, so Rome brought in sailors from the imperial fleet's naval base at Misenum, on the Bay of Naples, men who already knew sail and rigging in the wind.

In the centuries after the empire's fall, builders quarried old Roman monuments for marble and stone. The Pantheon survived whole because in AD 609 Pope Boniface IV turned it into a church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, so it was cared for instead of being torn apart.

Roads ran out of Rome like spokes. The first great one was the Via Appia, which the official Appius Claudius Caecus started in 312 BC; it ran straight south on tightly fitted lava blocks that people still walk on, first to Capua and later to the port of Brundisium. Romans prized it so highly that they called it regina viarum, the queen of roads.

The secret of Roman concrete lay in the earth around Pozzuoli, a town on the Naples coast: builders mixed lime and water with the local volcanic ash, called pozzolana after the town, and it formed a mineral glue that hardens even underwater. That is why Roman harbour walls have stood in the sea for 2,000 years.

A team from MIT led by Admir Masic showed in 2023 that the small white lumps of lime dotted through the mix let Roman concrete heal its own cracks. The lumps form when the concrete is hot-mixed with quicklime. When water seeps into a crack, they dissolve and crystallise again as calcium carbonate, gluing the crack shut; in tests, cracked concrete made this way sealed itself within two weeks.

The aqueducts brought water into the city from many miles away using nothing but gravity. Each channel sloped downhill the whole way, often falling only a few centimetres in a kilometre, barely enough to keep the water flowing without letting it stall. The Roman writer Vitruvius even laid down a rule for the gentlest slope a channel could safely have.

Rome's oldest marvel lies underfoot. In the 6th century BC, long before the empire, the Etruscan king Tarquinius Priscus had a huge stone drain built to empty the soggy hollow that later became the Forum into the Tiber. That drain, the Cloaca Maxima, or Greatest Sewer, still carries rainwater to the river some 2,500 years later, one of the oldest sewers in the world still in use.

rongorongo-the-lost-script-of-easter-isl.context_blurb:
Easter Island, Rapa Nui to its people, is a speck of land in the South Pacific with some 2,000 miles of open ocean on every side. Its people raised the giant stone moai, and they also carved rows of tiny signs, each about a centimetre tall, into wooden tablets. Those signs are called rongorongo.

Across the thousands of islands of Oceania, only Rapa Nui produced a glyph-script of its own, so rongorongo is often called the only writing ever invented in the whole Pacific. Scholars still debate whether it is full writing or a memory aid for chants. About 600 different signs are known: stylised people, plants and seabirds such as the frigatebird.

The style is called reverse boustrophedon. Every other line is carved upside down, so a reader starts at the bottom left, reads one line across, then turns the entire tablet upside down, a full 180 degrees, to read the next.

In 1862 Peruvian slave raiders carried off the island's trained tablet-chanters, and one islander later told Bishop Jaussen that no one was left who could read the signs. Egyptian hieroglyphs and Maya glyphs once fell silent too, but scholars learned to read them again, and a stone carved in more than one script, the Rosetta Stone, unlocked the hieroglyphs. Rongorongo has no such key. Only about two dozen inscribed objects survive, and the script is still completely undeciphered, one of the very last such scripts in the world.

rotorua.context_blurb:
Rotorua is a lakeside town in the volcanic heart of New Zealand's northern island, built right on top of live volcanic ground. Steam drifts out of gardens and roadside parks, mud bubbles in hot pools, and geysers roar a short walk from the shops. The Te Arawa Maori have lived beside these hot springs for centuries and still use them every day.

The first thing a visitor notices is the smell. Hot rock deep below leaks hydrogen sulphide up through the soil, the same gas that makes rotten eggs stink, so the town wears the nickname Sulphur City. Locals even joke about Rotten-rua.

In the Whakarewarewa valley the ground hisses and spits. The star is Pohutu, Maori for big splash, the largest active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere, which goes off as often as twenty times daily and hurls scalding water up to 30 metres. In Whakarewarewa village the families of Te Arawa still cook without fire or stove: they lower flax baskets of seafood, corn and greens on cords into a naturally boiling hot spring, Parekohuru. They also set wooden steam boxes over vents in the ground.

Pohutu has a herald. A smaller geyser beside it reliably shoots up 7 to 9 metres a few minutes ahead of Pohutu, so guides call it the Indicator. Its real name, the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser, dates from a royal visit in 1901, when people saw that its three-part plume looked like the three feathers on the Prince of Wales's badge.

South of town at Wai-O-Tapu lies the Champagne Pool, a steaming blue pool 65 metres across that fizzes with rising bubbles of gas. Its famous orange rim is a crust of arsenic and antimony minerals that crystallise from the hot water.

Rotorua is no lone hot spot: it sits at the northern end of the Taupo Volcanic Zone, a belt running down the centre of the North Island to the volcanoes of Tongariro. Here the crust is being stretched thin, and magma rises close enough to boil the groundwater.

That zone holds a world record. In the past 350,000 years it has poured out some 3,900 cubic kilometres of lava and more, in over 300 eruptions. That makes it the most productive source on Earth of rhyolite, a pale, silica-rich lava that tends to explode rather than flow.

ryoan-ji-kyotos-garden-of-stone.context_blurb:
Ryoan-ji is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan, and its rock garden is among the most famous works of art in the country. It is a dry landscape, karesansui in Japanese: a rectangle of raked white gravel with fifteen stones set in it, a low earthen wall behind, and no stream or pond. Visitors sit on the wooden veranda and simply look.

The only green inside the garden is moss, a thin skirt of it around the foot of each stone. Everything else is gravel and rock. Yet the temple grounds outside that courtyard hold a large old pond, Kyoyochi, dug long before the rock garden. For centuries people called it Oshidori-ike, the Mandarin Duck Pond, after the mandarin ducks that came every year to spend the winter on it.

Each morning a monk combs the gravel into ruler-straight furrows, with rippling rings around every stone. In the classic reading of a dry garden, the gravel is water, the open sea, and the stones are islands or mountain peaks rising out of it, a whole seascape made without a drop.

The fifteen stones sit in five groups, placed so that from any spot on the veranda one of them always hides behind another, and you can count fourteen at most. Temple tradition offers one exception: only a person who has reached inner enlightenment, it is said, can see all fifteen together.

The low wall behind the stones has its own quiet beauty: soft brown blotches like drifting clouds. No one painted them. The builders boiled the wall's clay with rapeseed oil, and over the centuries that oil has slowly wept out through the surface, staining it. The Japanese prize this beauty of age and weathering, wabi-sabi.

Close by stands a small stone basin for water, carved with four characters around its square hollow. Alone, each character is only half of one. The empty centre, a square shaped like the character for mouth, completes all four. Together they read 'I know only contentment', a Zen lesson about needing nothing more than you already have.

salar-de-uyuni.context_blurb:
High on the Altiplano, the treeless plateau of the Bolivian Andes, lies the Salar de Uyuni, a white plain more than 3,600 metres up that stretches dead flat to every horizon. No hill, plant or bird breaks it. Spread over 10,582 square kilometres, it is the largest salt flat on Earth, about a hundred times the size of the Bonneville Salt Flats in the United States.

After the rare rains, a thin film of water lies perfectly still across the crust, and the salar becomes the largest natural mirror in the world, some 129 kilometres across, where sky and salt blur into one.

With no stone or timber for hundreds of kilometres, people build with what the plain gives them. Hotels such as the Palacio de Sal are made of cut blocks of salt: the walls, the floors, even the beds and tables.

The whole salar varies in height by less than a metre, which makes it the flattest big surface anywhere. It is so bright and smooth that space agencies use it to calibrate satellite instruments, and NASA's ICESat checked its altitude readings against it to within about 2 centimetres.

Where did so much salt come from, some 10 billion tonnes of it, far from any sea? The salar is the dried floor of Lake Tauca, an ancient lake that filled the basin during the Ice Age and evaporated some 12,000 to 13,000 years ago, leaving its salt behind. Under the crust lies a hidden brine holding one of the world's great stores of lithium, the soft metal in phone and electric-car batteries. Bolivia holds roughly a fifth of the known supply, though that is the store in the ground, not what has been mined.

Near the middle of the salt rises Incahuasi, a rocky island in a white sea. It is a fossil coral reef stranded high above any ocean, proof that the salar was once under water. Thousands of giant cacti crowd its slopes, growing about a centimetre a year, and the tallest reach 12 metres and are more than a thousand years old.

The salt stays because the water cannot leave. Rivers run into the basin from the Andes, but none flows out to any sea, so water escapes only by evaporating, and its salt piles up. Geographers call such a closed basin endorheic, meaning flowing within. The Dead Sea is famously salty for the same reason: it too lies in a sealed basin with no outlet to the ocean.

samarkand-the-registan-and-timurs-blue-c.context_blurb:
Samarkand, in today's Uzbekistan, was one of the great cities of the Silk Road, and in the late 1300s it became the capital of the conqueror Timur, also called Tamerlane. He dragged in the finest craftsmen from the lands he sacked and set them to dressing his city in tile, so that its domes and arches still glow turquoise above the dusty plain.

The heart of the city is the Registan, a Persian name meaning sandy place: a vast paved square that was once Samarkand's marketplace and the ceremonial centre of Timur's empire, framed by three towering madrasas, or Islamic colleges.

Islamic sacred art almost never shows living creatures, but the Sher-Dor, built on one side of the square in the 1600s, breaks the rule. Its name means Lion-Bearing. Across its great doorway two striped tiger-lions chase white does, and each cat carries a rising sun with a human face on its back, an echo of old Zoroastrian sun symbols.

Timur himself lies in the Gur-e-Amir, a tomb finished in 1404 under a bright-blue ribbed dome, about 15 metres wide, that swells outward like a ripe melon. Up a nearby slope runs the Shah-i-Zinda, the Living King, an alley of over twenty tombs dressed in blue tile. It is named for Kusam ibn Abbas, the Prophet Muhammad's cousin. In the old tale, enemies cut off his head while he prayed, and Kusam picked it up, carried it down into a deep well, and lives there still. That is oral legend, not history.

Timur wanted his great mosque, Bibi-Khanym, to outdo every other in Islam, and he paid for it with the plunder of his Indian campaign. Its outer walls ran 167 metres and its main dome rose some 40 metres. But the builders rushed it up between 1399 and 1404, and within a few years bricks were dropping from that great dome. A Samarkand legend tells it differently: the architect lost his heart to Timur's queen and would not complete the mosque until she granted him a single kiss. The kiss, the story says, burned a mark onto her cheek, and the furious Timur ordered women to veil their faces. It is a folk tale, not recorded history.

The third madrasa on the square, the Tilya-Kori, built from 1646 to 1660, also served as the city's main Friday mosque, and its name means Gilded, because its prayer hall glitters with gold leaf laid over intricate patterns on the walls and the domed ceiling.

When Uzbekistan became independent of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Sher-Dor mosaic of striped cats and their suns turned into a national emblem, and today it is printed on the country's 200-som banknote.

The ribbed dome over Timur's tomb outlived his empire: his descendants, the Mughals, carried its bulging shape to India and repeated it for two centuries, at Humayun's Tomb in Delhi and, most famously, at the Taj Mahal in Agra.

Over Timur's grave lies a dark-green slab of nephrite, the biggest single piece of jade known anywhere, which his grandson Ulugh Beg brought from the east. The stone had first graced the palace of a Chinese emperor; later a Chagatai khan, a descendant of Genghis Khan, had it cut down to serve as his throne.

Ulugh Beg was more astronomer than conqueror. Around 1428 he built an observatory on a hill outside the city, and its main instrument was the Fakhri sextant, a curved stone arc with a radius of about 40 metres, sunk partly into a trench in the hillside. In its day it was the largest astronomical instrument in the world.

Working only by eye, without a telescope or a precise clock, he timed the year in the 1430s at 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes and 15 seconds, which missed the true value by under a minute. That was closer than Copernicus came a century later.

Samarkand's last story is a famous legend. The Soviet scientist Mikhail Gerasimov unsealed the conqueror's grave in mid-June 1941 to examine the skeleton, and a tale later spread that an inscription warned anyone who disturbed Timur would let loose an invader worse than he had been. Two days later, on 22 June, Hitler's Germany invaded the Soviet Union. Historians call it coincidence, and people close to Gerasimov said the curse was made up.

samba-and-bossa-nova-rio-de-janeiro.context_blurb:
Rio de Janeiro moves to two of the world's most famous rhythms. Samba, loud and pounding, rose from the city's Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods and became the beating heart of Carnival. Bossa nova, its cool, hushed younger cousin, was born decades later near the beaches of Rio's South Zone, and both have carried the city's sound around the world.

Samba began in the early 1900s in a dockside district nicknamed Little Africa. Women who had moved from Bahia, the tias baianas, opened their homes for parties, and the most famous host was Tia Ciata. At those gatherings, drumming and dance from Africa met the rites of Candomblé, and a new urban music grew out of the mix: samba.

Rio's police in the 1920s often harassed Black street drummers simply for playing. Around 1929 musicians in the Estácio neighbourhood answered by founding Deixa Falar, Let Them Talk, the first organised Carnival group of its kind, and marching as one body also gave them some protection. Other neighbourhoods copied the idea, and today rival samba schools compete every year for the Carnival crown.

For decades the parade wound through ordinary downtown streets. Then in 1984 Rio opened the Sambadrome, a permanent parade avenue some 700 metres long, designed by the architect Oscar Niemeyer, with grandstands for about 90,000 people.

Each school marches behind its bateria, a huge drum band. The biggest drum, the surdo, pounds out the deep master beat that every other player and dancer follows, the heartbeat of the band. Above it wails the cuíca, a friction drum: the player rubs a stick fixed inside the drumhead with a wet cloth and presses the skin to slide the pitch into a laughing squeak or a moan. The cuíca is named after a Brazilian opossum famous for the very same screech.

Pelo Telefone, which means By Telephone, is usually named the first samba ever recorded: the musician Donga registered it in late 1916, and it set the 1917 Carnival alight. Some scholars think another tune beat it by a little, so the honour is disputed.

In the late 1950s, in Rio's South Zone, the guitarist João Gilberto found a way to fold a whole samba band's rhythm into the strumming of one classical guitar, and he sang over it almost in a whisper, a style called bossa nova, the new trend.

Its greatest song began with a walk to the beach. One day in 1962 two regulars at the Veloso bar, the poet Vinícius de Moraes and the composer Tom Jobim, watched a 17-year-old, Heloísa, stroll past on her way to the sand, as she did every day. They wrote a bossa nova about her and named it after the neighbourhood and beach she was heading for: The Girl from Ipanema, now one of the most recorded songs in history.

san-francisco.context_blurb:
San Francisco crowds a hilly peninsula on the coast of California, at the narrow mouth of one of the world's great natural harbours. Its fog, its cold water, its steep hills and its restless ground shape everyday life there, from the famous bridge to the streets.

In 1846 the explorer John C. Frémont gave the name Golden Gate to the strait that leads from the ocean into the bay, picturing it as a golden gateway to the trade of the Pacific. He named it some eighteen months before anyone found gold in California.

When the bridge across that strait was built, the U.S. Navy asked for black-and-yellow stripes so ships could pick it out in fog. The consulting architect Irving Morrow refused. He liked the reddish primer the steel arrived in and chose one bold colour, International Orange, bright enough to pierce the mist and warm enough to suit the green hills and blue water.

For some two hundred years Spanish captains cruised this shore and missed the vast bay hidden behind its narrow mouth. In November 1769 an expedition under Gaspar de Portolá, travelling overland, sighted the bay at last from the high crest of Sweeney Ridge. No ship sailed in through the Golden Gate until 1775.

The city's hills were too steep for ordinary streetcars, so in 1873 Andrew Hallidie opened the first cable car line. A cable runs without stopping in a slot beneath the street, and when the gripman pulls his tall lever back, a grip under the car clamps onto that moving cable and the car is towed uphill. San Francisco's cars are the last hand-operated system of their kind on Earth.

Summer surprises visitors: on a July afternoon the city can sit in chilly fog while towns an hour inland swelter. The cause is the cold California Current, which runs down the coast and drags frigid deep water up to the surface, cooling the sea air just offshore until its moisture condenses. The heat inland then sucks that fog bank through the strait and over the hills.

The same cold water guarded Alcatraz, a federal prison on a rocky island about 1.25 miles from the waterfront. The walls were not the real barrier: the bay's water hovers around 50 to 55 F, cold enough to kill, and its ripping currents can sweep a swimmer right out to sea. In 1962 three prisoners paddled off on homemade floats and were never seen again.

Building the bridge was deadly work. Joseph Strauss, the chief engineer, slung a movable safety net under the deck, the first on a job that size. It caught nineteen men who fell, and they called themselves the Half Way to Hell Club. Eleven workers still died, ten of them when a platform tore through the net in February 1937.

At dawn on 18 April 1906 the San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other, ruptured off the city. The shaking broke both the gas mains and the water mains, so fires raged unchecked through the city for three days and did most of the damage. Some 25,000 buildings were lost, and more than 3,000 people died.

In 1989 the Loma Prieta quake hit during the World Series. Most of the city held, but the worst shaking hit the Marina District. The Marina is built on loose rubble, sand and bay mud dumped as landfill for the 1915 world's fair, and when it was shaken, the waterlogged fill lost its strength and flowed like liquid. Geologists call this liquefaction; buildings there sank, tilted and burned while homes on bedrock stood.

Lombard Street's steepest block falls about 27 feet for every 100, a 27 per cent grade. In 1922 the city rebuilt it as eight tight switchbacks, which cars zigzag down at 5 miles an hour.

The Golden Gate is also a great drain, the single outlet for the rain and Sierra snowmelt of about 40 per cent of California. The Sacramento River, draining the north, and the San Joaquin, draining the south, join in the broad Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta and flow out through the bay to the Pacific.

santorini-the-caldera-behind-the-atlanti.context_blurb:
Santorini is a Greek island in the Aegean Sea, but it is really the broken rim of a volcano. Ferries steam into a deep blue bay ringed by cliffs some 300 metres tall, with the white towns of Fira and Oia perched along the top. Around 1600 BC the volcano, then called Thera, tore itself apart in one of the greatest eruptions people have ever witnessed.

The bay is a caldera: the giant basin left when a volcano's summit collapses into its emptied interior, letting the sea flood in. Santorini's is about 12 by 7 kilometres and up to 385 metres deep. A crater, by contrast, is only the small vent at a volcano's mouth.

The volcano is sleeping, not dead. At the centre of the bay two low islands of black rock have pushed up. The younger, Nea Kameni, New Burnt Island, has been growing from the seabed in eruption after eruption since the collapse, and it now stands about 114 metres high. Its older twin is Palea Kameni, Old Burnt Island.

On the island's south coast lies Akrotiri, a Bronze Age town buried in ash as completely as Pompeii, its three-storey houses, painted walls and even clay water pipes still in place. Yet it held almost no treasure. For years the only gold object found there was a little hollow ibex, a wild mountain goat, discovered in 1999 tucked in a wooden box that sat inside a clay chest.

Stranger still, archaeologists found almost no human bodies: unlike Pompeii, whose victims left hollows in the ash that are now cast in plaster, Akrotiri was nearly empty of the dead. Warned by earthquakes, its people seem to have left in good order, taking their valuables, before the blast came.

And what a blast it was: Thera hurled ash and pumice some 35 kilometres up, deep into the stratosphere, the high layer of the atmosphere that holds the ozone layer. Ash and gas thrown that high can dim sunlight around the world for years.

The archaeologist who dug up Akrotiri, Spyridon Marinatos, believed the island's catastrophe lived on in memory for centuries. He tied it to Plato's tale of Atlantis, an island realm swallowed by the sea in a single day and night. It is a popular idea, but most scholars reject it, because the dates and the geography do not fit.

seoul-palace-city-on-the-worlds-stranges.context_blurb:
Seoul lies in a basin of granite peaks divided by the wide Han River, and it has been the capital of Korea for most of the last 600 years. Today it is home to about ten million people, its tiled palace roofs sit among glass towers, and only a short drive to the north the Korean peninsula is cut in two.

At its heart stands Gyeongbokgung, the main palace of the Joseon kings, founded in 1395 by King Taejo, its name drawn from an old book of Chinese poems that wishes the new dynasty bright, lasting blessings. Twice a day guards in silk robes still change the watch at its painted main gate, Gwanghwamun.

Uphill behind the palace, the Bukchon quarter, once home to Joseon's officials and nobles, keeps rows of hanok, traditional Korean houses whose heavy grey tile roofs curve upward at the eaves around walled courtyards.

Inside a hanok the family lived at floor level, because the floor was the heater. In the system called ondol, a fire in the kitchen sends its hot smoke along stone flues beneath a thick masonry floor, warming the room from below before the smoke escapes up a chimney outside. Elders and honoured guests got the place closest to the fire, where the floor was warmest.

About 50 kilometres north of the palaces runs the Demilitarized Zone, a strip some 250 kilometres long and 4 kilometres wide that crosses the whole peninsula. It was created by the armistice of July 1953, which stopped the Korean War without a peace treaty, and despite its name, fences, watchtowers and mines make it one of the most heavily guarded borders on Earth.

Seoul has a wild side too: just north of the city rises Bukhansan, the mountain north of the Han, whose bare granite domes and forest trails became a national park in 1983. Few big cities anywhere hold a hiking park like it within their limits.

The palace carries scars. In 1592, during the Imjin War, Japanese invaders burned Gyeongbokgung. The kings did not rebuild it: the blackened site lay in ruins, abandoned, for some 270 years, until the regent Heungseon Daewongun raised it again in the 1860s. Much of what visitors see is that 19th-century rebuilding.

The DMZ, meanwhile, has become something no general planned: with people shut out since 1953, its old rice paddies have turned back into wetland and forest, an accidental wildlife refuge. Endangered red-crowned cranes now spend the winter in the mined no-man's-land.

Mountain and palace were always linked. Joseon's founders followed pungsu, Korean geomancy, which holds that a guardian mountain at one's back marks a lucky site. They read the line of Bukhansan's ridge, to the north, to choose exactly where Gyeongbokgung would stand.

sequoyah-and-the-cherokee-syllabary.context_blurb:
Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith, born around 1770 in Tuskegee, in what is now Tennessee, deep in the southern Appalachian homeland of the Cherokee. He never learned to read any language at all. Yet he watched settlers capture words on paper, decided his own people should have that power too, and spent years making it happen.

What he made, from scratch, was a complete way of writing the Cherokee language. Very few people in recorded history have invented a script alone, and Sequoyah is the only one known to have done it without being able to read.

His script is a syllabary, not an alphabet: each symbol stands for a whole syllable, such as ga, no or hi, about 85 in all. That made it astonishingly quick to learn, and a Cherokee speaker who knew the symbols could read within a few days or, at most, a few weeks. The Cherokee National Council adopted the script in 1825.

At first his neighbours, and even his wife, feared the marks were witchcraft, and he was tried as a sorcerer. To prove the marks carried real speech, Sequoyah and his daughter Ayoka, about six years old, were shut in separate rooms, and she read aloud words he had written that she could not possibly have overheard.

In 1828 the nation's printers at its capital, New Echota, brought out the first Native American newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, with Sequoyah's symbols and English side by side. Its first editor was Elias Boudinot.

Some of the shapes came from a settler's spelling book, so a Cherokee sign may look like a D or an R. But Sequoyah could not read English and had no idea what sounds those letters made, so he gave every borrowed shape a brand-new Cherokee sound of its own.

The giant sequoias of California are popularly said to be named in his honour, but that is a story, not a proven fact. Stephan Endlicher, the Austrian botanist who gave the genus its name in 1847, left no explanation. Some scholars think he took it from the Latin sequi, to follow, because the tree's number of seeds per cone followed in sequence after those of related trees.

The script survived the Trail of Tears, the forced removal west in 1838, and now it appears on street signs and in immersion classrooms in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the capital of the Cherokee Nation. It even types on phones and laptops, because the syllabary joined Unicode, the shared code behind the text on every screen.

serabit-el-khadim-the-alphabet-born-in-a.context_blurb:
Serabit el-Khadim is a lonely hilltop in the Sinai desert of Egypt where, nearly four thousand years ago, the pharaohs sent workers to dig turquoise. Around 1800 BC people there cut a few dozen crude marks into the stone, and those marks became the ancestor of almost every alphabet now in use, from Greek and Latin to Hebrew, Arabic and our own ABCs.

The writers were not priests or royal scribes: they were the mine's own labourers, Semitic-speaking workers from Southwest Asia and the Nile Delta who had seen Egyptian hieroglyphs and simplified them for their own tongue. Scholars call the script Proto-Sinaitic and still argue over its exact century.

Their trick is called acrophony, first-sound writing. They borrowed a handful of hieroglyphs and let each picture stand for just the opening sound of the word it showed. The picture of a house, bayt, stood for b and became our B, while the ox head, alp, became our A.

For years the marks were taken for doodles. In 1916 the Egyptologist Alan Gardiner spotted one short group of signs that kept coming back, read each by its first sound, and got l-b-'-l-t, meaning to Baalat, the Lady. Baalat was the miners' name for Hathor, the Egyptian goddess worshipped at Serabit as Mistress of Turquoise, so the word Gardiner read was the name of the mine's own goddess. A goddess's name, spelled out sound by sound, proved the marks were an alphabet.

seville-the-inland-gate-to-the-americas.context_blurb:
Seville, the capital of Andalusia in southern Spain, sits on the Guadalquivir River, and for two centuries it was the gateway between Spain and its empire in the Americas. Treasure fleets unloaded New World silver on its quays, and that wealth raised one of the grandest cathedrals on Earth beside a tower that began life as a minaret.

That tower is the Giralda, about 96 metres tall, and its lower half is old brick that the Almohads, the Muslim rulers of the city, raised between 1184 and 1198 as the minaret of their great mosque. When Christian Seville took over, it did not pull the tower down; between 1558 and 1568 it set a Renaissance belfry on top.

Inside there are no stairs at all: thirty-five broad, gently sloping ramps wind around the solid core, wide enough for a rider to go all the way up on horseback. By tradition the muezzin rode to the top to call the faithful to prayer.

In 1568 a bronze statue of Faith, El Giraldillo, about 4 metres tall and weighing some 1,500 kilograms, was set on the summit, where it swings round to face the wind like a weathervane. From the Spanish girar, to turn, the whole tower took its name.

Beside it, on the cleared site of the mosque, builders worked from 1401 to 1506 on a church so huge that its canons reportedly said people would think them mad. Seville Cathedral, some 126 metres long, is the largest Gothic church on Earth, and when it was finished it took the title of largest cathedral from Hagia Sophia.

Inside lies Christopher Columbus. His coffin is not buried: four crowned bronze bearers, standing for the old kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre, lift it aloft on their shoulders as if in an endless procession. In 2024 DNA tests confirmed that the bones in Seville really are his.

The city's riches came from a strange choice of port. Seville lies about 90 kilometres inland, reached only by sailing up the winding Guadalquivir, yet from 1503 its House of Trade held a royal monopoly, and every ship to or from the Americas had to register there. The monopoly moved to Cádiz in 1717.

shanghai-the-bund-facing-the-future.context_blurb:
Shanghai stands near the mouth of the Yangtze on China's east coast, astride the Huangpu River. In the 1800s foreign powers carved it into trading enclaves and it became one of Asia's great ports; since 1990 it has sprouted a forest of skyscrapers. Its two riverbanks now face each other like the past and the future.

On the western shore of the Huangpu stands the Bund, a waterfront of stately European-style banks, hotels and trading houses, some 52 historic buildings in Gothic, Baroque, Neoclassical and Art Deco dress. They went up after China's defeats opened its treaty ports to British, French, American and Japanese traders. The name is not Chinese: the British who built the waterfront borrowed bund, an embankment or dyke, from Hindustani, a language of India. The Chinese call it Waitan, the outer bank.

Across the water blazes Pudong, where rice paddies and warehouses stood until 18 April 1990, when China threw the district open to developers almost overnight. Within a generation its riverfront became the first place on Earth where three supertall towers rose within a few blocks. Tucked into the old town is the Yu Garden, pavilions, ponds and rockeries crammed into two hectares under the Ming dynasty, which the official Pan Yunduan built between 1559 and 1577 as a peaceful retreat for his aging father, not for himself.

The tallest of Pudong's giants is the Shanghai Tower, 632 metres high, whose glass skin twists through 120 degrees between the ground and the top, a corkscrew that spills the wind and cuts the load on the building by almost a quarter. It is China's tallest building.

Shanghai also built the first commercial high-speed maglev. Since 2004 its wheel-less trains, floating on magnets, have raced about 30 kilometres out to Pudong International Airport in under eight minutes, at up to 431 kilometres an hour. For seventeen years no regular passenger train anywhere was faster.

Back on the Bund, the HSBC Building of 1923 still keeps two bronze lions at its door, polished by passing hands. Its owners boasted that no building anywhere between the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait was as luxurious, a stretch covering much of the globe.

In the old town a zigzag walkway, the Nine-Turn Bridge, leads across a lotus pond to the Huxinting Teahouse of 1784. Folklore says the builders bent it on purpose: evil spirits can travel only in straight lines, so the sharp turns keep them out.

shibam.context_blurb:
Shibam is a walled town in the Wadi Hadhramaut, a long desert valley in Yemen, and it looks like a city of the future built out of earth. About 500 tower houses crowd together inside one defensive wall, rising five to eleven storeys, and the British explorer Freya Stark, who crossed the Hadhramaut in the 1930s, made its nickname stick: the Manhattan of the desert.

Unlike Manhattan's steel and glass, every tower is made of sun-dried mud brick, the earth of the valley shaped into blocks and baked hard by the sun.

Desert gales ought to tear such tall earthen buildings apart. But the builders hid a skeleton inside them, a lattice of timber beams laced through the mud walls, which ties each tower together so it can take the sideways push of the wind.

Weight is the other danger, since soft, heavy mud brick piled more than 30 metres high ought to slump. The builders' main answer is a taper: each wall is about 1.2 metres thick at the bottom and narrows to about 0.4 metres at the top. Smaller bricks go into the upper floors, so a wide base carries a light crown.

shwedagon-pagoda-yangon.context_blurb:
The Shwedagon Pagoda crowns Singuttara Hill in Yangon, the largest city of Myanmar, and it is the holiest Buddhist shrine in the country. Its great bell-shaped stupa, a solid mountain of brick some 99 metres high, is sheathed in more than 20,000 gold plates, so the whole hill seems to glow at sunset.

Ordinary pilgrims keep it golden themselves: they buy thin squares of gold leaf and press them onto the lower stupa by hand.

The four covered stairways each end at a gateway guarded by a pair of chinthe, white-bodied, gold-headed beasts like lions. They are so famous that they appear on Myanmar's money.

At the very tip sits a golden orb set with 4,351 diamonds, and on its point rests one great diamond of about 72 carats. The old craftsmen angled it so that from the right spot on the terrace at dawn or dusk it flashes colours, which most accounts give as red, then green, then white.

By tradition four Buddhas of the present age each left a relic here: a staff, a water filter, a scrap of robe and, holiest of all, eight hairs from the head of the Buddha Gautama. Because the hairs are believed to lie inside, worshippers walk around the stupa clockwise and barefoot.

The shrine's bells have their own tale. British troops who seized Yangon carried off the great bronze Singu Min bell, 23 tons and cast in 1779, as loot, but it slid from the barge and sank in the river, and their engineers gave up on it. The Burmese lashed rafts of bamboo beneath the bell until it floated up, and it hangs in its pavilion to this day.

Around the base stand eight planetary posts, because the Burmese week has eight days: Wednesday is cut in two at six in the evening, and its second half belongs to Rahu, the shadow-planet. Each post bears an animal, and Rahu's is a tuskless elephant, while Wednesday morning has an elephant with tusks. Worshippers pour water over the post of the day they were born.

The custom of giving gold goes back, tradition says, to Shin Sawbu, a 15th-century queen of Bago, who gave gold equal to her own body weight to gild the stupa. She set the pattern for the pilgrims who followed.

sigiriya.context_blurb:
Sigiriya is a sheer tower of rock standing about 180 metres above the forested plains in the middle of Sri Lanka, the hardened granite plug of a long-dead volcano. In the late 400s a king named Kashyapa made it a royal capital in the sky, and the rock still carries his paintings, his gardens and the scratched poems of the visitors who came after him.

Kashyapa set his palace on the roughly flat summit, a court floating high above the plain.

The only way up ended at a gatehouse built as a colossal brick lion crouched against the cliff, and the last stair led between its paws and into its open mouth. The rock was called Sinhagiri, Lion Rock, a name worn down over time to Sigiriya. The head fell long ago, and only the giant paws, each about 3 metres long, remain.

Halfway up the face, under a shallow overhang, survive about two dozen of the cloud maidens: life-size paintings of bare-shouldered celestial women, among the oldest frescoes in Sri Lanka. They are the remnant of a band that once stretched 140 metres along the cliff.

Below them runs the Mirror Wall, brick coated in lime plaster polished so glassy that, tradition says, Kashyapa could see his own reflection as he passed.

Long after the king, travellers kept climbing up to admire the maidens, and they scratched short poems into that polished plaster. Over 1,500 of these verses, written between the 8th and 10th centuries by governors and housewives alike, can still be read.

Kashyapa built partly out of fear. He had taken the throne by murdering his father, and his half-brother Moggallana had escaped abroad to gather troops. In 495 they came. As the armies met, Kashyapa's men swung aside to avoid a swamp, and thinking himself deserted, the king took his own life on the battlefield below his rock. Sigiriya then passed to Buddhist monks.

At the foot of the rock his engineers laid out symmetrical water gardens, fed through buried pipes of clay and pressure chambers. Their round fountains, carved from plates of limestone, sit level with the paths, and after some 1,500 years they still spurt water when the monsoon rains come.

silk-chinas-two-thousand-year-secret.context_blurb:
Silk is the shining thread spun by silkworm caterpillars, and for thousands of years China alone knew how to turn it into cloth. The Chinese state guarded the secret so closely that only the finished cloth, never the silkworms, was allowed to travel west.

The craft is astonishingly old. Diggers at a Yangshao farming settlement from the Stone Age, in Henan in central China, turned up a fragment of woven silk from about 3630 BC, the oldest silk cloth ever found. It had been used to wrap a child for burial, a sign that silk was treasured as precious and sacred from the very dawn of the craft.

Much later, the cloth travelled the long caravan roads west, some 6,400 kilometres across the deserts of Central Asia toward Persia and Rome. The caravans all began their journey at Chang'an, today's Xi'an, the old imperial capital that anchored the eastern end of the route. For two thousand years the traders had no single name for the network; the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen called it the Silk Road only in 1877.

singapore.context_blurb:
Singapore is a small island city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula in Southeast Asia, beside one of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth. Founded as a British trading post in 1819 and independent since 1965, it has turned a cramped tropical island into a city of gardens, towers and ground that did not exist a lifetime ago.

It lies only about 137 kilometres, some 85 miles, north of the equator, where the sun stands nearly overhead all year, so Singapore has no summer or winter, only warmth and downpours nearly all year round.

The coastline keeps moving outward. By land reclamation, piling imported sand into the shallow sea, Singapore has grown from about 582 square kilometres in the 1960s to about 723 today, nearly a quarter bigger, the fastest growth of any country on record.

Gardens by the Bay, beside Marina Bay, is famous for its 18 Supertrees, steel towers 25 to 50 metres tall draped with ferns, vines and other living plants. The tallest carry solar cells and rain collectors, and every night they glow in a light show. At Jewel Changi Airport, rain caught on a glass roof plunges 40 metres through a round hole in the dome: the Rain Vortex, the tallest indoor waterfall on Earth.

The greenery is policy. From 1967 Lee Kuan Yew, the country's first prime minister, set out to make the young nation a lush, tree-lined city, and he planted a tree himself nearly every year. Singapore took a new nickname to match: the Garden City.

Fresh water is scarce on so small an island, so in 2008 Singapore finished the Marina Barrage, a dam that shut Marina Bay off from the sea. Rain slowly flushed out the salt, and the bay at the heart of downtown became a reservoir of drinking water.

Next door to the Supertrees, the Flower Dome shelters desert succulents, baobabs and olive trees in cool, dry air under a single sweep of glass and steel, and in 2015 it entered the record books as the largest glasshouse in the world with no columns to hold up its roof.

The sand ran short when Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam stopped selling it, so in 2016 Singapore borrowed a centuries-old Dutch method: ring a patch of sea with a dike and pump the water out. Land made this way is called a polder, and it needs far less sand.

West of the city, engineers merged seven small islets into one artificial island of more than 3,500 hectares, finished in 2009: Jurong Island. The country has no oil of its own, yet the island processes roughly a million and a half barrels daily.

Singapore grew rich on one narrow sea-gate. The Strait of Malacca, the quickest way by sea from the Indian Ocean to the Pacific, runs past the island, and near the city it narrows to only 2.8 kilometres.

skara-brae-and-neolithic-orkney.context_blurb:
On the windswept Bay of Skaill, on Orkney, an island group north of mainland Scotland, lies a Stone Age village so complete that you can still see where its people slept. People lived in it for some six hundred years, from about 3200 to 2500 BC, before sand swallowed it for thousands more.

One winter in 1850 a gale stripped away the turf covering a dune by the bay and laid bare the stone walls beneath: Skara Brae, the best-preserved Neolithic village in Western Europe.

It is astonishingly old. Many people imagine the Great Pyramid of Giza, built around 2560 BC, as the dawn of history. But Skara Brae beats the Great Pyramid's age by several centuries: it was already a busy village long before that pyramid rose, and before Stonehenge too.

Windblown sand covered the village gently and completely, sealing its beds, dressers and tools just as the villagers left them, and so it is nicknamed the Scottish Pompeii. No volcano was involved; the name only compares how well both places were preserved.

The furniture still stands because Orkney had almost no trees, so the villagers made their beds, seats and dressers out of flat slabs of local stone instead of wood. Stone does not rot.

Against the Atlantic gales they set the houses close together and joined them with low passages, only about a metre high and roofed with slabs of stone, so people could go from home to home without stepping into the storm. Packed rubbish of ash, bone and shell insulated the double stone walls.

Almost every house has a small stone cubicle built into its thick wall, room for one person and connected to stone-lined drains running under the village. That is why archaeologists believe each cubicle was an indoor toilet, a comfort most Orcadians would not have again until the 20th century. The reading is likely but not certain.

Skara Brae was one corner of a great ritual landscape. Nearby, at the Ness of Brodgar, stood a temple complex whose biggest building was closed for good around 2400 to 2200 BC with an enormous farewell feast. In its ruins excavators found the shin-bones of some 400 cattle slaughtered for the occasion.

st-petersburg.context_blurb:
St Petersburg spreads across the marshy islands where the Neva River meets the Baltic Sea, in the far northwest of Russia. Tsar Peter the Great founded it in 1703 as Russia's window on Europe, forced his nobles to build palaces there, and made it the capital of the empire for two centuries. Its canals, palaces and strange summer light make it unlike any other Russian city.

In the weeks around midsummer, darkness never quite falls. The sun slips only just below the horizon, so even at midnight the sky glows brightly enough to read outside: these are the White Nights. They are not the true midnight sun, because the sun does set, if only briefly, and crowds stay out on the embankments far into the night.

The city sits on about 42 islands of the Neva delta, threaded by some 60-odd rivers and canals and tied together by over 300 bridges, and that maze of islands and waterways earned it the name the Venice of the North.

Peter chose ground everyone called unbuildable. On 27 May 1703 work began on the first structure, the Peter and Paul Fortress, on little Hare Island in the delta, and the whole capital grew outward from it. Conscripted peasants and Swedish prisoners of war drained the swamp and hammered endless wooden piles into the mud, and so many thousands of them died that people called St Petersburg a city built on bones.

The tsars' Winter Palace now holds the Hermitage, and Catherine the Great started its collection in 1764 by buying about 225 paintings. With some three million works and objects, it is the second-largest art museum in the world, behind only the Louvre in Paris. In its cellars works a colony of cats, first brought in by Empress Elizabeth in the 1740s to hunt the rats and mice. Each cat still gets a name and a passport.

St Petersburg is also a working seaport. From spring to autumn the great bridges over the Neva lift open every night, around 1 a.m., so that ocean-going ships can pass along the river. Anyone caught on the wrong bank waits for them to close near dawn.

No church on Earth holds more mosaic than the one Russians call the Savior on Spilled Blood, whose walls and vaults shine with over 7,500 square metres of it. Its name marks the spot where, in 1881, a bomb killed Tsar Alexander II.

Outside the city, at Peter's summer palace of Peterhof, over a hundred fountains have splashed every summer since 1721 without a single pump. Water gathered from springs on the Ropsha Heights, some 22 kilometres away and about 90 metres higher, flows down by gravity and arrives with enough pressure to leap skyward. The tallest jet, about 20 metres, rises from the Samson Fountain, where a gilded Samson tears open the jaws of a lion. The lion is Sweden's emblem, and the statue celebrates Russia's victory over Sweden.

The Bronze Horseman, Peter rearing on his horse, stands on the Thunder Stone, a single granite boulder of about 1,500 tonnes. For months, 400 men hauled it overland on a sled riding on a bed of bronze balls, with no animals or machines.

Both the frozen winters and the glowing summers come from one fact, how far north the city lies: at about 60 degrees north, it sits so far from the equator that the sun barely sets near midsummer and barely rises in deep winter. In those dark months the Neva locks in ice.

stockholm.context_blurb:
Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, stands where the fresh water of Lake Mälaren empties into the salt Baltic. Rather than hugging one shore, the city leaps from island to island across the channels, so water, bridges and boats are everywhere, and its medieval core has survived almost untouched.

Old Stockholm is spread over 14 islands at the lake's outlet, stitched together by bridges, and Swedes once called it the city between the bridges.

The old town, Gamla Stan, is packed onto one small island and dates to the 13th century, one of the best-preserved medieval centres in Europe. Its tightest lane, the stepped alley Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, squeezes down to about 90 centimetres, barely the width of a person's shoulders.

East of the city the coast shatters into the Stockholm Archipelago: islands, islets and skerries, bare rocks too barren to build on, scattered far out to sea. Counts vary, but there are roughly 30,000 islands in all.

Even the subway is a wonder. More than 90 of the metro's roughly 100 stations are painted, sculpted or blasted straight into the bedrock and decorated by over 150 artists, and at T-Centralen blue vines climb the raw stone. People call it the longest art gallery in the world.

In August 1628 crowds lined the harbour to cheer the Vasa, the tallest, best-armed warship Sweden had ever built. She sailed barely 1,300 metres on her maiden voyage before she capsized and went down in the harbour, in full view of the crowd, and about 30 people drowned.

The fault lay in her design. Her builders mounted two whole gundecks of heavy bronze guns up high and left too little ballast in the bottom. So a light gust heeled her over, and the sea poured in through her open lower gunports.

The Baltic then saved her. Its water is too cold and too low in salt for the shipworm that eats oak hulls elsewhere. When the Vasa was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom, about 98 per cent of her original oak survived. She stands whole today in her own museum.

The islands themselves are still rising. In the last Ice Age, ice sheets a kilometre thick pressed the crust down, and since they melted the land has been springing back, a process called post-glacial rebound. It lifts the Stockholm region about 3 millimetres a year and pushes new skerries out of the sea.

stone-town-zanzibar.context_blurb:
Stone Town is the old heart of Zanzibar City, on the island of Zanzibar off the coast of Tanzania in East Africa. For centuries African, Arab, Indian and European traders met in its maze of narrow alleys, and under the sultans of Oman the island grew rich on spices and, darkly, on the slave trade.

The town is famous for its doors, more than 500 of them, hand-carved from heavy wood. A family put up the carved door first, before the walls of the house, and its carvings announced the owner: verses of the Qur'an for the devout, a fish for a fisherman, lotus flowers and chains for prosperity.

The name comes from the building stone: while villages along the coast were built of mud and thatch, Stone Town's merchants quarried fossil coral from the reef and cut it into blocks for tall houses. In 2000 the old town became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Many of the oldest doors are studded with big brass spikes, though Zanzibar never faced a siege. The idea came from India: there, studs on fort gates stopped war elephants from smashing them down. In Zanzibar the spikes became pure show, a badge of a merchant's wealth.

That wealth came from cloves: the Omani rulers spread clove plantations across the island, and by the mid-1800s Zanzibar grew more cloves than anywhere on Earth, so traders called it the Spice Island.

In 1946 a boy named Farrokh Bulsara was born to Parsi parents in a house in these alleys, and after his family moved to England he became Freddie Mercury, the singer of Queen. The house is now a museum.

Said bin Sultan, the ruler of Oman, astonished everyone around 1840 by moving his capital away from Muscat to Stone Town. The riches pouring in from the rich trade of the Indian Ocean, above all his East African cloves, had grown larger than all of Oman's own income.

The trade had a cruel side. The biggest slave market in East Africa stood here, where captives from deep in the interior were bought and sold. After Britain forced the market to close, the Anglican Christ Church Cathedral rose on the site from 1873. Its altar stands exactly where the market's whipping post once stood. Beneath, the cramped cells where captives waited to be sold survive.

In 1883 Sultan Barghash built a ceremonial palace on the seafront, Beit-al-Ajaib, the House of Wonders. It earned the name as East Africa's first building with an elevator and Zanzibar's first with electric light.

stonehenge-salisbury-plain.context_blurb:
Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain, the rolling chalk downland of southern England: a ring of colossal standing stones, some still capped by stone beams, raised in stages over many centuries by Stone Age and early Bronze Age people whose names are lost. Where its stones came from, and how they travelled, is still being worked out today.

The builders treated stone like timber. Around 2500 BC they carved a knob, a tenon, on top of each upright and a hollow, a mortise, under each lintel, then dropped one onto the other: a mortise-and-tenon joint, borrowed from woodworking.

At midsummer the rising sun climbs over an outlying block, the Heel Stone, and shines straight along the monument's main axis, so the circle marks the summer solstice. It works as a 5,000-year-old calendar of the turning year.

The lintels were also joined end to end, with tongue-and-groove joints: a tongue carved on the end of one slotted into a groove cut in the next, linking the whole capping ring into one unbroken hoop. No other prehistoric stone circle has anything like it.

The Heel Stone has a legend of its own. In the folk tale the Devil boasted that the stones could never be counted, and when he spotted a friar counting them in secret, he flung a stone at the man. It struck the friar's heel and bounced off, leaving the dent that gave the Heel Stone, or Friar's Heel, its name.

Stonehenge is built of two kinds of rock. The smaller bluestones, 2 to 4 tons each, came from the Preseli Hills of Wales, some 230 kilometres away, among the farthest any stones were moved in ancient times. At the centre lies the Altar Stone, a flat slab about 5 metres long that visitors once walked over. Much of it is hidden because a huge sarsen, Stone 55, toppled over and still lies across it.

The giant sarsens of the outer ring were a mystery until 2020, when a team led by the geographer David Nash read their chemical fingerprint and traced 50 of the 52 to West Woods near Marlborough, only about 25 kilometres north.

In Wales, digs at the bluestone quarries showed the stones were cut around 3400 BC but not raised at Stonehenge until about 2900 BC. Many archaeologists now suspect the bluestones first stood in an older circle in Wales that was later taken down and moved, though that is still a hypothesis.

In 2024 laboratory tests brought a bigger surprise: the six-tonne Altar Stone is not Welsh at all but comes from the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland, more than 700 kilometres away. No stone in any Neolithic monument is known to have travelled farther. Because hauling it that far overland, before the wheel reached Britain, would have been extraordinary, researchers think it was most likely shipped by sea, along Britain's coasts.

Two sarsens still keep a secret. Stones 26 and 160 do not share the West Woods signature, so they must have come from a different source, still unknown.

summits-left-unclimbed-out-of-reverence.context_blurb:
Across Asia stand a few great mountains that people have chosen not to conquer. Climbers could try for their tops, but local faith holds the summits sacred as the homes of gods, and kings, governments and mountaineers have agreed to leave them alone. Not every holy mountain is off-limits, though: some are climbed precisely because they are holy.

On the border of Bhutan and Tibet rises Gangkhar Puensum, 7,570 metres high, whose name means White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers. It is the highest mountain on Earth that no one has ever climbed. Four expeditions failed in the 1980s, and then Bhutan, where the high peaks are revered as dwellings of the gods, banned climbing on them altogether.

In Nepal stands Machapuchare, the Fish Tail, named for its forked summit and sacred to the Gurung people as a home of Shiva. Only one team has ever tried it. In 1957 a British party under Jimmy Roberts got within about 50 metres of the top and turned back, because they had promised King Mahendra, as the price of their permit, to leave the summit untouched. They kept the promise, and no permit has been issued since.

Kangchenjunga, the world's third-highest peak at 8,586 metres, straddles Nepal and Sikkim. The first men to climb it, Joe Brown and George Band in 1955, halted a few steps short of the true summit, keeping their word to Tashi Namgyal, the ruler of Sikkim, that its very top would stay untouched. Many climbers still follow that custom.

Kawagarbo, Yunnan's highest mountain, in southwest China, has never been climbed. The Tibetans who live beneath it believe that if any person stood on its summit, the warrior god who guards them would abandon them. In 1991 an avalanche killed all 17 members of an expedition there, and in 2001 the local government banned climbing for good.

Mount Kailash, a black pyramid of rock in western Tibet, is holy to four faiths at once, Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Bon, and pilgrims walk the path around its base. Unlike Kangchenjunga, its top has never even been tried: no expedition has ever set out for the summit, and China forbids climbing it.

Fuji, the tallest mountain in Japan and an active volcano, is the reverse. It is sacred in Shinto belief to Konohanasakuya-hime, a goddess, and shrines crown its summit. Each year, in the July-to-September climbing season, about 300,000 people climb it, many of them pilgrims going up to worship at the top.

svalbard-and-the-global-seed-vault.context_blurb:
Svalbard is a cluster of cold, mountainous Norwegian islands in the Arctic Ocean, roughly halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole. The ground there is frozen solid, polar bears roam beyond the few small towns, and inside one of its mountains lies a vault built to save the world's farming from catastrophe.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, near the town of Longyearbyen, opened in 2008 to hold spare copies of food-crop seeds from gene banks in more than 80 countries, so that farming could start again after a disaster. Its single entrance juts out of a snowy slope, and the press calls it the doomsday vault.

Engineers drilled it 130 metres into a mountain of permafrost, ground that never thaws and has been frozen for millennia. Machines chill the seeds to minus 18 degrees, but a power cut would hardly matter, because the frozen rock would keep them cold, and it would take some 200 years to warm the chambers to zero.

Longyearbyen, at about 78 degrees north, is the northernmost town on Earth with more than 1,000 people. Beyond its last houses lies polar bear country, so by long custom residents carry a rifle whenever they head out of town.

The vault was meant to wait for some distant disaster, but in 2015 it made its first withdrawal, 128 crates of seed: chickpeas, lentils, barley and wheat. They belonged to a gene bank in Aleppo whose researchers had to flee during Syria's civil war. The seeds were regrown in Lebanon and Morocco and later deposited again.

In 2017 headlines claimed the vault had flooded, after a warm winter sent meltwater into the entrance tunnel. The water got only about 15 metres in and froze there, long before it reached the seeds, which sit behind a second sealed door. None were harmed, and Norway later rebuilt the tunnel to keep water out.

Longyearbyen's small cemetery stopped taking burials around 1950. People had found that the bodies of townsfolk who died in the 1918 flu pandemic were still preserved in the frozen ground, never having decayed. Researchers later dug some up hoping to study the virus, and since then the dead have been flown to mainland Norway.

sydney.context_blurb:
Sydney, Australia's largest city, wraps around one of the finest natural harbours on Earth, on the country's southeast coast. British convicts and their guards founded it in 1788, and today two neighbouring icons rise from its blue water, a steel arch bridge from 1932 and a white-roofed opera house from 1973, both set against warm golden sandstone.

On Bennelong Point, a slim point of land poking into the harbour, stands the Sydney Opera House, opened in 1973, its roof a crowd of huge white curving shells that lean together like sails filling with wind. The point is named for Bennelong, an Aboriginal man who lived alongside the first governor, Arthur Phillip, and a fort and later a tram depot stood there before both were cleared for the building.

Across the water, the Sydney Harbour Bridge of 1932, among the widest long-span steel arches on Earth, makes such a great curved silhouette that Sydneysiders nicknamed it the Coathanger.

The shells nearly defeated the engineers, because each seemed impossible to cast. Utzon, the Danish architect, solved it in 1961: every shell is a piece sliced from one huge imaginary sphere, so all share a single curve and could be made in common moulds. The shells are clad in about a million glazed Swedish tiles in two shades of white, glossy white and matte cream, laid in a chevron pattern so the roof shimmers in changing light.

Visitors can do something on the bridge that few great bridges allow: clipped to a safety line, they climb on foot right up the steel arch to its summit, 134 metres above the water.

The harbour itself, Port Jackson, is a drowned river valley. When Ice Age ice melted and the seas rose, the ocean flooded the old valleys, leaving a coastline of deep inlets that branch far inland, the feature geographers call a ria. When Governor Phillip sailed the First Fleet in, in 1788, he wrote that no harbour in the world was finer, with room for a thousand warships of the line to ride in perfect security.

The bridge's opening in 1932 had a surprise: before Premier Jack Lang could cut the ribbon, Francis de Groot, a man in military uniform, rode forward on horseback and slashed it with his cavalry sword. He declared the bridge open in the name of the people, was arrested, and the ribbon was tied again.

Its sea cliffs, the rocky Heads guarding the harbour, and its stately old buildings share one warm honey colour, the Hawkesbury sandstone that the whole city rests on. Braided rivers laid it down grain by grain some 230 million years ago, in the Triassic, when the first dinosaurs were appearing.

The opera house had a sad ending for its creator. Worn down by fights over money and control, Utzon resigned in 1966 and left Australia, and Australian architects completed the building without him. He won architecture's Pritzker Prize in 2003 and died in 2008 without ever once returning to Australia to see his masterpiece.

ta-prohm.context_blurb:
Ta Prohm is one of the temples of Angkor, in the jungle of northwest Cambodia. The Khmer king Jayavarman VII built it as a great Buddhist monastery, consecrated in 1186 as Rajavihara, the Royal Monastery. Today giant trees sit on its roofs and their pale roots pour down the walls, and it is the picture most people carry of a lost temple swallowed by the forest.

In the early 1900s French restorers at Angkor cleared the jungle off one temple after another. At Ta Prohm they chose differently: they propped the ruins up so they would not fall, then left them wrapped in the forest, as a nod to the popular taste for the picturesque. The conservator Maurice Glaize said it had merged with the jungle without yet becoming part of it.

That wild look made it a film star: in 2001 Lara Croft: Tomb Raider sent Angelina Jolie racing through its root-choked galleries, and locals have called it the Tomb Raider temple ever since.

Most of the great roots belong to the silk-cotton tree, which towers over the ruins, with smaller strangler figs among them. The trees did not grow up from the ground: birds dropped seeds on the gallery roofs, and the roots crept down through the walls, prying the stones apart as they went.

The monastery was enormous in its day, and its founding inscription boasts that nearly 80,000 people were needed to serve it, among them 615 dancers, 18 high priests and 12,640 people living inside the walls. Scholars suspect the king's scribes inflated the numbers.

taj-mahal.context_blurb:
The Taj Mahal stands on the bank of the Yamuna River at Agra in northern India, a vast white tomb inside a walled garden of long pools. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built it over roughly two decades and finished it in 1653, and it is often called the most beautiful building in the world.

It is a monument to grief. In 1631 Shah Jahan's wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their fourteenth child, and the emperor raised the tomb over her grave. For two years he wore no fine clothes and banned music.

Its brick core is sheathed in Makrana marble, quarried in Rajasthan more than 300 kilometres away and hauled to Agra by oxen and elephants, because no stone closer at hand was as white. Nothing coats it: the marble, faintly translucent, takes on whatever light falls on it, so the tomb blushes pink at dawn, blazes white at noon and glows gold under a full moon.

The two richly carved tombs in the great domed hall are false ones, called cenotaphs. Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal actually lie one floor below, in a plain vault, their faces turned toward Mecca, following a Mughal custom that kept the true graves simple and hidden.

Each of the four tall, thin minarets around the platform tilts about two degrees outward, on purpose. The builders were planning for an earthquake: if one ever struck, the towers would topple away from the dome instead of onto it.

The flowers and vines that seem painted on the marble are really cut gemstones, chips of agate, jasper, carnelian and lapis polished and set flush into the white stone, as many as 64 pieces in a single blossom. The craft is pietra dura, called parchin kari in India.

A famous legend says Shah Jahan planned a black marble twin across the river for his own tomb, linked to the first by a bridge. Dark ruins on the far bank seemed to prove it, but when archaeologists dug there in the 1990s, they found ordinary white marble blocks that age had turned black. There never was a black Taj.

tallinn.context_blurb:
Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, sits on the Baltic coast across the Gulf of Finland from Helsinki. Its medieval old town, a tangle of cobbled streets and steep red roofs inside a towered stone wall, is one of the best-preserved in Europe, and it grew rich in the Middle Ages as a trading port.

What makes the old town rare is that it was never bombed flat or turned into a museum: people still live, shop and work in it every day, along a 13th-century street plan that survives almost intact. UNESCO listed it in 1997.

In its 16th-century prime the town wall ran about 2.4 kilometres, stood up to 16 metres high and carried 46 towers. About half of it still survives: nearly 2 kilometres of wall and some two dozen towers.

Tallinn is really two towns. The merchants built the lower town by the harbour, while rulers held Toompea, the upper town on its hill, which passed from Danes to German knights, then to Swedes and Russians. Today Estonia's parliament, the Riigikogu, meets in Toompea Castle at the top.

The lower town's guildhalls and spires were paid for by trade, because Tallinn belonged to the Hanseatic League, the great medieval alliance of merchant towns around the Baltic and North Seas.

The spire of St Olaf's Church shows how rich the town became. By tradition it soared to about 159 metres and made St Olaf's the tallest building in the world from 1549 until lightning burned it in 1625. Historians think the real height was nearer 115 to 125 metres, so the record is a claim, not a certainty. Lightning has struck the steeple eight times or more.

Toompea itself is no man-made mound. It is part of the Baltic Klint, a long wall of pale limestone that follows Estonia's northern shore for hundreds of kilometres. Geographers call such a long, steep step from high ground down to low ground an escarpment, and its 20- to 30-metre drop gave the upper town a wall of rock before anyone built one.
