tambora-and-the-year-without-a-summer.context_blurb:
Mount Tambora is a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia. In April 1815 it tore itself apart in the largest eruption in recorded human history, and the haze it flung into the sky chilled the harvests of Europe and North America, half a world away, the following year.

Its roar carried about 2,600 kilometres to Sumatra, so like cannon fire that the soldiers stationed there were fooled. Believing a nearby post was under attack, the troops marched out to defend it. Stamford Raffles later wrote that almost everyone took the noise for distant guns.

Some 71,000 people died. Only about 11,000 were killed by the eruption itself, by the ash, the glowing flows of hot rock and the tsunamis. Tens of thousands more died of starvation and disease in the weeks and months that followed, because the ash had smothered the crops of Sumbawa and the islands nearby.

The eruption spread so much haze around the globe that 1816 brought freak cold far away. New England saw June snow and summer frosts, and harvests failed across Europe and North America. People remembered 1816 as the Year Without a Summer, and Americans joked about Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.

By Lake Geneva that dark summer, a group of English writers was stuck indoors at Lord Byron's villa, and Byron set them a contest: who could write the best ghost story? Mary Shelley, only eighteen, accepted the challenge and started the novel that became Frankenstein.

The failed harvests sent the price of oats soaring, and feeding a horse became too expensive. In 1817 the German inventor Karl Drais showed off a wooden running machine that needed no horse, and it is counted as the direct forerunner of the bicycle.

How could one mountain cool the planet? Tambora lofted some 60 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed a thin veil of sulphate droplets that spread around the world and lingered for more than a year. The droplets reflected much of the incoming sunlight straight back out into space, and the globe cooled by about half a degree.

The eruption also erased a whole small kingdom on Sumbawa, with its people and its language. In 2004 the volcanologist Haraldur Sigurdsson dug through some 3 metres of ash and found one of its houses, with two of its inhabitants lying where the blast caught them, beside iron tools and bronze bowls. The lost kingdom became known as the Pompeii of the East.

tartan-and-the-kilt-highland-scotland.context_blurb:
Tartan is the criss-cross patterned wool woven for centuries in the Highlands of Scotland, and the kilt is the garment most famously made from it. Both became symbols of Highland identity, were banned after a failed rebellion, and came back in a burst of romance that invented some of the traditions people now think are ancient.

Every tartan grows from one small block of coloured stripes that repeats again and again across the cloth, and weavers call that block the sett. Fix the sett and the whole tartan follows.

The oldest Highland garment was the great kilt, the feileadh mor: a single length of tartan, four to six yards long, belted at the waist with the top thrown over the shoulder. Tradition pictures a clansman on the open hills at night unbelting it and rolling himself up in it like a blanket. The tailored knee-length kilt came later.

Tartan-like cloth is very old in Scotland. The oldest piece ever found, the Falkirk tartan, dates from about the 3rd century AD. It survived because someone used the checked scrap to plug a clay pot and buried it, sealing in a hoard of almost 2,000 Roman silver coins.

After the Jacobite Rising of 1745 was crushed at Culloden in 1746, the government in London passed the Dress Act, which outlawed the wearing of the plaid, the kilt and tartan by Highland men and boys entirely. A first offence meant six months in prison; a second meant transportation, being shipped across the ocean to the plantations for seven years. The ban lasted 36 years, until 1782.

The idea of one fixed tartan for every clan is younger than it looks. It took hold during King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh, when the novelist Sir Walter Scott staged a tartan pageant and coaxed the clan chiefs into parading in their own matching patterns. The king himself wore a kilt so short that he added pink tights.

A great many clan tartans called official come from a book of 1842, the Vestiarium Scoticum, which pretended to reproduce an old manuscript that had gone missing and was later exposed as a forgery. Its authors were the Welsh-born Allen brothers, who called themselves the Sobieski Stuarts and falsely claimed to be grandsons of Bonnie Prince Charlie.

temperate-rainforests-the-cool-wet-giant.context_blurb:
Most people picture rainforest as steamy jungle on the equator, but some of the wettest, mossiest forests on Earth grow in cool places. Along the misty west coasts of the middle latitudes, from the Pacific Northwest of North America to southern Chile and New Zealand, sea winds drench the mountains and raise forests of giant trees dripping with moss.

In Washington State's Hoh Rain Forest, about 140 inches of rain fall each year, and every trunk is shaggy with moss and lichen. Yet the climate is cool, not tropical, which makes the Hoh a temperate rainforest, a forest with a rainforest's soaking but without the heat. Its giants are Sitka spruce and western hemlock.

In 2006 two climbers, Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor, found the tallest tree, indeed the tallest living thing, known anywhere, in the foggy coastal forest of northern California: Hyperion, a coast redwood 116 metres high. That is taller than a 35-storey building, and its exact spot is kept secret.

Walk the Hoh and you may see young hemlocks and spruces standing in a dead-straight, evenly spaced line. They sprouted along a fallen giant, a nurse log, whose rotting wood filled with moss and soil, and when the log finally crumbled away, the young trees were left standing in a row that traces where it lay.

The rain comes from the mountains. On the ocean side of the Olympic Mountains, wet Pacific air is pushed up the western slopes, cools as it climbs, and drops its water before it can cross the peaks. The forest there gets over 140 inches a year, while dry scrub a mere 15 miles beyond the crest gets about 8.

Far to the south lies the Pacific Northwest's mirror twin. Along the Chilean coast, pressed between the Pacific and the Andes, grows the Valdivian rainforest, named for the city of Valdivia and soaked by up to 6,000 millimetres of rain a year. Only the Pacific Northwest has a bigger temperate rainforest.

New Zealand's far southwest, Fiordland, is wetter still: westerly gales off the Tasman Sea are forced over its mountains, so Milford Sound catches about 8,000 millimetres of rain on some 200 days a year. Dense forests of southern beech wrap the glacier-carved fiords that name the region.

These cool forests hold a surprise. A 2009 Australian study found that, acre for acre, temperate rainforest locks away even more carbon than tropical rainforest, about 377 tonnes per hectare above ground against 171. Because they are cool, their fallen wood rots slowly, and the carbon piles up.

tenochtitlan.context_blurb:
Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztecs, the Mexica, founded around 1325 on islands in a shallow lake high in the Valley of Mexico. By 1519, when Hernán Cortés and his Spanish soldiers arrived, it held some 200,000 people or more, a city of temples, canals and gardens rising from the water. Modern Mexico City stands on top of it.

The Mexica built on an island in Lake Texcoco, a shallow, salty lake ringed by mountains, and the island had no room for fields. Their legend explains the choice: Huitzilopochtli, their god, had promised them a home where they would see an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus, a nopal, growing in the swamp, and when they saw it, they built there. That eagle on its cactus sits at the centre of Mexico's flag today.

With no fields, they made their own. They built long garden beds out into the shallows, heaping up mud and decaying plants and tying them in place with the roots of willows. These chinampas, often called floating gardens though they were rooted to the bottom, could yield up to seven crops a year.

Canals ran between the garden plots and people moved about mostly by canoe, so the astonished Spanish called the city the Venice of the New World.

Three broad causeways joined the island to the shore, running north to Tepeyac, south to Iztapalapa and west to Tlacopan. Gaps in them were spanned by wooden bridges that the Mexica could lift out, cutting the city off from any army. Cortés had to fight past exactly that defence.

The lake was too salty to drink, so from around 1418 a stone aqueduct brought fresh spring water from the wooded hill of Chapultepec. It had two channels side by side, so that one could be scrubbed clean while the other kept flowing and the city never ran dry.

The chinampas outlived the empire: in Xochimilco, in southern Mexico City, boatmen still pole flat boats along canals between working garden plots.

In the holy centre of the city rose the Templo Mayor, a stepped pyramid crowned by twin shrines, one to Huitzilopochtli, lord of war and of the sun, and one to Tlaloc, who ruled rain and lightning.

Just north lay Tlatelolco, Tenochtitlan's twin city, whose market amazed the Spanish: gold, obsidian blades, turkeys, herbs and cotton cloth changed hands among crowds that Cortés put at 60,000 a day.

In 1521 Cortés and his native allies besieged the city for more than 90 days, cut its aqueduct and razed it, after smallpox had already swept through. The Spanish built their capital on the ruins, and because it flooded again and again, over the following centuries they drained Lake Texcoco almost completely away.

In 1978 workers digging beneath downtown Mexico City struck a carved stone disc over three metres wide that shows Coyolxauhqui, the moon goddess, cut to pieces in myth by her brother Huitzilopochtli. It led archaeologists straight to the buried Templo Mayor.

The lake has its revenge. Modern Mexico City rests on the soft clay of the old lakebed. As the clay dries and squeezes together, the ground sinks, a process called subsidence, and some districts drop up to 50 centimetres a year. The Metropolitan Cathedral visibly leans.

teotihuacan.context_blurb:
Teotihuacan lies in the Valley of Mexico, north of today's Mexico City: a vast ruined city of pyramids, temples and apartment blocks laid out on a single grid. Around 500 CE it was among the largest cities on Earth, home to more than a hundred thousand people, and it was already an empty ruin by the time the Aztecs found it centuries later.

Its spine is a dead-straight road some 40 metres wide. Long after the city emptied, the Aztecs took the flat platforms lining it for the tombs of ancient lords and named it the Avenue of the Dead. They were wrong: the platforms are temple bases, not graves. Beside the avenue stands the Pyramid of the Sun, some 65 metres high on a base nearly 230 metres square, one of the biggest pyramids in the world.

For all that archaeologists have dug up, one simple fact has never been recovered: what the builders called themselves. They left no readable record of it, so scholars just call them the Teotihuacanos. Even the city's name is borrowed: the awed Aztecs named it in their own Nahuatl language, Teotihuacan, usually translated as the birthplace of the gods.

Ordinary families lived in broad stone apartment compounds of a single storey, their inside walls bright with murals. The most famous, at Tepantitla, shows a mountain gushing water while tiny people swim, sing and gather flowers below, and scholars usually read it as a watery paradise for the dead, an afterlife tied to the rain god Tlaloc.

The city grew rich on obsidian, a volcanic glass that could be knapped into razor-sharp blades. Most obsidian is plain black, but the hills of the Sierra de Pachuca yielded a rare kind that shimmered golden-green, and Teotihuacan's control of it made its blades easy to spot hundreds of miles away.

When the Feathered Serpent Temple was dedicated, around 150 to 200 CE, its builders made a terrible offering: more than 200 people, many with their hands bound, were sacrificed and buried in pits beneath and around it.

Teotihuacan was a magnet for migrants from across Mesoamerica. In one neighbourhood, Tlailotlacan, archaeologists uncovered graves, burial urns and carvings made in the style of a distant valley: it was a quarter of Zapotecs from Oaxaca, who kept their homeland's customs far from home.

In 2015 the archaeologist Sergio Gómez finished digging out a tunnel beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple that had been sealed for some 1,800 years. Among jade statues, shells and pyrite spheres, his lamps lit pools of liquid mercury on the floor, which he thinks stood for an underworld river or lake.

At the north end of the avenue, the 43-metre Pyramid of the Moon was shaped so its outline copies the silhouette of Cerro Gordo, the sacred mountain behind it, and from the avenue pyramid and peak read as one.

The whole city is turned about 15.5 degrees east of true north, and the tilt is deliberate. The Pyramid of the Sun lines up with sunrise and sunset on particular dates, such as sunrise on 11 February and 29 October, dates that probably anchored the ritual calendar.

Around 550 CE the city's great buildings were set on fire deliberately. Because the flames targeted the elite buildings along the avenue rather than ordinary homes, most archaeologists now blame a revolt by the city's own people, probably sharpened by drought, rather than a foreign invasion.

the-aksum-obelisks-stelae-of-axum.context_blurb:
Aksum, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, was the seat of a mighty ancient kingdom that traded across the Red Sea with Rome, Arabia and India. At the edge of the town stands a field of giant carved stone pillars, called stelae, raised more than 1,600 years ago, among them some of the largest single stones people ever cut and stood on end.

The most famous, the Obelisk of Axum, rises 24 metres and weighs some 160 tonnes. What astonishes builders is not its size but that the whole pillar was carved out of one single block of stone, a hard, granite-like rock called nepheline syenite.

Its faces imitate a many-storeyed Aksumite tower-house, with false windows and beams rising storey above storey. At its base the carvers cut false doors, and in them they added a lock and keyhole, as if the monument were a lived-in home. Instead of a pointed tip it ends in a rounded crown like a half moon, and the marks of old fittings show it once wore a metal cap, thought to be sheets of bronze.

The stelae were grave markers: rock-cut burial chambers run beneath the field, and the greatest and most finely carved stones stood over the tombs of kings and nobles.

In 1937 soldiers of Fascist Italy, which had invaded Ethiopia, cut the obelisk into three pieces and shipped it away, and Mussolini's government raised it in Rome as a war prize. In 2002 lightning struck it there and cracked the stone, because three steel bars that the Italians had run through it acted as a lightning rod, so when Ethiopia later stood it up again, the steel was replaced with bars of Kevlar fibre, the material in bulletproof vests. After 68 years abroad it came home in 2005, flown back in three sections aboard a giant Antonov cargo plane, one of the heaviest air cargoes ever carried.

Ethiopian Orthodox Christians hold that Aksum's church of Saint Mary of Zion guards the Ark of the Covenant, brought from Jerusalem by Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. In this living tradition a single monk, chosen for life, keeps watch and alone may see it.

Beside the standing stones lies the Great Stele, about 33 metres long and over 500 tonnes, perhaps the largest single stone ever cut to stand as a monument. It probably fell while it was being raised and never stood at all; as it toppled it crushed a stone chamber below it, and it lies where it fell.

The stone came from Gobo Dura, some 4 kilometres to the west, and had to be dragged without wheels or a river to float it. Local tradition says teams of elephants hauled the blocks into place, though that is tradition rather than proven fact.

Aksum was a world power. King Endubis made it, around AD 270, the first state south of the Sahara to strike its own coins of gold and silver. In the 3rd century the Persian prophet Mani named it one of the four great kingdoms of the Earth, alongside Rome, Persia and China.

the-alps.context_blurb:
The Alps are the great mountain wall of Europe, curving for about 1,200 kilometres through the heart of the continent. They are snowy, steep and young, still being squeezed upward, and they have given the world a sport, an ancient frozen man and one of the great ideas of geology.

No single country owns them: the range touches eight nations, Monaco on the Mediterranean, France, Switzerland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and, at the eastern end, Slovenia.

Its crown is Mont Blanc, White Mountain, a dome of ice and rock 4,808 metres high at the meeting point of the French, Italian and Swiss borders, the highest peak in Western Europe.

On 8 August 1786 Jacques Balmat, a crystal hunter, and Michel-Gabriel Paccard, a doctor, both from Chamonix, became the first people to stand on its top, a climb remembered as the birth of alpinism, the sport of high mountaineering. The sport takes its very name from these mountains.

Geneva's Horace-Bénédict de Saussure, a scientist, had offered a cash prize for that first ascent back in 1760. In 1787, a year after the prize was won, he climbed Mont Blanc himself, with porters hauling cases of scientific instruments so that he could spend days taking measurements at the top.

Mountaineers can come across fossil shells of sea creatures high on the peaks. The Alps rose as the African plate pushed north into Europe and closed the sea that lay between them, the Tethys Ocean, shoving its old sea floor kilometres into the sky.

The range is Europe's water tower: its snow and glaciers feed rivers that run to four different seas. Among them, the Rhine begins as Alpine meltwater in eastern Switzerland, as do the Rhône and the Po.

In September 1991 two hikers in the Ötztal Alps, on the border of Italy and Austria, found a shrivelled body melting out of the ice, and scientists showed that the man, soon nicknamed Ötzi, had died about 5,300 years ago. He is the oldest intact human mummy known. His axe blade was made of nearly pure copper, which proved that metalworking had reached the Alps by about 3300 BC, earlier than scholars had believed.

The collision was so violent that whole sheets of rock slid tens of kilometres and folded over, so that older rock now lies on top of younger rock, and geologists call these far-travelled slabs nappes, from the French for tablecloth.

In 1837, after years studying Alpine glaciers, Louis Agassiz told Swiss scientists at Neuchâtel that immense sheets of ice had once buried much of Europe. He read the evidence in moraines, stray boulders and polished bedrock; most of his audience refused to believe him, but he was right, and the idea of the Ice Age was born.

the-amazon.context_blurb:
The Amazon is the giant river of South America. It rises in the Andes of Peru, gathers a thousand tributaries, and rolls east across Brazil to the Atlantic through the largest tropical forest on Earth. No river anywhere carries so much water, and almost everything about it is outsized.

Roughly one-fifth of the river water reaching the world's oceans comes out of the Amazon, a greater flow than the next seven rivers in size added together. Yet it usually loses one contest, because the Nile is generally counted the longer river. The title is disputed: some surveys that follow a different source make the Amazon the longest.

Its width changes with the seasons: in the dry season a broad stretch runs about 11 kilometres across, but at the peak of the annual flood the same stretch can swell past 48 kilometres, so a boat in mid-river cannot see either bank.

From its mountain source to the ocean, not a single bridge spans the main river; there are none anywhere along it. The one bridge in the whole river system, opened at Manaus in 2011, crosses a tributary, the Rio Negro. The banks are the problem: they are soft, waterlogged wetland that shifts as the river rises and falls by up to 10 metres a year. A bridge would need very deep foundations and miles of raised approaches, and with few roads nearby, factories at Manaus find it cheaper to ship their goods by boat.

At Manaus two rivers meet. The pale Rio Solimões carries fine silt from the Andes. The Rio Negro is black, stained like strong tea by tannins leaching out of rotting leaves and plants in the forest. For about 6 kilometres they run side by side in one channel without mixing, because they differ so sharply in temperature and speed: the Negro is warm, about 28 degrees, and slow, while the Solimões is cooler, about 22 degrees, and fast. Brazilians call it the Meeting of the Waters.

Twice a year, at the spring tides near the equinoxes, the incoming Atlantic tide pushes a wave up the river mouth, against the flow. This tidal bore, the pororoca, a Tupi name usually translated as great roar, can stand 4 metres high and race hundreds of kilometres upstream. The Brazilian surfer Picuruta Salazar rode a single pororoca in 2003 for about 37 minutes, covering some 12.5 kilometres. A pororoca surfing championship has been held every year since 1999.

Every year the central Amazon rises and falls about 10 metres, and the floodwater spreads deep into the jungle for months, making a drowned forest called the várzea, where fish swim among the trunks.

The river's start is as surprising as its end. It rises as snowmelt on Nevado Mismi in the Peruvian Andes, only about 160 kilometres from the Pacific, yet it turns east and crosses the whole continent to the Atlantic. At the mouth, the flood of river water is so great that it freshens the ocean into a vast low-salt plume reaching more than 100 kilometres offshore and covering nearly a million square kilometres.

the-andes.context_blurb:
The Andes run down the whole western edge of South America, some 7,000 kilometres from Venezuela in the north to Chile's far south, the longest mountain chain on Earth. Volcanoes, salt flats, high lakes and plateaus crowd among their peaks, and the Inca built an empire in their valleys.

Most ranges can be crossed in a couple of hours, but in the central Andes the far side can lie 700 kilometres from the coast. That breadth comes from several parallel mountain chains, called cordilleras, marching side by side, with high basins and plateaus caught between them.

More than fifty Andean peaks rise above 6,000 metres, crowded close together, and only the Himalayas of Asia, home to all fourteen of the world's peaks over 8,000 metres, pack in more giants.

Lake Titicaca, on the border of Bolivia and Peru at 3,810 metres, is the largest lake in South America by surface area, and it is often called the highest large lake that boats can navigate. Andean peoples have held it sacred for thousands of years.

Caught between the eastern and western cordilleras spreads the Altiplano, a bare, windswept tableland about 3,750 metres high across Bolivia, Peru, Chile and Argentina. Only the Tibetan Plateau of Asia is larger and loftier.

On the high border of Chile and Argentina rises Ojos del Salado, 6,893 metres, a snow-capped volcano that is the highest volcano anywhere on the planet.

Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, but Earth bulges at the equator. Chimborazo in Ecuador, standing almost on the equator, is 2,585 metres lower than Everest, yet its summit reaches about 2 kilometres farther from the centre of the Earth, the point on the planet's surface farthest from its core.

The Andes exist because of what happens just offshore. There the oceanic Nazca plate dives beneath the South American plate in a subduction zone, and the sinking slab melts and rises to feed the volcanoes. The grinding still shakes the land with earthquakes.

On Chile's northern coast, the Atacama is a reddish wilderness of salt and stone, walled off from moist air by the Andes on one side and a coastal range on the other, and it is the driest desert anywhere outside the polar regions. NASA tries out its Mars rovers there, and some of its weather stations have never recorded rain.

the-appalachians.context_blurb:
The Appalachian Mountains run some 2,000 miles down eastern North America, from Canada through New England to Alabama. From the air they are ridge after ridge, low and rounded and wooded, gentle where the Alps are jagged. That softness hides one of the oldest and strangest stories of any mountains on Earth.

A range's rounded shape is a sign of great age: young mountains stay sharp because they are still rising faster than they wear down, while old ones are ground into smooth, low ridges over immense spans of time. The Appalachians have been eroding for more than 240 million years.

Their highest point is Mount Mitchell in North Carolina's Black Mountains, 6,684 feet tall, the highest summit in North America east of the Mississippi. Its windy top is colder than its height suggests.

Their first uplift came some 480 million years back, when life was only beginning to colonise the land. The first true trees did not appear until about 100 million years later, so these forested mountains are literally older than forests.

They are older than something in space, too: in 2023 a study led by Sascha Kempf, using dust measurements from NASA's Cassini probe, suggested that Saturn's rings may have formed within the last 100 to 400 million years. The rings' age is still debated, but even the oldest estimate is younger than the Appalachians.

The soft ridges are the stumps of a giant. Some 300 million years ago Africa rammed into North America and pushed up the Appalachians as a wall of high, snowy peaks, perhaps 15,000 feet or more, as tall as the Himalayas are today.

That same collision helped weld most of the world's land into one supercontinent, Pangaea, and the range formed its central spine.

When the Atlantic began to open, some 200 million years ago, it split the range and carried its pieces off on separate continents. Geologists match the Appalachians' rocks to Scotland's Highlands and Morocco's Atlas mountains, which were once a single unbroken chain with them. Centuries later, Scottish Highlanders who emigrated to America settled in the Appalachians, unknowingly returning to a broken-off piece of their own mountains.

the-aral-sea.context_blurb:
The Aral Sea lies in Central Asia, shared by Kazakhstan to the north and Uzbekistan to the south, in the middle of a desert. Within living memory it was the fourth-largest lake on Earth, full of fish and islands. Then Soviet planning drained it, in one of the worst environmental disasters people have ever caused, and only now is part of it coming back.

Its name, from an old Turkic word, is usually translated as Sea of Islands, for the more than 1,000 islands that once dotted it. With most of the water gone, the name now reads like a cruel joke.

The disaster was a choice: from the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the two great rivers that fed the sea into irrigation canals to grow cotton, which they called white gold, across the desert. Starved of inflow, the sea evaporated, and more than 90 per cent of its water was lost.

The dry seabed became the Aralkum, a desert of salt and sand that geographers call the newest desert in the world, made within a single human lifetime.

The retreating water also uncovered the past. In July 2001 the shrinking sea exposed ground off the Kazakh shore that had been some 20 metres under water. There archaeologists found Kerderi, a lost medieval town called Aral-Asar with a domed tomb, lived in around the 14th century. The sea had shrunk and grown before.

The old seabed is caked with salt, pesticides and fertiliser from decades of farming, and the wind lifts tens of millions of tonnes of this poisoned dust every year. Scientists have traced it as far away as the glaciers of Greenland.

For decades a small island in the sea, Vozrozhdeniya, Rebirth Island, was left off Soviet maps. It was a secret biological-weapons test site where anthrax and plague were tried out, and as the water fell it joined the mainland, raising fears that buried germs could be reached.

Yet the story has a hopeful turn. In 2005 Kazakhstan finished the Kokaral Dam, which sealed off the smaller northern part of the sea and kept the Syr Darya's water there. The North Aral rose more than 12 metres and grew fresher, and the native fish came back to breed, years sooner than anyone had forecast.

the-arctic-ocean-and-the-north-pole.context_blurb:
The Arctic Ocean caps the northern end of the globe, almost completely enclosed by Asia, Europe and North America. For most of the year its surface is a crust of floating sea ice, and in its middle, with no land beneath it at all, sits the North Pole.

Of Earth's five oceans, the Arctic Ocean ranks smallest and shallowest, covering about 14 million square kilometres with an average depth of roughly 1,000 metres. It is so nearly landlocked that you could almost walk around it.

Stand at the North Pole and there is no ground under your boots: you are on drifting sea ice only a few metres thick, floating on ocean about 4 kilometres deep. That is why nothing permanent can be built there. The South Pole is the opposite, rock under a deep ice cap.

The Arctic has just one doorway to the Pacific, the Bering Strait between Siberia and Alaska, only 82 kilometres wide and 40 to 50 metres deep. All its other links run to the Atlantic. In the Ice Age, when sea levels fell, the strait drained into a chilly grassy plain as much as 1,000 kilometres across called Beringia, a land bridge between Asia and America, until the returning sea flooded it some 11,000 years ago.

Icebergs off Greenland look like sea ice but are something else. Sea ice is frozen seawater. An iceberg is fresh water that froze on land: a chunk breaks away from the end of a glacier, a process called calving, and drifts out to sea.

At the Pole the sun rises and sets only once a year. It climbs above the horizon around the March equinox and circles the sky without setting for about six months, then sinks around the September equinox for about six months of unbroken night.

Sonar mapping found a hidden mountain range, stretching some 1,800 kilometres between Ellesmere Island and the New Siberian Islands: the Lomonosov Ridge, rising more than 3,000 metres from the seabed and splitting the deep Arctic into two basins. It is claimed by Denmark, Canada and Russia alike, because it could decide where seabed borders run.

The ice itself travels. A current of drifting ice, the Transpolar Drift, carries anything frozen in off Siberia across the Arctic, past the Pole and out through the Fram Strait in two to four years. Fridtjof Nansen of Norway froze his ship, the Fram, into it on purpose in 1893, and about three years later it emerged near Svalbard, just where he had predicted.

the-atacama.context_blurb:
The Atacama Desert stretches about 1,000 kilometres down the Pacific coast of northern Chile, a stony waste of gravel, salt and dunes under an almost cloudless sky. It is famous for its dryness, but it also holds fog-fed life, sudden flowers, giant telescopes and the oldest mummies made by human hands.

Antarctica is technically the driest desert of all, so the Atacama's title is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth, where some weather stations have gone more than a century without recording rain. In its driest heart, soil and climate clues point to a dry spell of about 400 years, roughly from 1570 to 1971, with no significant rain at all.

Still, the desert is not lifeless. On most mornings a dense, chilly fog, the camanchaca, rolls inland off the cold Humboldt Current, and lichens and cacti drink their water straight from it.

The same dryness makes the sky astonishingly clear, with more than 200 cloudless nights a year, far from city lights. So the world's richest nations have spent billions building world-class observatories on its high plateaus. On the Chajnantor plateau, 5,000 metres up, where workers carry bottled oxygen, 66 dish antennas work together as one telescope, ALMA, which sees about ten times more sharply than the Hubble Space Telescope.

The soil near Yungay is so dry and empty of life that scientists treat the Atacama as Earth's best stand-in for Mars, and NASA tests its rovers there. In 2003 scientists ran the old Viking lander's life tests on that soil and found almost no microbes, the same result they would expect on Mars.

Outside San Pedro de Atacama, an oasis town, is the Valle de la Luna, or Valley of the Moon, a maze of salt ridges carved by the wind. As blazing day turns to freezing night, the salt crust expands and shrinks, and in the silence the ground is heard crackling and popping.

To the south spreads the Salar de Atacama, where pink flamingos wade in turquoise lagoons above a brine richer in lithium than any other on Earth, holding roughly one-quarter of the world's known reserves.

Once every few years an unusual downpour wakes seeds that have waited underground a long time, and a few weeks later the desert vanishes under millions of wildflowers. Chileans call it the desierto florido, the flowering desert.

On a hillside of Cerro Unita, desert people of around 1000 to 1400 CE outlined the Atacama Giant, some 86 metres tall, the largest ancient human figure drawn on the land anywhere. Its purpose is debated, but by one leading theory lines from its head tracked the moon, so that it worked as a calendar to follow the seasons and predict the rains.

On the coast, some 7,000 years ago, the Chinchorro people made mummies, dismantling each body, drying it, and putting it back together on a frame of sticks and reeds. The oldest, a child dated to about 5050 BC, is about 2,000 years older than any Egyptian mummy.

the-atacama-the-driest-place-on-earth.context_blurb:
In northern Chile, between the Pacific and the Andes, lies a desert where some weather stations have run for years, even more than a decade, without catching any rain worth measuring. Its soil resembles moon dust more than earth, and three forces at once keep it that way.

That desert is the Atacama, the driest place on Earth outside the frozen poles. Antarctica is technically drier, but it is a polar desert, in a class of its own.

Even so, life clings to the shore. Almost daily a heavy grey fog from the chilly ocean, the camanchaca, drifts inland and moistens the hills enough to keep fog oases, called lomas, green with lichens, algae and cactus.

Around Yungay the soil is so empty of life that NASA spent four field seasons testing a rover there, drilling the ground and feeding samples to life-detecting instruments, as practice for searching for life on Mars.

The dryness has three causes. The Andes block rain from the east, and dry air sinks over the desert from the great high-pressure zone of the South Pacific. The third works from the sea: the cold Humboldt Current flows north along the coast and chills the water so much that hardly any of it evaporates to make rain.

Some coastal villages have no river, almost no rain and only salty groundwater, so they harvest the fog itself. People string mesh nets across the hills to catch the camanchaca, and a net of about 40 square metres can gather some 200 litres of fresh water a day.

The clear, dry skies draw astronomers. On the 2,635-metre summit of Cerro Paranal, the European Southern Observatory runs the Very Large Telescope, four telescopes with 8.2-metre mirrors which can be joined into one giant instrument. Higher still, at 5,000 metres on the Chajnantor plateau, ALMA links 66 dish antennas into one instrument that gathers faint radio light from galaxies as they form.

Once every few years a lone downpour wakes seeds that have slept in the ground, and between September and November some 200 kinds of wildflower carpet the sand, a bloom Chileans call the desierto florido. Chile set aside a national park to guard the bloom.

The desert also preserves the dead: its rainless air and its salty, nitrate-rich soil have preserved bodies naturally for up to 9,000 years, with no wrappings at all. Near Arica the Chinchorro people made the oldest deliberate mummies on Earth, the Chinchorro mummies, beginning around 5050 BC, about 2,000 years before Egypt.

the-bagpipes-contested-home.context_blurb:
The bagpipe is famous as the sound of Scotland, but no one can say for sure where it was first invented. Every bagpipe works the same way: a squeezed bag of air feeds a fingered melody pipe, the chanter, and one or more pipes that drone a steady note beneath the tune, and cousins of the instrument are played across Europe and beyond.

It is far older than its Scottish fame. The Roman historian Suetonius wrote that the emperor Nero, who loved performing in public, vowed to appear playing a reed pipe fed from a bag squeezed under the arm.

Earlier still, Greek writers described a pipe set in a swollen bag of animal hide, and they called it the askaulos, from askos, wineskin, and aulos, reed pipe: a wineskin-pipe.

In the rainy northwest of Spain, in Galicia and Asturias, the local bagpipe, the gaita, is a badge of the region, cherished there the way Scots cherish their Highland pipes.

Ireland's pipes are the gentle opposite of Scotland's loud, mouth-blown battle pipes. The uilleann pipes, which took shape in the early 1700s, are played sitting down, and the bag is filled not by the mouth but by a small bellows pumped with the arm. Uilleann means elbow, the joint that works the bellows, and the dry air it supplies keeps the tone sweet.

the-bay-of-fundy-highest-tides-on-earth.context_blurb:
The Bay of Fundy is a long arm of the Atlantic between the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and its tides are the greatest on Earth. Twice a day the sea floods in and drains out so far that boats lie on bare mud and then float again, and people walk across sea floor that will be deep under water a few hours later.

The record belongs to Burntcoat Head in Nova Scotia, where the gap between low and high water reaches some 16 metres, as tall as a four-storey house, and in 1975 Guinness recognised the Bay of Fundy's tides as the greatest in the world.

On the New Brunswick shore the tide has carved the Hopewell Rocks, pillars of sandstone that stand 12 to 21 metres high. The water eats away their softer bases faster than their tops, so many are wider above than below, like flowerpots crowned with shrubs and small trees. At low tide visitors walk around them; hours later kayaks float past.

Each tide moves about 100 billion tonnes of seawater in and out, roughly twice the combined flow of all the rivers on Earth, so more water than every river on the planet put together.

The returning tide can overpower a river and send a single wave racing upstream against its current, a tidal bore. In July 2013 surfers rode a Petitcodiac River bore all the way to Moncton, some 29 kilometres, setting a record for North America.

At Cape Split, a finger of cliff in the upper bay, the tide tears past at about 8 knots, and the churning water sends a deep, hollow roar up into the clifftop forest. Locals call that sound the Voice of the Moon, a fitting name, since the moon's pull drives the tides.

At Saint John the river tumbles over hidden rock ledges into the bay, but twice a day the rising tide overwhelms it, and the rapids turn around and churn upstream, uphill. These are the Reversing Falls, and boats can pass only in the few minutes of slack water in between.

Why are the tides so huge? The water in the bay rocks from end to end and back in about 13 hours, and the Atlantic tide beats about every 12 and a half, so each new tide comes just in time to push the slosh higher, like a well-timed push on a swing. Scientists call this matching of rhythms resonance.

Fundy's all-time high water arrived on the night of 4 to 5 October 1869, when a hurricane's surge landed on an extreme tide; the sea broke through the Minas Basin dykes, flooded the marshland, and at Burntcoat Head the water peaked near 21.6 metres. The storm is remembered as the Saxby Gale, after Stephen Saxby, a Royal Navy instructor who had predicted extreme tides for that very day almost a year before and was mocked until the storm proved him right.

the-bering-land-bridge-beringia.context_blurb:
In the ice ages, vast ice sheets held so much water that the sea sank as much as 120 metres below today's level. Between Siberia and Alaska, where Asia and North America now almost touch, the sea floor rose out of the water as dry land, and for thousands of years the two continents were joined.

The Swedish botanist Eric Hultén named that lost land Beringia in 1937, after Vitus Bering, the Danish-born explorer who sailed into the strait in 1728.

It took surprisingly little to make it. The Bering Strait is 82 kilometres wide, but its floor lies on average only about 40 to 50 metres down, so a modest fall in sea level was enough to turn the whole strait into land.

Beringia was no frozen white waste. Fierce, dusty winds kept it nearly free of snow. It was a cold, dry grassland of grasses and herbs grazed by great Ice Age beasts, and scientists call that vanished world the mammoth steppe.

It was huge, too: at its greatest it covered some 1.6 million square kilometres, as large as British Columbia and Alberta put together, a whole grassy country between two continents. Rising seas drowned it around 11,000 years ago.

Only a few of its high points still poke above the sea: the Diomede Islands, Big Diomede belonging to Russia and Little Diomede to Alaska, just 3.8 kilometres apart. The International Date Line runs between them, so they are nicknamed Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Island.

Beringia was one of several lands the ice ages opened and then swallowed. The same fall in sea level bared the floor of today's North Sea, a plain of rivers and marshes joining Britain to Europe where Stone Age hunters lived and fished, and that drowned land is Doggerland. A tsunami from the Storegga Slide, a vast undersea landslide off Norway, swept across it around 6150 BC.

the-blues-the-mississippi-delta.context_blurb:
The Mississippi Delta is a hot, flat stretch of cotton country in the American South. About a century ago, among Black families who had been enslaved and then worked the fields as sharecroppers, a new music was born there: the blues. From the Delta it travelled north to Memphis and Chicago, and it fed rock and roll.

Its most famous sound is a guitar that seems to weep like a human voice. Delta players slid a smooth glass or metal tube, often the broken-off neck of a bottle, along the strings so the notes bent and cried, a technique called the bottleneck slide.

The blues grew out of older music of the fields, the work songs and field hollers that Black labourers sang across the cotton rows, one voice calling out a line and the others answering back. That call and response passed straight into the blues, where the guitar answers the singer.

Near Cleveland, Mississippi lies Dockery Farms, a vast cotton plantation; around 1900 Charley Patton and other early bluesmen lived and played on it, and it is often called the birthplace of the blues. B.B. King, standing there, said that everything started on that spot.

Patton, often named the father of Delta blues, was a wild showman whose rough voice reportedly carried 500 yards without a microphone, and long before rock stars tried it, he played his guitar behind his back to delight the crowd.

Nearly every Delta blues song rides on the same frame, the twelve-bar blues: twelve measures on just three chords, repeating so that anyone can join in.

Outside Clarksdale, two highways meet at a lonely crossroads. Legend says Robert Johnson, who disappeared for a while as a fumbling player and returned a master, went there at midnight and sold his soul to the devil. It is folklore, first told about another bluesman, Tommy Johnson. The truer story, researchers found, is long night practice with his mentor Ike Zimmerman, who took him to play among the graveyard tombstones, where they could play undisturbed.

Highway 61, the Blues Highway, runs from New Orleans up through the Delta to Memphis and beyond, and bluesmen rode it north out of the cotton fields. Bob Dylan named a 1965 album after it.

W.C. Handy, a bandleader, spent nine hours waiting for a late train in 1903 at the little station at Tutwiler, Mississippi. Beside him a ragged stranger made his guitar moan by sliding a knife blade along the strings, singing about the place where the Southern crosses the Dog. Handy called it the strangest music he had ever heard.

The Dog was a railroad, the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley line, nicknamed the Yellow Dog for its mustard-yellow cars, which crossed the Southern Railroad at Moorhead. Handy wove it into a song of 1914.

Many bluesmen, Elmore James among them, learned first on a diddley bow, a single wire nailed to a porch or wall and plucked while a glass bottle slid along it, a homemade instrument any poor child could build.

the-camino-de-santiago.context_blurb:
The Camino de Santiago, the Way of St James, is a pilgrim road across northern Spain to the city of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, where tradition holds that the apostle St James the Great is buried. Pilgrims have walked it since the Middle Ages, and huge numbers still do, some for faith and some for the journey itself.

The best-loved branch, the Camino Francés, runs about 800 kilometres from the French village of Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. On day one, walkers climb over the Pyrenees, the mountain wall between France and Spain, and drop down to Roncesvalles. There, in 778, Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed, the battle behind the Song of Roland.

The way is marked simply: pilgrims follow painted yellow arrows and wear its ancient emblem, a scallop shell. Its grooves fan out and meet at one point, like the roads of Europe meeting at Santiago.

Roughly a third of the distance in, the road swaps the green hills for the Meseta, the lofty, level, treeless plateau of Castile, some 220 kilometres between Burgos and León. One stretch runs about 17 kilometres without a village, shade or water.

The goal is the cathedral built over the tomb of St James. By legend, a hermit in the 800s was led night after night to a place in the forest by a light shining in the night sky, and there he found the forgotten tomb. The spot came to be read as Campus Stellae, field of stars, the likely root of the name Compostela.

Those yellow arrows are mostly one man's work. O Cebreiro's parish priest, Elías Valiña, set out in 1984 in his battered Citroën 2CV and marked the whole road from Roncesvalles to Santiago, painting arrows from a bucket of leftover yellow road paint.

O Cebreiro itself sits in the mist at 1,296 metres, on the last mountain before Galicia. Among its lanes stand pallozas, round stone houses thatched with rye straw and built without chimneys, a style people have lived in there since Celtic days. Some families shared them with their animals into the 20th century.

For many the walk does not end at the cathedral. They go on about 90 kilometres more, to Cape Finisterre on the Atlantic, which the Romans called Finis Terrae, the end of the earth. It is not truly the westernmost point of the peninsula, but there pilgrims watch the sun sink into the ocean.

the-caspian-sea.context_blurb:
The Caspian Sea lies between Europe and Asia, ringed by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan. It covers about 371,000 square kilometres, an area bigger than Germany, and no channel joins it to any ocean. Its shores hold oil, ground that burns, and a gulf saltier than almost any water on Earth.

For all its name, the Caspian is the world's largest lake, the biggest by both area and volume, holding roughly 40 per cent of all the lake water on the planet. It is called a sea for its size and its salt.

Great rivers pour into it, yet not one flows out. The Caspian is a closed basin: its water escapes only by evaporating into the air under the sun, so its size is a balance between the rivers filling it and the sunshine drying it.

One river matters most: the Volga, Europe's longest river, supplies about 80 per cent of the inflow, so the Volga's flow mostly sets whether the sea climbs or drops. The level has swung by whole metres within a lifetime.

Outside Baku a wall of fire some 15 metres wide leaps from a bare slope of the Absheron Peninsula, fed by gas leaking up through the rock, and no rain or snow can put out Yanar Dag, the Burning Mountain. Fires like it gave Azerbaijan the name Land of Fire.

The Caspian tastes faintly salty, with roughly one-third of seawater's saltiness, because it is a leftover of a real sea, the Paratethys, which once spread across ancient Eurasia and was cut off from the world ocean about 5.5 million years ago as the land rose.

On the eastern shore, in Turkmenistan, the shallow gulf of Kara-Bogaz-Gol evaporates so fast in the desert heat that the loss outruns any inflow, so Caspian water rushes in by a narrow strait to replace it, and dries away in turn. It leaves blinding salt flats and a lagoon about as briny as the Dead Sea.

The Ateshgah, a five-sided fire temple near Baku, was built over gas vents, and its altar fire lit itself for centuries, drawing Zoroastrian, Hindu and Sikh pilgrims. Years of gas extraction nearby starved the vents, and in 1969 the flame went out. Today gas piped in from outside keeps the altar lit for visitors.

the-colosseum-romes-flavian-amphitheatre.context_blurb:
The Colosseum rises in the middle of Rome, the largest amphitheatre the Roman world ever built. It opened around AD 80 and held some 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights and wild-beast hunts. Even half-ruined and stripped of its marble, it is the biggest Roman building still standing and the symbol of the city.

Its builders never used the name everyone knows. Vespasian started it, his son Titus dedicated it in AD 80, and the arena took the name of their family, the Flavian dynasty: the Flavian Amphitheatre.

The popular name came later: beside the arena stood a bronze giant some 30 metres tall, the Colossus of the emperor Nero, and around the year 1000 people began calling the arena after the statue. Colosseum means the place by the Colossus.

That fits, because the ground had been Nero's. The arena stands at the heart of his private estate around the Golden House, where he had flooded a private artificial lake, and Vespasian drained it and built a public arena on its bed. An emperor's playground became a gift to the people.

A crowd of 50,000 could leave in minutes, because wide passages called vomitoria, from the Latin for spewing out, poured spectators through the stands toward the 80 numbered entrance arches round the outside. It is the same trick a modern stadium uses.

On hot afternoons a vast canvas awning, the velarium, shaded the seats, and only sailors, brought from the navy's base at Misenum near Naples, had the skill with rope, mast and canvas to rig it.

Under the arena floor of sand-covered boards, the emperor Domitian dug the hypogeum, a two-storey maze of tunnels equipped with trap doors, pulleys and lifts. When a trap door sprang open, snarling wild animals seemed to burst out of nowhere into the arena. There were no engines: every cage rose some 7 metres to the floor, wound up by a capstan worked by as many as eight men. With some two dozen lifts, running them all at once took about two hundred men, hidden below the sand.

In 2014 engineers rebuilt one of those lifts with Roman materials and hand tools, and for the first time in over 1,500 years a live animal, a wolf, rode up into the arena. It was rewarded with a biscuit.

Roman writers claimed the first games included a mock sea-battle on a flooded arena. Historians doubt it, because once Domitian had dug out the two levels of tunnels beneath the floor, there was no watertight basin left to fill.

The pale travertine walls are pocked all over with small holes. The Romans set the blocks largely without mortar, binding them with some 300 tons of iron. In the Middle Ages scavengers chiselled those iron clamps out of the stone to melt them down, leaving the pockmarks.

the-congo.context_blurb:
The Congo River drains the great rainforest of central Africa, the second-largest tropical forest on Earth, from a basin of about 4 million square kilometres. It loops across the heart of the continent, crossing the equator and then crossing back, before it bursts into the Atlantic, and almost every fact about it is extreme.

Near its mouth the riverbed plunges about 220 metres deep, making the Congo the world's deepest river. In that blackness some fish have evolved with no eyes at all, and scientists first grasped the depth when fish hauled up from the bottom showed the bends, the injury divers get from rising too fast.

Most rivers swell in the wet season and shrink in the dry, but the Congo pours out almost the same flood all year. It is the only major river that crosses the equator twice, so part of its basin always lies in a rainy season while the rest is dry, and rain is always falling somewhere to feed it.

Its old Kikongo name, nzadi, is popularly translated as the river that swallows every other river, though some linguists think the word simply meant river. The nation south of the river took the name Zaire from it, from 1971 to 1997.

On opposite banks of the lower river stand Brazzaville, seat of government of the Republic of Congo, and Kinshasa, which rules the much larger Democratic Republic of Congo, and leaving aside Vatican City inside Rome, they are the closest pair of capitals of any two countries on Earth.

Below them the river is pinched into a gorge and thunders over Livingstone Falls, a staircase of about 32 cataracts named for the explorer David Livingstone, which drops some 270 metres and carries more water than any other waterfall on the planet.

Every second some 41,000 cubic metres of Congo water reach the sea, and only the Amazon delivers more.

Its work does not end at the coast. Far out under the ocean, surges of sediment roaring down the seabed like avalanches, the strongest underwater currents ever recorded, keep carving the Congo Canyon, a gorge with walls up to 1,100 metres high cut some 500 kilometres across the sea floor.

the-coriolis-effect-why-the-storms-spin.context_blurb:
Earth spins, and anything that moves freely across it for long enough seems to curve. Seen from the ground, winds, ocean currents and even bullets are nudged sideways by the turning planet. This apparent curve is the Coriolis effect, and it decides which way the great storms of the world spin.

Seen by satellite, Caribbean hurricanes whirl counterclockwise and cyclones off Australia clockwise, and the cause is Earth's rotation: the planet turns beneath the moving air, so storms curve opposite ways north and south of the equator.

North of the equator, the effect bends every freely moving thing to its right, so a marksman's bullet fired a thousand yards in Sacramento lands a few inches off target. South of the equator, everything bends to the left of its path instead.

On the equator itself the Coriolis effect drops to zero, and a storm needs that sideways push to wind itself up. That is why typhoons almost never form right on the line, and why Pontianak, an Indonesian city sitting on it, has almost never been hit by one.

At the equator line outside Quito, guides show tourists a basin draining one way on one side and the other way on the other. Careful tests show it is a myth: at the size of a sink the Coriolis effect is far too weak, and the shape of the drain and leftover swirl in the water decide the direction.

Over great distances the effect is real. In World War I Germany's Paris Gun fired shells about 75 miles, and each stayed in the air for nearly three minutes. Its gunners had to allow for Earth's rotation, which pushed each shell sideways and also stretched its range by several hundred metres.

the-darkest-skies-on-earth-where-the-mil.context_blurb:
In most of the world, city light now hides the night sky, and few people alive have seen a truly dark one. A handful of remote places still have them: high, dry, clear and far from any town, such as Chile's northern desert, Namibia's wild reserves and the high country of New Zealand. There the stars blaze, and the Milky Way can throw a shadow.

The greatest of these lies in northern Chile: the Atacama Desert, which no desert outside the polar regions can match for dryness. Its observatories enjoy more than 200 cloudless nights a year.

Its dryness has several causes, and the first is the Andes, which rise along Chile's eastern side and cast a rain shadow, wringing wet air dry before it can cross. Along the coast, the cold Humboldt Current sweeps up from the south and chills the air above the sea so that it cannot rise into rain clouds.

Even so, the coast is not without water: a dense, chilly sea mist called the camanchaca drifts in from the Pacific, and plants and villagers comb drinking water straight out of it.

High on the Chajnantor Plateau, above 5,000 metres, 66 dish antennas called ALMA listen together for the faint radio whisper of chilly gas and dust clouds in which stars and planets form.

On Cerro Paranal stand the four telescopes of the Very Large Telescope, and their names come from the Mapuche language: Antu means Sun and Kueyen Moon, while Yepun is the evening star and Melipal the Southern Cross.

On nearby Cerro Armazones, engineers are building the Extremely Large Telescope, whose single mirror, about 39 metres across, is made of 798 six-sided segments. No telescope on the ground will be larger.

Astronomers grade darkness on the nine-step Bortle scale. Under the blackest class, the glowing centre of the Milky Way, in Sagittarius and Scorpius, is bright enough to throw a shadow on the ground. On the very darkest nights a second shadow can appear, cast by Venus, which at its brightest shines at magnitude -4.9, outshone only by the Sun and Moon.

In Namibia's NamibRand Nature Reserve, the nearest neighbours are about 100 kilometres off and no artificial light breaks the horizon. In 2012 it became the first International Dark Sky Reserve in Africa, with the strictest Gold Tier rating.

Before sunrise at Aoraki Mackenzie, a dark-sky reserve in New Zealand, a dim wedge of light rises from the eastern horizon, tilted along the path the Sun will take: sunlight scattered by dust lying between the planets. Old skywatchers called it the false dawn, but its proper name is the zodiacal light.

the-dead-sea.context_blurb:
Between Israel and Jordan, in the sun-baked trough of the Jordan Rift, lies the Dead Sea, a long lake of heavy, glassy water ringed by white salt crusts and bare desert cliffs. It is a place of extremes, and it is shrinking.

Its shore is the lowest dry ground on the planet, about 430 metres below sea level. The surface keeps dropping; in 2025 it was measured at a record 439.78 metres below.

Try to duck under and the water will not let you. It is so heavy with dissolved salt, about 1.24 kilograms a litre, that it pushes a swimmer straight back up to the top. Bathers famously lie back and read a newspaper.

The water is about 34 per cent salt, almost ten times saltier than the ocean, so fish and water plants cannot live in it. Only after unusually rainy winters can salt-loving microbes and a red alga briefly bloom.

The salt has a simple cause. The Jordan River flows in, but no river flows out; geographers call such a closed lake endorheic. Its water can leave only by slowly evaporating into the dry desert air, and the salt the river brings stays behind and grows ever more concentrated.

Today the lake is vanishing. The two countries draw off the Jordan's water upstream, the shoreline falls about a metre a year, and more than 6,000 sinkholes pit the old seabed. As the sea retreats, fresh groundwater seeps in and dissolves layers of salt buried underground, and the hollowed ground caves in. In 2015 one swallowed enough of the beach at Ein Gedi to close it.

Mount Sodom, a 210-metre ridge by the southwestern shore, is essentially solid salt, rock salt from top to bottom, and it sits on a salt layer that reaches some 2.3 kilometres down.

Among its salt pillars, one salt column has long been called Lot's wife. In the biblical story, as Lot's family escaped from Sodom before its destruction, she turned to look back at the burning city and became a pillar of salt. It is a place legend, not established fact.

the-didgeridoo-arnhem-land-australia.context_blurb:
Arnhem Land is a wild region of rivers, rock country and eucalyptus forest in the tropical north of Australia, home to the Yolngu and other Aboriginal peoples. From here comes the didgeridoo, a long wooden pipe that pours out one deep, unbroken hum, with no tune at all, and it is among the most ancient wind instruments that people still play.

Makers do not drill or carve the bore: they hunt the bush for living eucalyptus branches that termites have eaten hollow. The insects strip out the dead heartwood but leave the living outer wood, so the tree survives and the maker gets a ready-made tube.

Because a rough mouthpiece hurts the lips, the maker finishes the blowing end with a moulded ring of beeswax that seals softly against the mouth.

Players can hold one drone for more than 40 minutes by circular breathing. While snatching a breath in through the nose, the player squeezes the air stored in the puffed-out cheeks into the pipe, so the note never breaks.

The Yolngu call the instrument the yidaki, and across northern Australia it has at least 45 local names. Didgeridoo is an outsiders' word, an English coinage that imitates its droning sound, first printed around 1908.

It is often said to be 40,000 years old, but there is no evidence for that. The firm proof is a rock painting at Ginga Wardelirrhmeng on the Arnhem Land plateau, in which a player performs with song men at a ceremony, and it is about 1,500 years old.

the-door-to-hell-darvaza-gas-crater.context_blurb:
In the middle of Turkmenistan's Karakum Desert lies a crater about 70 metres across that is full of fire. Its light carries for miles over the dark dunes, travellers camp beside it in yurts, and locals call it the Door to Hell. It is not a volcano: people made it, by accident.

By the standard account, in 1971 a Soviet rig drilling for gas broke into a cavern underground, the ground caved in, and poisonous methane began pouring out. Rather than let it spread, the engineers lit the escaping gas to burn it off safely, expecting the fire to die within days. The exact date and even the deliberate lighting are disputed, because the Soviet records are lost or secret.

It never went out: the crater has burned without stopping for more than 50 years.

Turkmenistan's leaders now want it put out, because the fire is burning away valuable natural gas that the country could sell, and leaking methane besides. Engineers have drilled wells nearby to capture the gas, and the flames have shrunk.

the-east-african-rift-a-continent-tearin.context_blurb:
Across eastern Africa runs a crack in the Earth some 6,000 kilometres long, the East African Rift,, running from the Afar region of Ethiopia south to Mozambique. Along it a whole continent is slowly being torn in two on dry land, and the tearing has raised volcanoes, filled some of the deepest lakes on Earth and made landscapes found nowhere else.

Geologists have already named the two halves. The larger western piece is the Nubian plate, and the smaller eastern piece, being pulled away from it, is the Somali plate.

The rift splits into two great branches, the Eastern and the Western, with over fifty volcanoes strung along them. Towering by itself above the Tanzanian grasslands is Mount Kilimanjaro, capped with ice, Africa's highest peak.

In the Western Rift, about 12 kilometres north of the city of Goma in Congo, rises Nyiragongo, and its summit crater holds a lava lake, once some 600 metres deep and one of the largest on Earth. In January 1977 the lake suddenly emptied through cracks in the volcano's lower slopes. Its lava is so runny that it races downhill, and that flow, clocked at about 60 kilometres an hour, is the fastest lava flow ever recorded. It killed at least 50 people.

In northern Tanzania, near Lake Natron, Ol Doinyo Lengai erupts a lava found at no other volcano, carbonatite, at only about 540 to 590 degrees. Lava that cool cannot glow orange, so its fresh flows come out jet black. Rain and volcanic gases soon go to work on it, and within hours or days they turn the black rock into pale minerals such as trona and calcite, until the whole cone is snow-white.

In Ethiopia's scorching Danakil Depression, the shield volcano Erta Ale, the smoking mountain, holds a lava lake that has churned without cooling since at least 1906, and people have nicknamed its southern pit the gateway to hell. No lava lake anywhere has lasted longer.

Where the floor of the Western Rift cracked and sank, it opened a basin now filled by Lake Tanganyika, about 1,470 metres deep, and only Lake Baikal in Siberia is deeper.

Below Nyiragongo, where Congo meets Rwanda, lies Lake Kivu, whose deep water holds about 65 cubic kilometres of methane and 256 of carbon dioxide under pressure, so geologists count it as one of only three known exploding lakes. Some 2 million people live on its shores.

the-everlasting-storm-catatumbo-lightnin.context_blurb:
In northwestern Venezuela, where the Catatumbo River runs into the southwest corner of Lake Maracaibo, a thunderstorm builds over the same stretch of water almost every night. It flashes for hours at a time on well over a hundred nights a year, and people call it the everlasting storm.

Seen from the shore at full strength, it looks like an almost unbroken strobe of light: 16 to 40 flashes a minute for about nine hours a night, mostly from 7 in the evening to 5 in the morning.

For three centuries sailors steered by it. Because the glow hung over the same place nearly every night, they called it the Beacon of Maracaibo and used it as a natural lighthouse to find the port in the dark.

Long before that, the Barí people who lived by the lake had their own explanation: the flashes were clouds of fireflies gathered to honour the ancestors. Their neighbours the Wayuu saw the lightning as the spirits of the dead.

The storm keeps coming back because of the land around it. Mountains, the Andes among them, wall the lake on three sides. Warm, wet air rising off the lake collides with cool air spilling down from the Andes, and the mountains funnel the winds together so the storm rebuilds over the same warm water.

In 2014 Guinness World Records gave the lake the title of the planet's lightning capital, with about 250 flashes per square kilometre each year, taking it from Kifuka, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Tour guides once claimed that methane seeping from the oily marshes fed the storms. Scientists doubt it: if gas were the fuel, the lightning should be strongest in the dry season, yet the storms peak in the rainy months, when gas should matter least.

In early 2010 the storm went dark for about six weeks, and frightened locals feared it was gone for good. A severe drought, brought by El Niño, had dried out the whole region, and when the rains returned, so did the lightning. The storm now shines on the flag of Zulia state, around the lake.

the-four-great-inventions-of-ancient-chi.context_blurb:
China's Four Great Inventions are papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass, technologies that began in China and transformed the world as they spread west, centuries before Europe had them. In 1620 the English philosopher Francis Bacon praised printing, gunpowder and the compass for remaking the world, without realising that all three had come from China.

The oldest printed book that carries a date shows how early Chinese printing began, and where it was kept is a wonder of its own. The Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture printed in 868 AD, spent close to a millennium sealed in a bricked-up room at the Mogao Caves, a cliff near Dunhuang, an oasis on the Silk Road, honeycombed with hundreds of Buddhist shrines. The caves are also called the Caves of the Thousand Buddhas. In 1900 their caretaker, Wang Yuanlu, opened the hidden room, and in 1907 the archaeologist Aurel Stein bought the scroll, which now rests in the British Library.

the-gamelan-java-and-bali.context_blurb:
On the Indonesian islands of Java and Bali, the gamelan is the heart of court, temple and village music: an orchestra of gongs, tuned metal keys and drums whose shimmering, layered sound carries far through the evening air. Every village once owned its own set, and Western composers from Debussy onward fell under its spell.

Almost the entire orchestra, the gongs and the metal-keyed instruments called metallophones, is cast from bronze, and a big Javanese set can hold 70 to 80 instruments.

No two gamelans share a tuning; each set agrees only with itself. Yet all of them rest on two ancient scales: sléndro, with five notes to the octave, and pélog, with seven. A full Javanese set really holds two orchestras, one for each scale.

One great gong rules them all, the gong ageng, historically up to 135 centimetres across, and its deep boom closes each long musical cycle. The gamelan's spirit is said to live inside it, and players leave flowers, food and incense before it.

On Bali two players sit face to face, and each plays only half of a dazzling melodic line, filling the gaps the other leaves. Interlocked, their notes run at four to eight times the speed of the main melody, so it sounds like one impossibly fast player, a technique called kotekan.

In Java the gamelan also accompanies wayang kulit, the shadow-puppet play, in which one puppeteer, the dalang, moves every flat leather puppet behind a white screen, speaks every voice and cues the orchestra all night until dawn. The tales come from epics like the Ramayana.

Bali has a performance with no instruments at all. In the kecak, between fifty and a hundred men, stripped to the waist, sit in rings and chant a fast, interlocking cak-cak-cak, voicing the monkey army of the Ramayana. It is not ancient: the German painter Walter Spies and the Balinese dancer Wayan Limbak shaped it in the 1930s from an older trance ritual.

the-ganges.context_blurb:
The Ganges is the great river of northern India. It is born from a glacier high in the Himalaya and flows some 2,500 kilometres across the crowded plains to the Bay of Bengal, giving water and food to hundreds of millions of people. To Hindus it is also holy, and its banks are lined with temples and pilgrims.

Its source lies more than 4,000 metres up in Uttarakhand, where meltwater gushes out of an ice cave at the snout of the Gangotri Glacier. The cave mouth is called Gaumukh, the cow's mouth, because it is said to look like a cow's muzzle. Pilgrims trek for days to reach it.

Hindus revere the river as a living goddess, Ganga, and believe that bathing in her can wash away sin.

Hindu legend tells how she came down. King Bhagiratha won the right to bring the heavenly river to earth so that her waters could cleanse the ashes of his forefathers, but her crash to earth would have smashed the world apart. Shiva stepped beneath the torrent and caught her in his matted hair, letting her out gently in many small streams.

The holiest city on the river is Varanasi, a city lived in for thousands of years. About 88 wide flights of stone steps, the ghats, lead down into the river, packed with bathers before sunrise, and the grandest, Dashashwamedh, hosts a nightly fire ceremony. Varanasi is also called the Great Cremation Ground: the dead are burned beside the river and their ashes given to it. Dying and being cremated there is believed to grant moksha, the soul's release from the endless cycle of rebirth.

Near the Bay of Bengal the Ganges meets the Brahmaputra, and together, joined by the Meghna, they build the biggest delta in the world, across Bangladesh and eastern India.

Pilgrims long said Ganges water could sit in a jar for months without spoiling. Testing it in 1896, Ernest Hankin, a British scientist, saw untreated river water destroy cholera germs in about three hours. Later researchers credited bacteriophages, natural viruses that kill only bacteria, though the idea is still debated. Today parts of the river are badly polluted.

the-ganges-from-gaumukh-to-the-ghats-of-.context_blurb:
The Ganga, as Indians call the Ganges, is India's holiest river. It begins as meltwater high in the Himalaya and runs some 2,500 kilometres across the northern plains to the Bay of Bengal, passing sacred meetings of rivers and the stepped stone banks of Varanasi, where pilgrims come to bathe, pray and say goodbye to their dead.

Every drop starts in one river of ice, the Gangotri Glacier, about 4,000 metres up in the Himalaya of Uttarakhand.

The water drips from the glacier's snout at a place called Gaumukh: gau means cow and mukh means mouth, so the name means the cow's mouth, because by local tradition the jagged ice looked like a cow's head.

In its first wild descent from the ice, the stream goes by another name, the Bhagirathi, after King Bhagiratha, whose penance in legend brought the river down from heaven.

At the hill-town of Devprayag the Bhagirathi meets the green Alaknanda head-on, and only below that confluence is the united river called the Ganga.

Down on the plains at Prayagraj, the Yamuna joins in plain sight, and by Hindu belief an unseen third river, the Sarasvati, flows in beneath the sand. The meeting place, the Triveni Sangam, or confluence of three, is the river's holiest bathing spot. Every few years, by the lunar calendar, its banks host the Kumbh Mela, and the 2025 festival drew some 400 million bathers, the largest gathering of people in history.

At Varanasi the river bends in a long crescent, and 84 stone ghats, stepped embankments, line the west bank for about 7 kilometres, all facing the sunrise. Across the water, the far shore is only an empty sandbank, a bare stretch of sand with nothing built on it.

The ceremonial heart is Dashashwamedh Ghat, whose name means ten-horse sacrifice, where every evening young priests swing tiered brass lamps of fire out over the dark water in the Ganga Aarti. They chant to drums as crowds watch from the steps and from boats.

Two ghats are cremation grounds where pyres burn day and night. The older and holier is Manikarnika Ghat, the jewelled earring, already named in a 5th-century inscription of the Gupta age.

The ghats look endlessly old, but most of today's stone steps and riverside palaces were built in the 1700s by the Marathas, an alliance of Deccan chiefs and queens, among them Ahilyabai Holkar.

Near the sea the Ganga meets the Brahmaputra, which rises in Tibet and wraps around the eastern Himalaya, and together they build the world's biggest delta. Their channels braid through the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest on the planet and home of the Bengal tiger, before the glacier's water finally reaches the Bay of Bengal.

the-global-conveyor-belt-thermohaline-ci.context_blurb:
Beneath the restless surface currents of the oceans runs a far slower, deeper flow that links every sea on Earth into one loop: the global conveyor belt. It carries heat around the planet, it has no pump, and a drop of water may spend a thousand years riding it.

The belt runs in two stacked lanes. Warm Atlantic water flows north at the top, in the sunlight, and once it has chilled it makes the long trip back south by crawling along the deep sea floor. The oceanographer Wallace Broecker made the picture famous.

Scientists call it thermohaline circulation: thermo means temperature and haline means salt, the water's saltiness, and together they decide how heavy seawater is.

The motor lies between Greenland and Iceland. There, each winter, the sea's top layer becomes icy cold and extra salty, grows so dense that it sinks straight down into the deep sea, and that sinking drags the whole planet-sized loop along behind it.

No current in the sea is slower than the deep branch, which inches along at a few centimetres a second, slower than you walk. But it is as wide as the world, so the belt moves over a hundred times as much water as the Amazon.

In the Denmark Strait, dense cold water pours over a cliff on the sea floor in a hidden waterfall about 3,500 metres high, about three times taller than Angel Falls, the highest falls on dry land.

Around Antarctica the densest water of all is made each winter as the sea freezes. New sea ice is almost fresh, and it sheds its salt, which is packed into the water just beneath the ice, making that water extra salty and heavy, so it sinks. This Antarctic Bottom Water, much of it formed in the Weddell Sea, slides down the slopes and spreads across the floor of every ocean, carpeting the deepest abyss of the world.

Water that sinks off Greenland now may spend about 1,000 years in darkness, passing from one ocean to another before it surfaces again, probably in the North Pacific.

The engine has stalled before. About 12,900 years ago Lake Agassiz, a vast meltwater lake in North America, broke through the ice holding it back and poured fresh water into the North Atlantic. Scientists think the sinking faltered, and the Northern Hemisphere slid back into near-ice-age cold for about a thousand years, a spell called the Younger Dryas, though the exact trigger is debated.

Today melting Greenland ice is freshening the North Atlantic, and scientists watch for a slowdown. The film The Day After Tomorrow showed one freezing the world in days, but the real science says any genuine slowdown would unfold over several decades. A full collapse this century is judged unlikely.
