the-gobi.context_blurb:
The Gobi sprawls across some 1.3 million square kilometres of southern Mongolia and northern China, a high, dry, windswept land of extremes. It is famous for its bones as much as its emptiness: some of the world's most celebrated dinosaur fossils have come out of its red rocks.

It is a cold desert, defined by dryness, not heat. Summer can bake past 45 degrees, but in winter the bare ground loses its warmth to the night sky, and the cold can plunge to about minus 40 degrees.

It is not a sea of sand either. Only about 5 per cent of the Gobi is dunes; most of it is bare rock and gravel, wind-scoured stony plains.

The reason for its dryness lies to the south. The Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas form a barrier some 5,000 metres high, and the summer monsoon drops its rain on their far side, soaking India. The Gobi lies in their rain shadow, where only dry, spent air arrives.

Roy Chapman Andrews, an American fossil hunter, brought a convoy of cars and camels in 1923 to a cliff of glowing red sandstone that he named the Flaming Cliffs, and there his team found the first dinosaur eggs ever recognised. They proved that dinosaurs hatched from eggs.

The Khongoryn Els, one of the Gobi's rare fields of sand, are dunes up to 300 metres high and 100 kilometres long. When a slope of sand avalanches, the whole dune booms a deep, droning hum, like a distant aircraft engine, and locals call them the Singing Dunes.

In 1971 diggers in the Gobi's Djadochta rocks uncovered the Fighting Dinosaurs: a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops, buried together some 75 million years back when a dune collapsed on them, still locked in combat. The raptor's sickle claw is hooked into the throat of the Protoceratops, while the Protoceratops has bitten down on the raptor's arm.

The desert is spreading. Along its southern edge grassland vanishes at about 3,600 square kilometres a year, and its dust storms reach Beijing. In 1978 China launched the Great Green Wall, officially the Three-North Shelter Forest Program, to plant a vast belt of trees across its dry north and hold back the sand.

the-grand-canyon.context_blurb:
The Grand Canyon is a vast gorge in northern Arizona, in the American Southwest, 277 miles long, up to 18 miles wide and more than a mile deep. Its walls step down in bands of red, cream and grey rock, and at the bottom, almost too far to see, runs the river that made it.

A single river did the carving: the Colorado River, which over millions of years cut the whole gorge, grain by grain, a mile straight down. No earthquake split it open; it took only water and time.

The walls hold dozens of coloured rock layers, never folded or scrambled, the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top. So geologists read them like pages in a book, each band a chapter from a vanished world of seas, beaches and deserts.

High in the walls lies a pale cream stripe, the Coconino Sandstone, made from the sand of desert dunes some 280 million years old. That damp sand caught the trackways left by reptiles and amphibians, more than 20 kinds of footprint trail, long before the first dinosaurs.

The Kaibab Limestone that forms the canyon's rim is crammed with fossil clams, corals, sea lilies and shark teeth, because about 270 million years ago that rim rock was itself the floor of a shallow sea, later lifted a mile into the sky.

The rocks are ancient, but the gorge is young. By the leading view, the Colorado carved the canyon to roughly its present shape only some 5 to 6 million years ago, though some geologists argue for a much older start.

At the very bottom the layers end in the Vishnu Schist, dark, hard, twisted and glittering, about 1.74 billion years old. It was forged 10 to 15 miles deep inside the Earth's crust, squeezed and baked until it folded like taffy, and only later lifted and laid bare.

Isolated buttes of rock more than 1,000 feet high stand on the canyon floor. Clarence Dutton, exploring in the 1800s, gave them the names of gods and goddesses, so maps label each one a Temple: Vishnu Temple, Shiva Temple, Isis Temple and Zoroaster Temple.

In one spot you can lay your hand across two layers that touch: 525-million-year-old Tapeats Sandstone sitting right on the 1.74-billion-year-old schist. More than a billion years of rock is missing at that seam, never laid down or worn away, and geologists call it the Great Unconformity.

In a side canyon at Supai, Havasu Creek glows turquoise as it spills over terraces into pool after pool. Both the colour and the terraces come from lime minerals dissolved in its spring water, which scatter light blue-green and slowly build the stone ledges.

The Havasupai village of Supai has no road at all, and it is the only place in the United States where the mail still arrives by mule train, led down a trail some eight miles long.

The canyon is still deepening, and not only because the river keeps cutting: the whole Colorado Plateau has been rising for millions of years, lifting into the river's blade as it saws downward.

John Wesley Powell, a Civil War veteran who had lost an arm, took ten men and four wooden boats down the uncharted river in 1869, the first expedition through the canyon. Mapmakers had called the gorge the Big Canyon, and in 1871 Powell renamed it the Grand Canyon.

the-great-aletsch-glacier-swiss-alps.context_blurb:
The Great Aletsch Glacier in the Bernese Alps of southern Switzerland is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps, a river of ice about 23 kilometres long that pours from the high snowfields near the Jungfrau down toward the Rhone valley. Dark stripes of rubble run down its back where its feeder glaciers merged.

Visitors can watch it from above: a train climbs to the Jungfraujoch, a station cut into the rock at about 3,450 metres, the highest railway station in Europe.

At Konkordiaplatz four streams of ice flow together into one, and the ice there is about 900 metres thick, nearly reaching the rock of the hidden valley beneath.

A glacier leaves its signature on the land. A river saws a narrow, V-shaped notch, but the enormous weight of moving ice grinds a valley into a broad U shape with steep sides, so a broad U-shaped valley is one of the surest signs that ice once filled it. Yosemite and Lauterbrunnen are famous examples.

The glacier has retreated about 3.2 kilometres since 1870, baring rock that had been under ice for centuries. Near its snout the freshly uncovered ground is first claimed by hardy pioneer plants, the opening stage of new life there.

Alpine glaciers are Europe's water towers, storing winter snow as ice and releasing it as meltwater through the dry summer. The Aletsch's meltwater feeds a small river, the Massa, which flows on into the Rhone, one of Europe's great rivers.

the-great-barrier-reef.context_blurb:
The Great Barrier Reef runs for more than 2,300 kilometres along the coast of Queensland, in northeastern Australia, through the Coral Sea. It is a world of coral gardens, fish and islands, and all of it is alive: every bit was built by tiny animals.

It is the largest structure on Earth made by living creatures, so vast that it can be picked out from low orbit and has been photographed from space. The old claim that it shows from the Moon is a myth.

Its coral covers some 344,400 square kilometres of sea, about the size of the whole of Italy.

A coral may resemble a colourful stone or a little shrub, yet each one is a colony of thousands of tiny animals, each called a polyp, smaller than a fingernail. A polyp draws dissolved limestone from seawater and builds itself a stony skeleton, and over thousands of years those skeletons, stacked together, built the reef.

Seen from a deck, it seems a single wall of coral, but from the air the truth appears: it is a system of about 2,900 separate reefs and 900 islands scattered across the sea.

A pilot spotted one of them from the air over Hardy Reef, in the Whitsundays, in 1975: a coral patch only about 17 metres across that is naturally shaped like a perfect heart. Heart Reef is now one of the most photographed sights on the reef.

The living reef is a newcomer, between six and nine thousand years old, growing on the drowned remains of reefs far more ancient. As the last Ice Age ended, melting ice raised the sea by about 120 metres, and the rising water flooded the shallows above the old reefs, giving coral fresh sunlit ground to grow on.

Once a year, shortly after the full moon of November, almost the whole reef spawns at once: billions of polyps release their eggs and sperm together in a mass spawning. Divers caught in it describe an upside-down snowstorm, as countless tiny coloured bundles drift upward through the water.

The spawning always happens at night, because most of the fish that eat plankton are asleep then, so far more of the drifting eggs survive.

If the water remains too hot for several weeks, about a degree above the summer average for a month, corals bleach. They get their colour from algae living in their tissues, and under heat stress they expel them. Because coral tissue is see-through, its own bare limestone skeleton then shows through, ghostly white. A bleached coral is alive but starving, and it can die if the heat lasts.

the-great-blue-hole-belize.context_blurb:
Out in the Caribbean off Belize, in the middle of a pale turquoise coral lagoon, lies a nearly perfect circle of deep, dark blue: the Great Blue Hole, about 318 metres across and 124 metres deep. From the air it looks like a door into the sea floor, and the French explorer Jacques Cousteau made it famous in 1971.

It is a marine sinkhole, a drowned pit in limestone, not a crater.

You cannot see it from the beaches of Belize: it lies about 70 kilometres out to sea, near the middle of Lighthouse Reef, a small ring of coral, an atoll, around a lagoon.

In the last Ice Age, so much water was locked in glaciers that the sea stood some 120 metres lower, and this spot was dry land with a limestone cave inside it. When the ice melted and the ocean rose, the cave's roof collapsed and the sea poured in.

Divers in the hole found huge stalactites hanging from its overhangs, and all of them tilt by roughly 5 degrees in one direction. A stalactite always grows straight down as water drips from its tip, so geologists conclude that the whole limestone slab tilted after the stalactites had grown in the dry cave.

Below about 90 metres there is no oxygen, no light and no life, and the still, black water is poisoned with hydrogen sulfide, the gas that makes rotten eggs stink.

The floor is carpeted with conch shells: anything that falls or crawls in sinks through the poisoned layer, suffocates and cannot climb out, and with no currents to sweep them away, the shells stay where they fell. Divers call it the conch graveyard.

The Blue Hole is part of the Belize Barrier Reef, which Charles Darwin, in 1842, called the finest reef of the West Indies. It is the largest reef in the Western Hemisphere, and only one reef on Earth is bigger: Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

the-great-caves-waters-underground-cathe.context_blurb:
Some of the grandest spaces on Earth are hidden underground. Over millions of years, rainwater made faintly acidic seeps into limestone and dissolves it, hollowing out passages, halls and shafts, from the endless tunnels of Kentucky to a Vietnamese chamber with its own jungle and clouds.

Mammoth Cave runs beneath the rolling hills of central Kentucky, a maze of passages in limestone mapped for more than 685 kilometres, and it is the world's longest cave, over one and a half times the length of the runner-up.

Mammoth formed where acidic water dissolved a thick bed of limestone some 330 million years old. Its big passages survive because a hard layer of sandstone caps the limestone like a roof and keeps them from collapsing.

Son Doong, in Vietnam's jungle, contains the biggest cave passage known, over 5 kilometres long, 200 metres high and 150 metres wide. Explorers say a Boeing 747 could fly through it without its wings touching the walls. A farmer, Ho Khanh, found it in 1990, and British cavers first surveyed it in 2009.

In two places its roof fell in long ago, opening huge skylights called dolines. Where the daylight floods in, a real jungle of trees has grown on the cave floor, a rainforest inside a mountain. The chambers are so vast that in summer, warm, damp air from the cave's river meets cooler air and condenses into drifting clouds. Outside, the jungle may swelter at 37 degrees while the cave stays near 22 to 25.

Jim White, a teenage cowboy, noticed an opening in the ground of the New Mexico desert in 1898 and climbed down a homemade wire ladder, the first person to explore Carlsbad Caverns. Its Big Room, nearly 1,220 metres long, is the largest cave chamber in North America.

In Slovenia a rugged limestone plateau, the Kras, gave all such landscapes their name: scientists first described its caves, sinkholes and vanishing streams, so geographers everywhere call land of dissolving rock karst.

Most caves are dissolved from the top down. New Mexico's Lechuguilla Cave was eaten from the bottom up, by sulfuric acid rising from oil deposits below, and it is hung with gypsum chandeliers up to 6 metres long. Cavers broke into it in 1986 after following wind roaring up through its floor, and it is now sealed to all but approved scientists. Geologists call caves formed this way, from below, hypogene.

The deepest caves of all, Krubera and Veryovkina, the only two known to drop more than 2 kilometres, both sink into a single limestone mountain mass in the Caucasus of Abkhazia, the Arabika Massif. Krubera's Russian nickname, Voronya, means Crow's Cave, for the crows that nest in its entrance pit.

the-great-ice-ages-and-their-orbital-pac.context_blurb:
Some twenty thousand years ago, ice sheets thousands of feet thick sprawled across Canada and the northern United States, and glaciers buried much of northern Europe. That was only the latest of many great freezes. Again and again the ice has crept south and melted back, and it left its fingerprints everywhere: lakes, scratched rock, drowned lands, and ice caps that never melted at all.

Look at a map of North America and you can see the claw marks. The Laurentide Ice Sheet pushed south in great tongues of ice that gouged out a row of deep basins, and when the ice drew back about 14,000 years ago, its meltwater filled them to make the five Great Lakes. Between them the lakes contain over one-fifth of Earth's fresh surface water, about 22,800 cubic kilometres. Spread evenly over the 48 contiguous states, that water would flood the whole country roughly 10 feet deep, or about 9.5 feet to be exact.

In New York's Central Park the ice signed its name on Umpire Rock, a bare hump of bedrock polished smooth and scored with long parallel scratches called glacial striations. The scratches run north to south, the track of ice grinding southward over the city, and at its peak that ice stood roughly 1,000 feet thick above Manhattan. Geologists call that whole age of repeated freezes the Pleistocene, an epoch running from about 2.58 million years ago to 11,700 years ago. Each advance carved lakes and lowered the seas before the ice pulled back again.

With so much water locked up in ice, the oceans sank about 120 metres. The bed of the North Sea became dry country with rivers, grassland and roaming hunters, linking Britain by land to France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, and scientists call it Doggerland. The sea crept back between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago and finally cut Britain off from the mainland around 6500 BCE. In 1931 a trawler's net brought up a barbed antler harpoon some 22 centimetres long, made by a hunter who fished there between about 10,000 and 4,000 BCE, when the seabed was still land.

In two places the ice age never really ended. Greenland is still mostly buried under an ice sheet up to about 3.4 kilometres thick, and at its base lies ice that settled as snowfall roughly a million years ago. Antarctica's ice is heavier still. Its weight has pushed the continent's bedrock hundreds of metres down, the way a sleeper sinks into a soft mattress, and if the ice ever went, the land would rise again over thousands of years in a slow spring-back that geologists call isostatic rebound.

At its thickest, near the Astrolabe Subglacial Basin, Antarctic ice reaches almost 4.8 kilometres. If all of it melted, the oceans would climb by about 53 metres, call it 50, enough to redraw every coastline on Earth. That ice is also a time machine. At Dome C, high on the plateau, scientists from Concordia Station drilled the EPICA core about 3,270 metres down to just above the bedrock. Every layer is a year of snow with bubbles of real ancient air sealed inside. Its record reaches back roughly 800,000 years, and its trapped bubbles are the oldest samples of ancient air ever recovered.

Read from top to bottom, the Dome C ice shows about eight great freezes, one roughly every 100,000 years. In the 1920s the Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković worked out why the cold keeps such regular time. Earth's orbit slowly stretches and rounds again over about 100,000 years, the tilt of its axis nods back and forth every 41,000 years, and the spinning axis wobbles like a top every 23,000. Together these slow orbital rhythms are called the Milankovitch cycles, the pacemaker of the ice ages.

Yet the closest match hides a real puzzle. The freezes keep step best with the 100,000-year stretching of the orbit, and that cycle barely alters how much sunlight reaches Earth in total. Why the weakest push sets the master beat is still argued over, with ideas ranging from feedbacks in the ice and oceans to subtler timing effects, and scientists call it the 100,000-year problem.

the-great-mosque-of-djenn.context_blurb:
Djenné is an old trading town on the inland delta of the Niger River in Mali, and its Great Mosque rises over the market square on a platform about 75 metres on each side, lifted 3 metres above the ground. The building standing now dates from 1907, a rebuild in the traditional Sudano-Sahelian style on a holy site where the first mosque went up in the 13th century.

It is the largest mud-brick building on Earth, as big as a cathedral and made from nothing but sun-dried earth. Each of its three minarets, about 16 metres tall, is crowned with an ostrich egg, said to stand for fertility and purity.

All over the walls jut the toron, bundles of palm wood that stick out about 60 centimetres. They are not decoration but permanent scaffolding, built into the walls so that workers can climb them every year.

Why climb every year? Mud melts in the rain, and without care the walls would wash away. So each year, before the wet season, Djenné re-skins its mosque in a festival called the crépissage. The work falls not to paid crews but to the people of the town themselves, a whole crowd of ordinary men and women. Guided by the guild of master masons, the barey ton, the men swarm up the toron to smear on fresh mud while the women carry water, and the giant building is plastered by hand in about a single day. Neighbourhood teams race to finish first, cheered on by drummers.

Inside, the vast prayer hall stays cool through the fierce heat of the Sahel with no fans or machines at all. The earthen walls, some 16 to 24 inches thick, work like a heat battery: they soak up the blazing warmth of the day and give it back slowly after dark.

Three kilometres away lies the town's ancestor, Djenné-Djenno. Founded around 250 BC and abandoned around AD 1400, it ranks among the oldest cities found south of the Sahara, home at its height to perhaps 20,000 merchants, goldsmiths and iron-workers. When the archaeologists Susan and Roderick McIntosh dug into its mound, they found the treasure that made it famous: terracotta figurines up to half a metre tall, many of them bearded horsemen.

the-great-pyramid-of-giza.context_blurb:
On the Giza plateau, at the edge of modern Cairo, the Great Pyramid rises out of the desert, the largest of three pyramids and some 4,500 years old. More than two million blocks of limestone went into it. Ancient Greek travellers put it on their list of the Seven Wonders of the World.

Of all seven, only the Great Pyramid still stands; fire, war and earthquakes destroyed every other one, from the Colossus of Rhodes to the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. It was built as a tomb: the pharaoh Khufu, whom the Greeks called Cheops, raised it as his burial place around 2600 to 2560 BC, and his relative Hemiunu is thought to have been the architect.

Finished around 2560 BC at about 146.6 metres, it was taller than anything people had ever built, and it kept that title for more than 3,800 years, longer than any building before or since. Its builders were not slaves but paid, well-fed Egyptian crews who lived in a town beside Giza and were buried in tombs of honour near their king. They worked in proud gangs and daubed their gang names on the stones, and one crew called itself The Friends of Khufu Gang.

Its reign ended only around AD 1311, when the central spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England reached roughly 160 metres, a few metres higher. A storm blew that spire down in 1549, and it was never rebuilt.

The pyramid's four sides face the four points of the compass, lined up on true north with an average error of just 3 minutes and 38 seconds of arc, about 0.06 of a degree. Khufu's builders had no magnetic compass, and how they managed it is still debated. They also buried a ship for their king. In 1954 the archaeologist Kamal el-Mallakh opened a sealed pit beside the pyramid's south face, shut for 4,500 years, and found 1,224 cedar timbers laid out in order. Fitted back together, they made a complete full-sized ship, 43 metres long, probably meant to carry the king's spirit across the sky.

Deep inside, the King's Chamber is roofed with dark granite beams, the heaviest about 80 tonnes. That hard stone came from the quarries at Aswan, roughly 800 to 900 kilometres to the south, and boatmen floated it down the Nile. The outside once gleamed white, cased in polished Tura limestone. After an earthquake loosened the casing in 1303, Cairo's rulers carted the polished stones away and built them into the mosques and fortresses of their city. Stripped to its stepped core, the pyramid now stands about 138.5 metres high.

In 2013, at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient port on the Red Sea, diggers found the oldest inscribed papyrus ever discovered: the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew spent its days carrying white Tura limestone by boat up the Nile to Giza. It is a worker's-eye view of the pyramid going up in Khufu's reign.

Over the King's Chamber, Khufu's builders stacked five low, empty rooms, each capped with huge granite slabs, never meant to be entered. These relieving chambers spread the enormous weight of the stone above, so that the ceiling of the King's Chamber is not crushed. When they were opened in 1837, explorers found work-gang names painted on the hidden blocks.

Narrow shafts angle upward from the inner chambers. A well-known theory, fiercely contested, holds that the southern shaft, around 2500 BC, pointed at the three stars of Orion's Belt, which the Egyptians linked with the god Osiris. The northern shaft aimed near Thuban, the pole star of that age. Most archaeologists treat the idea as fringe, since the shafts are blocked by stone and could never have been used to watch the sky.

the-great-sphinx-of-giza.context_blurb:
Below the pyramids of Giza crouches the Great Sphinx, a lion about 73 metres long and 20 metres high with the face of a king. It is one of the largest and oldest statues on Earth, carved some 4,500 years ago.

Unlike the pyramids beside it, the Sphinx was never built up from blocks: its makers carved it in place, straight down into one natural ridge of limestone bedrock. That makes it the largest single-stone statue left from the ancient world.

Today it is bare tan rock, but it once looked very different. Flecks of red pigment still cling to the face, with traces of yellow and blue on the body, because the Sphinx was once painted in bright colours. A piece of its fallen royal beard is now in the British Museum.

The face is crisp while the body is crumbling, and the rock explains why. The Giza bedrock lies in layers, and the top layer, where the sculptors cut the head, is a harder, tougher limestone, so the face has kept its detail. The lower layers that form the lion's body are much softer, and thousands of years of wind and salt have eaten them into deep hollows.

And the missing nose? A popular story blames Napoleon's soldiers, firing a cannon for practice in 1798. But the Danish traveller Frederic Norden drew the Sphinx in 1737 already without its nose, decades before Napoleon was even born in 1769. The historian al-Maqrizi wrote that a man named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr smashed it off around 1378, angry that local people made offerings to the statue.

Between the great paws stands the Dream Stela, a granite slab some 3,400 years old. It tells how the young prince Thutmose IV dozed in the statue's shade, when sand covered it to the shoulders, and dreamed that the Sphinx promised him the crown: clear away the sand, and he would become pharaoh of Egypt. He cleared it, and around 1400 BC he took the throne.

The walls of the pit cut around the Sphinx are scored with deep, rounded vertical grooves. The geologist Robert Schoch claimed that heavy rain wore them, which would push the statue's age back to perhaps 7000 to 5000 BC. Mainstream geologists and Egyptologists reject that as pseudoarchaeology. They blame salt: water soaking into the porous limestone leaves salt behind, and each time that salt crystallizes it swells and flakes the surface away. And the archaeological evidence dates the Sphinx to about 2500 BC.

the-great-wall-of-china.context_blurb:
The Great Wall of China snakes across the mountains, deserts and grasslands of northern China, built to hold back the horse-riding raiders of the Mongolian steppe. It is not one wall at all but a vast web of ramparts, towers, trenches and forts, raised, abandoned and rebuilt by one Chinese dynasty after another for more than two thousand years.

A six-year survey, completed in 2012, added up every branch and fragment for the first time and reached a total of 21,196 kilometres, or about 21,000, more than half the distance around the equator. The stretch on all the postcards is Badaling, northwest of Beijing, the most visited and most heavily restored section: nearly 10 million people climbed it in 2018, so since 2019 officials have let in no more than 65,000 a day.

Many textbooks once claimed the wall can be seen from the Moon. It cannot. From some 384,000 kilometres out, the wall would look as thin as a single human hair viewed from about 3 kilometres off, far too fine for any eye. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said after his 2003 flight that he had not seen it at all.

The first border walls went up as early as the 7th century BC, centuries before China's first emperor. Around 221 BC that emperor, Qin Shi Huang, linked the older walls together, and later Han builders and, much later, the Ming raised and rebuilt walls of their own.

The grey stone wall of the travel posters, its battlements and watchtowers riding the hills near Beijing, was built mostly by the Ming, who raised about 8,850 kilometres of it between 1368 and 1644 against Mongol raids. They swapped the rammed earth of earlier walls for fired brick and cut stone.

Far to the west, in the Gobi and Gansu deserts, Han crews two thousand years ago had no stone to spare. They built in alternating layers of willow branches and reeds, packed with sand and gravel, the plant stems binding the fill the way steel rods bind concrete. Stretches near Dunhuang still stand after two thousand years of sandstorms.

At its eastern tip, near Shanhai Pass, the wall runs straight into the sea: Ming builders in 1579 ran a stone spur some 20 metres into the Bohai Sea, and because it looks like a dragon bending to drink, it is called Laolongtou, Old Dragon's Head.

Some two thousand kilometres west, the wall ends in desert at Jiayu Pass, a fortress begun in 1372 in Gansu that held the Hexi Corridor, a narrow gap on the old Silk Road. Its walls run 733 metres and stand about 11 metres high, and a stone tablet there hails it as the greatest pass under heaven.

Legend says the workers who died building the wall were sealed inside it. In the old tale, Meng Jiangnu wept so bitterly for her husband that a long stretch of wall fell and bared the bones beneath, a story told for over 2,000 years as a protest against the brutal forced labour, which was real and cost an enormous toll. Yet archaeologists have found no bodies in the wall. What they found was the Ming mortar: slaked lime mixed with sticky-rice soup, the rice starch making it so hard that, centuries on, weeds can barely take root in the joints.

The boast that the wall can be seen from space is older than spaceflight: William Stukeley, an English antiquarian, made it in a letter in 1754, two centuries before the first human flight into space in 1961. A 1932 newspaper cartoon then spread it worldwide.

the-greenland-ice-sheet.context_blurb:
Greenland is a vast Arctic island, some 2.17 million square kilometres of land, most of it north of the Arctic Circle, and an unbroken sheet of ice smothers nearly the whole of it. That ice is a frozen world of its own, with record cold, a hidden canyon, a buried crater, and rivers that drop out of sight.

Greenland counts as the largest island on Earth even though Australia, some 7.7 million square kilometres, dwarfs it, because Australia is classed as a continent and so is left off the island list.

The ice averages about 1,670 metres thick, and at its deepest it reaches some 3,490 metres, over 3 kilometres or roughly 2 miles of solid ice above the rock. Even so, it is only the second-largest ice sheet on the planet: its 2.9 million cubic kilometres of ice come to about an eighth of the load piled on Antarctica. A remote weather station on the summit ice logged about minus 69.6 °C on 22 December 1991, later confirmed as the lowest temperature ever measured anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Only Antarctica, near minus 89 °C at Vostok, has been colder.

If all of Greenland's ice melted, the oceans would rise about 7.4 metres, some 24 feet, enough to redraw coastlines worldwide. The weight of all that ice has bent the land itself. It has pressed the bedrock of central Greenland down to some 300 metres below sea level, so with the ice lifted away the middle of the island would be a sunken bowl beneath the level of the sea, ringed by coastal mountains.

The ice hides older landscapes too. In 2013 NASA's Operation IceBridge flew radar that sees through ice and found a buried canyon more than 750 kilometres long and up to 800 metres deep, with V-shaped walls and a flat floor that mark it as the work of an ancient river from before the ice came. It snakes north toward the fjord of Petermann Glacier.

Greenland's glaciers feed the sea with icebergs. The berg that sank the Titanic in April 1912 most likely broke off a Greenland glacier around 1909, then drifted for years, north into Baffin Bay and then south past Newfoundland.

Ice cores, long tubes drilled out of the sheet, hold year upon year of snow, a climate record in frozen layers. The famous GISP2 core, over 3 kilometres long, holds about 110,000 years of climate. The bubbles sealed inside its layers are real ancient air, so scientists can measure the old atmosphere directly instead of estimating it.

Each summer bright blue lakes and rivers of meltwater spread across the surface. Some of those rivers vanish down moulins, near-vertical shafts that the falling water drills straight through the ice to the bed, where it greases the ice so the glacier slips faster seaward.

In 2018 radar found a buried ring about 31 kilometres wide under Hiawatha Glacier, most likely blasted out by a giant asteroid impact, an iron rock perhaps 1.5 kilometres across. Early guesses tied it to a cold spell some 13,000 years ago, but in 2022 dating of its melted rock put the impact at about 58 million years ago, the best estimate so far.

On the west coast, Sermeq Kujalleq, also called Jakobshavn Glacier, once raced along at over 45 metres a day, faster than almost any other glacier on Earth. It is Greenland's biggest iceberg factory, shedding some 35 billion tonnes a year into the Ilulissat Icefjord, a World Heritage Site since 2004.

For years most people blamed warm air for the melting of Greenland's glaciers. Then researchers sounding the deep fjords found a second attacker below the waterline: warm, salty Atlantic seawater slips into the fjords and melts the underwater faces of the glaciers, undercutting them until the ice above snaps off. In one survey of 226 glaciers, the 74 that sit in deep fjords caused nearly half of Greenland's ice loss between 1992 and 2017.

the-gulf-stream-and-the-mild-edge-of-eur.context_blurb:
A warm river runs through the Atlantic Ocean. Born in the Gulf of Mexico, it pours out past Florida, runs north up the American coast and then swings across the ocean toward Europe, carrying tropical heat with it. Thanks to that current, northwestern Europe enjoys winters far milder than its northern position should allow.

Through the narrow Straits of Florida the Gulf Stream pushes about 30 million cubic metres of water every second, while all the rivers that empty into the Atlantic together add only about 0.6 million. South of Newfoundland it swells to some 150 million.

London, at about 51.5 degrees north, and Dublin, at 53.3, lie in the same band as Labrador, whose Canadian harbours freeze solid each winter, yet they are spared because the Gulf Stream's far, Europe-bound arm, the North Atlantic Drift, carries its warmth all the way to Britain and Ireland. The current clings to the American shore until Cape Hatteras in North Carolina, near 35 degrees north, where it leaves the coast and heads out across the open ocean toward Europe.

Sailors knew it long before mapmakers did. Nantucket whalers found its unseen edge without instruments by three signs: how the whales behaved, how warm the sea felt, and the colour of the water.

The warm water flows on up the whole coast of Norway, keeping harbours open through winter far inside the Arctic Circle, and one of them, Tromsø, became a famous gateway for polar expeditions setting out toward the North Pole.

The Gulf Stream is a true river in the sea, about 100 kilometres wide and not just a skin of warm water, for it reaches 800 to 1,200 metres down, with a surface speed near 2.5 metres a second.

On Scotland's north-west coast, at Inverewe Garden on Loch Ewe, about as far north as Moscow, the warm drift and a sheltering ring of hills let palm trees, eucalyptus and other subtropical plants flourish outdoors.

The current never runs straight; it swings in great loops. Now and then a loop pinches off as a warm-core ring, a spinning whirl of warm water 100 to 300 kilometres across that drifts away south-west and can last for months, sometimes up to a year.

The Gulf Stream has twins. Each ocean basin has its own swift, warm current running up its western side, which oceanographers call a western boundary current. In the Pacific it is the Kuroshio, Japanese for Black Current, named for its deep blue-black water, and it carries about 50 million tons of seawater a second past Japan, even more than the Gulf Stream.

In 1768 Benjamin Franklin, then a deputy postmaster in London, was puzzled that the royal mail packets crossed the Atlantic more slowly than merchant ships. His cousin Timothy Folger, a whaling captain from Nantucket, explained that the packets were sailing straight against a warm current that the whalers knew well and steered around. Folger sketched it from memory, and by 1769 it was printed in London as the first chart of the Gulf Stream. The whalers had warned the British captains, Folger said, but the captains thought themselves too wise to take advice from simple American fishermen.

the-ha-amonga-a-maui-trilithon.context_blurb:
On Tongatapu, the main island of the Kingdom of Tonga in the South Pacific, a giant stone gateway stands near the village of Niutoua. Two upright blocks hold up a heavy crossbeam 5.2 metres above the ground. It is about 800 years old, and it looks so like England's great prehistoric monument that people call it the Stonehenge of the Pacific.

Tongans call it the Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, a trilithon, which means a monument of three stones.

Its builders had no metal tools, cranes or wheels, and the stone they worked was coral limestone cut from Tongatapu's own reef, the pressed skeletons of ancient coral and the one building stone a low coral island has in plenty. Each pillar weighs 30 to 40 tonnes, and the crossbeam of roughly 15 tonnes drops into carved grooves so that its own weight locks it in place.

The king who raised it, Tuʻitatui, the 11th Tuʻi Tonga, left another stone nearby, the ʻEsi Maka Faʻakinanga. Tradition says it was his backrest: he leaned against it while holding court, so that with solid rock at his back no assassin could creep up on him. His name means strike the knee, said to be a warning to anyone who came too close.

The monument's name means the Burden of Maui. A haʻamonga is a carrying pole laid across the shoulders with a load hung at each end. Legend says the demigod Maui used one to bring the giant stones nearly 1,000 kilometres across the ocean from ʻUvea, the island also called Wallis. In truth the stone matches quarries on Tongatapu itself, so no voyage was needed.

At Muʻa, Tonga's old royal capital some 12 kilometres away, lie the tombs of the Tuʻi Tonga kings, the Langi: some 28 terraced pyramids with flat tops, built of huge stone slabs fitted together with no mortar.

In 1967 King Taufaʻahau Tupou IV, working with the historian Tevita Fale, argued that a small V-shaped notch on top of the crossbeam lines up with sunrise at the summer and winter solstices, which would make the gateway a giant stone calendar. It remains a theory, and the astronomer C.F. Velt argued that the notch is too small to sight by. What is certain is that Tuʻitatui raised it around 1200 AD as a ceremonial gateway into his royal compound at Heketā.

the-hadley-cell-and-the-30-degree-desert.context_blurb:
Spin a globe and a pattern leaps out: the great rainforests hug the equator, while a belt of the biggest deserts lines up roughly 30 degrees to either side of it. One vast loop of moving air, turning over between the tropics and the subtropics, makes both.

Over the Amazon and the Congo the sun stands nearly overhead and heats the air at the ground until it is rising toward the sky, billowing into towering thunderclouds that pour rain almost every day. That rising air is why the rainforests sit in a band along the equator.

The air drifts poleward high in the sky, cools, and sinks back down near 30 degrees north and south, and since sinking air cannot make rain, the ground beneath bakes under clear skies. That one descending branch lines up the deserts of the Sahara, Arabia, the Kalahari and Australia at matching latitudes in both hemispheres.

The whole loop, air rising at the equator, flowing poleward aloft, sinking near 30 degrees and blowing back toward the equator at ground level as the trade winds, is called the Hadley cell, after George Hadley, an English lawyer who loved physics more than law. He described it in 1735 to account for the slant of the trade winds, which come out of the northeast and not due east. Right on the equator, under the rising air, the surface wind hardly blows at all, because the air is moving straight up instead of sideways, and sailors dreaded that dead belt as the doldrums, where a becalmed ship could sit for weeks.

The rising seam where the northeast and southeast trade winds meet and lift is the Intertropical Convergence Zone. It follows the band of most direct sunshine north in the northern summer and south in the southern summer, switching on the monsoon rains of India and West Africa when it swings inland.

Near 30 degrees, under the sinking air, lie calm, cloudless belts of high pressure that sailors named the horse latitudes. Legend says Spanish ships carrying horses to the Americas lay becalmed there, ran short of water and threw the dying animals overboard, but that tale is probably folk etymology; a sailors' ritual called the dead horse, marking the end of an advance on their pay, is a better-documented source.

The equatorial air climbs 12 to 15 kilometres, about where airliners cruise, until it hits the tropopause, the lid of the troposphere where all weather happens, and only then does it turn toward the poles.

Over the oceans the sinking air parks great domes of high pressure. Over the North Atlantic it is the Azores High, also called the Bermuda High, a vast calm dome that dries the Sahara and keeps Mediterranean summers dry, while its southern edge pushes storm seeds from Africa out across the ocean to the Caribbean, where some grow into hurricanes.

Hadley guessed rightly that Earth's spin bends the winds, but his maths was not quite right. In 1835 the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis worked out the true rule, now called the Coriolis effect: on a turning planet, anything moving freely, from a wind to a long-range shell, is pushed rightward north of the equator and leftward south of it. It is why the trade winds slant and why hurricanes spin.

The loop is shifting. Satellite and weather records over recent decades show the cell widening on a warming planet, its descending dry edge creeping poleward by roughly 0.1 to 0.5 degrees of latitude per decade, dragging the subtropical dry belt toward the Mediterranean, California, southern Australia and southern Africa.

the-highest-clouds-on-earth-noctilucent-.context_blurb:
On summer nights in the far north and far south, between about 50 and 70 degrees of latitude, long after sunset, thin silvery-blue wisps can glow high in the darkening sky. They are the highest clouds on Earth, floating at the very edge of space.

They are noctilucent clouds, from the Latin for night-shining, a name given by the German scientist Otto Jesse, who first photographed them in 1887. The first confirmed sightings came in 1885, two years after the great eruption of Krakatoa.

Ordinary clouds stay low, and even high cirrus tops out near 12 kilometres, but noctilucent clouds drift 76 to 85 kilometres up, in the mesosphere, a frigid layer where hardly any other cloud ever forms.

They shine only in deep twilight, when the sun sits 6 to 16 degrees below the horizon. By then the ground and the low air lie in Earth's shadow, but the clouds, 80 kilometres up, still catch the sun's rays from below the horizon and glow. Their electric-blue tint comes from ozone, which soaks up the redder light as the low sunbeams skim through it.

Each tiny ice crystal needs a speck to freeze onto. NASA's AIM satellite, launched in 2007, found that about 3 percent of each crystal is meteor smoke, nanometre-sized dust left behind as meteors burn up at the edge of space. The ice forms only where the air falls below about minus 120 °C, and strangely the coldest such air sits over the summer pole, which is why these are summer clouds.

the-himalayas.context_blurb:
The Himalayas curve for some 2,400 kilometres across South Asia, from Pakistan to Bhutan, a wall of ice and rock between the Indian subcontinent and the highlands of Tibet. They hold Mount Everest, 8,849 metres high, and they are still rising, because the ground beneath them is in the middle of a slow and unfinished crash.

The name comes from Sanskrit, the ancient language of India: hima means snow and alaya means dwelling, so Himalaya means abode of snow. Behind the wall spreads the Tibetan Plateau, the highest and largest plateau on Earth, averaging about 4,500 metres and spread over some 2.5 million square kilometres, so vast that it stands out plainly from orbit, which earned it the nickname Roof of the World.

Everest is not done growing: it gains about 4 millimetres a year, some 40 centimetres a century, because two continents are colliding head-on, the Indian plate ramming straight into the Eurasian plate. This is not the kind of collision where a thin ocean plate dives under a continent and feeds a line of volcanoes; it is continent against continent. Earth has fourteen mountains over 8,000 metres, and all fourteen of them stand in the belt where India meets Asia: ten in the Himalaya proper and four, including K2 at 8,611 metres, in the neighbouring Karakoram.

India was not always part of Asia. It broke away from Gondwana, the old southern supercontinent that once joined Africa, Australia, South America and Antarctica, and for tens of millions of years it was a lone island continent, drifting north across the Tethys Ocean. So the grey rock on Everest's very summit is limestone that formed on the floor of the Tethys Ocean some 450 to 500 million years ago, and the collision scraped that old seabed thousands of metres into the sky. Just 6 metres below the top, geologists have collected fossils of trilobites and sea lilies.

The wall splits the weather too. Moist monsoon air is forced up the southern slopes, cools and drops its rain, then spills over the crest with nothing left, so the Tibetan side is a cold desert with less than 200 mm a year. In that same monsoon's path, the town of Cherrapunji, in the Indian state of Meghalaya, is soaked by more than 11,000 mm of rain a year, among the wettest inhabited places on Earth.

The Himalaya cradles some 15,000 glaciers, more ice than anywhere outside the Arctic and the Antarctic, and so geographers call it the Third Pole. Its ice and snow, with that of the neighbouring Hindu Kush, feed about ten of Asia's great rivers, the Indus, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra among them, and their water reaches roughly two billion people, about one in four of everyone alive.

Most plates creep along at only a couple of centimetres a year, but around 80 million years ago India raced north at some 15 centimetres a year, perhaps 20, about twice as fast as the quickest plate moving today. It struck Asia about 50 million years ago and is still shoving north a few centimetres a year.

Where the continents meet, the crust under southern Tibet has been stacked to about 70 kilometres thick, double the usual 35. Thick crust behaves like a floating raft or an iceberg: the more is piled up, the deeper its root sinks into the dense mantle and the higher its top rides, so the plateau's deep, buoyant root holds it aloft.

The range is so heavy that it bends the Indian plate down in front of it, like a diving board with a weight on its tip. That sag forms a long trough, a foreland basin, which fills with mud and sand washed off the peaks, and the result is the flat, fertile Ganges Plain. The mountains, by their own weight, built the lowland at their feet.

the-horn-the-arete-the-cirque-and-the-ta.context_blurb:
Glaciers are sculptors. Where ice once filled the high valleys of the Alps, Wales and England's Lake District, it left a whole kit of shapes behind: scooped bowls, knife-edge ridges, pointed peaks and small dark lakes.

The Matterhorn, above Zermatt in Switzerland and Breuil-Cervinia in Italy, is the classic. Over about a million years, four glaciers each ground a hollow into a different side of the mountain and ate inward until only a sharp stone pyramid was left, 4,478 metres high, its faces turned roughly toward the four points of the compass.

When the ice melts, small lakes are often left in those hollows, held behind low dams of moraine, the rubble a glacier bulldozes along and drops. Such a pool is a tarn, from the Old Norse tjorn, and England's Lake District alone holds about 197 of them, among them the Red Tarn beneath Helvellyn.

The hollow itself is a cirque, French for a natural amphitheatre, a bowl steep on three sides and open downhill, which the Welsh call a cwm and the Scots a corrie, from the Gaelic for a cauldron. Cwm Idwal in Snowdonia curves around the lake Llyn Idwal, and Britons once ranked it seventh among their country's natural wonders.

Where two cirques gnaw toward each other from opposite sides, only a thin wall of rock survives between them, an arete, French for a fish bone, sharp on both edges. On Snowdon, Crib Goch, the red ridge, is a crest thin enough that some people straddle it like a horse.

Wherever three or more cirques meet, the rock between them is worn down to a sharp point called a horn, and the Matterhorn is the textbook example. Its four faces are unequal; the western one alone rises some 1,400 metres of almost sheer rock.

Cirque walls stay so steep because the ice keeps quarrying them. While a glacier filled the bowl, a deep crevasse called the bergschrund, German for mountain cleft, gaped at its head, where the sliding glacier pulled away from ice frozen fast to the back wall. Meltwater seeped into cracks in the bared rock, froze, swelled and pried blocks loose, carving the wall ever steeper.

Charles Darwin, as a young man in 1831, walked through Cwm Idwal and noticed nothing. By 1842 a bold new idea, that great sheets of ice had once buried much of Britain, had taught naturalists to read the scratches, mounds and stranded boulders that ice leaves behind. Back in Cwm Idwal, Darwin saw at once that glaciers had carved the valley, and he wrote that a house burned down by fire could not have told its own history any more clearly.

the-humboldt-current-upwelling-and-the-w.context_blurb:
Off the Pacific shores of Peru and northern Chile, a cold current flows north out of the sub-Antarctic seas, hugging South America's western shore deep into the tropics. It is the Humboldt Current, and it shapes everything here: a chilly sea, a rainless desert, islands of bird droppings and one of the greatest fisheries on Earth.

Wade into the surf near the equator in Peru and you gasp, because the Humboldt drags cold water thousands of kilometres north and the sea can be as cool as about 16 °C, or 61 °F, so a tropical shore feels almost temperate. Cold water gives off little moisture and chills the air above it so that it cannot rise into rain clouds, and so the Atacama Desert stretches along this shore, the driest place on Earth outside the poles. Some spots there may have gone centuries without measurable rain.

The real wealth is under the water. Winds along the coast shove the sunlit top layer offshore, and cold, nutrient-laden water wells up from the depths to fill the gap, a process called upwelling. The nutrients feed huge blooms of plankton, and the plankton feed the anchoveta, a small anchovy. Peru's fishery grew into the richest on Earth, and its 1970 catch topped 12 million tonnes, roughly a fifth, or 20 percent, of all the fish caught on the planet.

The same food fed vast flocks of seabirds. On the Chincha Islands off Peru, where rain almost never falls, their droppings never washed away and built up over thousands of years into layers up to 60 metres thick, deeper than a twenty-storey building is tall. In the 1800s miners dug out this guano, from the Quechua word wanu, by the shipload.

Once every few years the water along Peru's coast warms up, the anchovy shoals vanish and the boats come home empty. The fishermen named the warm spell El Niño, the little boy, after the newborn Christ, because it peaks around Christmas. Scientists kept the name for the whole Pacific-wide warming, and its cool opposite is La Niña.

By the 1840s guano was Peru's greatest export and its biggest source of money, because it was the finest fertilizer in the world: its nitrogen and phosphorus brought worn-out farm soils in Europe and America back to life. The United States passed the Guano Islands Act in 1856, letting its citizens claim unclaimed guano islands, and Spain's seizure of Peru's richest deposits set off the Chincha Islands War of 1864 to 1866.

The engine of upwelling hides a twist. The coastal wind blows roughly along the shore, yet the surface water it drives moves off at right angles, out to sea. The Coriolis force of Earth's spin deflects the moving surface layer, a turn called Ekman transport, so the wind ends up pushing the water offshore and deep, cold water rises to replace it.

The anchoveta fishery, the world's largest, crashed in 1972 and has never fully come back. Years of overfishing had weakened it, and the United Nations later called the anchoveta the most heavily exploited fish in history, but the final blow was a strong El Niño. Its warm water floated on top of the cold like a lid and kept the upwelling from rising, so the plankton starved, and the anchovies with them.

El Niño reaches across the whole Pacific: while freak rain floods Peru and makes its coastal desert bloom, the same warm pool parches eastern Australia and Indonesia with drought and feeds raging bushfires, opposite disasters an ocean apart. Meteorologists call such a long-distance link a teleconnection.

The Humboldt has cousins. Off Namibia's desert shore near Lüderitz, the Benguela Current drives the strongest upwelling cell on the planet, and like the Humboldt it turns a cold sea and a barren coast into a great fishing ground. Mark the world's four big cold-current fishing grounds on a map, off Peru, Namibia, California and Morocco, and every one lies on the west-facing coast of a continent, where the prevailing winds blow toward the equator and, bent by Earth's spin, push the surface water offshore.

the-ice-age-painted-caves-lascaux-chauve.context_blurb:
In the limestone caves of southwestern France and northern Spain, Ice Age hunters painted horses, bison, lions and rhinos with charcoal, ochre and manganese. Lascaux, Chauvet and Altamira hold some of the oldest and most beautiful art people have ever made, so lifelike that the animals still seem to move across the rock.

At Altamira in northern Spain, a low ceiling teems with a herd of bison, painted over natural bulges in the rock that become their humped shoulders and bellies, and its beauty earned it the nickname the Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art.

Lascaux in France was found thanks to a dog: in September 1940 a dog named Robot ran down a hole where a tree had toppled near Montignac, and his owner, Marcel Ravidat, came back with three friends. Hoping for a secret tunnel to a nearby manor, the teenagers slid down the shaft on 12 September and landed in a cave blazing with paintings.

Lascaux opened to tourists in 1948, but up to 1,200 visitors a day breathed out moisture and carbon dioxide that fed mould on the ancient paintings, so in 1963 France shut the original, and today's crowds walk through exact full-size copies, Lascaux II and the newer Lascaux IV.

Chauvet Cave in France, discovered on 18 December 1994, holds horses, lions and woolly rhinos painted so skilfully that experts first guessed they were fairly recent, until radiocarbon dating proved them about 36,000 years old. They are among the oldest cave paintings known, and Chauvet was sealed from the start to spare it Lascaux's fate. Deep inside, explorers found a cave-bear's skull perched on a fallen slab of rock that lies flat like an altar table, with more cave-bear skulls scattered on the floor around it. Many scholars read that arrangement as a sign that Chauvet was a sacred place, not just a gallery.

Altamira's ceiling was found in 1879 by Maria de Sautuola, a girl of eight, who looked up and, so the story goes, called out to her father that there were oxen. When Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola showed the paintings to Europe's leading scholars, they dismissed them as a forgery, sure that Ice Age people could never have painted so well, and he died in 1888 still branded a fraud. Only after more painted caves turned up in France did the chief sceptic, Émile Cartailhac, publicly apologise, in a 1902 article titled the apology of a sceptic.

The painters left their signatures too. An artist pressed a hand flat to the wall and blew a mouthful of powdered pigment around it, sometimes through a hollow bone tube, then lifted the hand away to leave a pale outline that has lasted some 30,000 years. Hand stencils like these are found in caves right across Europe.

Yet Europe's caves are not the oldest. A painting in the Leang Tedongnge cave, on the tropical island of Sulawesi, shows a warty pig at full size, and in 2021 it was dated to 45,500 years ago at the least, which makes it the oldest known animal painting in the world.

the-ice-crystal-sky-sun-dogs-and-the-22-.context_blurb:
On cold days, when thin, high cirrus clouds drift across the sky, the Sun can sprout rings, false suns and shafts of light. Tiny six-sided ice crystals make them all, acting like millions of prisms and mirrors that bend and bounce sunlight at exact angles.

On a clear, frozen morning the low Sun can appear with two smaller bright spots, one on each side of it and level with it. Scientists call each one a parhelion, Greek for beside the sun, but farmers and sailors named the pair sun dogs, because they seem to follow the real Sun across the sky the way a dog trails its master.

Often a faint ring circles the Sun with the sun dogs perched on it: the 22-degree halo, the commonest of all ice halos. A hand held out at arm's length with the fingers spread covers about 20 degrees, almost exactly the ring's radius, so the halo seems to fit just inside your outstretched fingers.

A rainbow comes from round drops of liquid water, but a halo comes from ice crystals, six-sided prisms high in cold cirrus, and about 22 degrees is the smallest angle by which such a prism can bend light.

You do not always need clouds. Around Fairbanks, Alaska, on the coldest mornings, the air at street level fills with tiny drifting ice crystals, a glittering haze called diamond dust, and sun dogs and halos can hang right down among the houses under a cloudless sky.

At night over a city like Montreal, column-shaped ice crystals floating with their flat faces level can act like millions of tiny mirrors and throw a shaft of light straight up above a streetlamp, a light pillar. A pillar is made by reflection, not by prism-bending, and reflection does not split colours, so the shaft glows in just one colour, the colour of the lamp itself: orange above a sodium lamp, white above a low winter Sun.

Over Finland and other winter lands, the loveliest of the ice optics is the circumzenithal arc, a brief, bright band that bends like a grin around the top of the sky, an upside-down rainbow with purer colours than a real one. It is not rare at all, but it is missed because it hangs straight overhead, where hardly anyone thinks to look.

On 20 April 1535, for two hours after dawn, rings of light and false suns crowded the sky over Stockholm, and the reformer Olaus Petri read it as God's warning to King Gustav Vasa. The painting made of that sky, the Vädersolstavlan, or Sun Dog Painting, is the oldest known picture of sun dogs, and it is also the oldest surviving view of Stockholm in colour. A copy from 1636 hangs in Storkyrkan cathedral today.

the-inca-quipu-an-empire-written-in-knot.context_blurb:
In the 1400s the Inca ruled some ten million people from their mountain capital, Cusco, in the Andes of Peru. Royal roads ran for thousands of miles, storehouses bulged with grain, and officials collected tribute and even counted the population. Yet the Inca never wrote a word. They kept the records of a whole empire in knots.

The accounts hung on cords of knotted string, bundles of coloured strings that the Inca called quipu, also spelled khipu.

A quipu is a counting machine built on tens, and since identical knots can stand for different amounts, what a knot is worth depends on how high up the cord it sits: knots near the bottom count ones, knots above them tens, and higher still hundreds and thousands. A reader took in a number by position, with the fingers as much as the eyes.

To record a number such as 308, a knot-keeper tied three knots in the hundreds place and eight in the ones, and left the tens place empty, a bare stretch with no knot at all. That gap was the Inca zero, a placeholder used centuries before the idea reached much of Europe.

The knot-keepers, the khipukamayuq, inherited their job and needed prodigious memories, because one wrong colour, shape or position could change a record. A keeper carried a whole province's tribute, herds and grain stores in his cords and his head. By some colonial-era accounts, a keeper who got the imperial figures wrong could be put to death, though that claim rests on Spanish testimony rather than certainty.

Today scholars can read a quipu's numbers clearly, but whether its colours, cord order and knot patterns also carry words, names or stories remains undeciphered. In 2005 Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine argued that three figure-eight knots on one cord spell the place name Puruchuco, perhaps the first word ever read from a quipu.

Once Spain had conquered Peru, its churchmen called the quipus idols of the devil and a barrier to converting the Andean people, and the Third Council of Lima, meeting in 1583, ordered them destroyed. Thousands were thrown into bonfires and burned as idolatrous, and only about 1,400 pre-Columbian quipus survive today, most of them in museums.

the-indus-script-and-the-silent-seals-of.context_blurb:
Some forty-five centuries ago, in the river valleys of present-day Pakistan and northwestern India, the Indus Valley people built brick cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, with straight streets and covered drains. They left short inscriptions by the thousand, cut into seals and scratched on pots, in a writing that has kept its secrets ever since.

Since the script was first dug up at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, it has defeated every reader, and no one alive can read what a single seal says.

Most of the signs survive on coin-sized seals of polished stone, each pairing a single animal with a short row of symbols. The creature that appears far more often than any other is a one-horned beast that scholars nickname the unicorn, though it is almost certainly a bull drawn from the side, its near horn hiding the far one.

The texts are tiny, too: the longest ever found, cut into a copper plate dug up at Mohenjo-daro, has just 26 signs, about 25 in all. There is no long text anywhere, no story, law or letter, to give codebreakers a grip.

Iravatham Mahadevan, a linguist, listed 417 distinct signs in 1977, too many for an alphabet of 20 or 30 letters yet far too few for a script with one sign for each word. That puzzle has fed a real argument over whether the marks are true writing at all, or symbols that never recorded a language.

The Indus people traded far to the west. At Ur in Mesopotamia, where the Indus land was known as Meluhha, Indus seals have been dug up. An Akkadian cylinder seal names one man, Shu-ilishu, as an interpreter of the Meluhhan language, proof that people once spoke and translated the Indus tongue.

Yet even he cannot help. The Rosetta Stone unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs, and scholars read Greek's Linear B too, because they could tie the signs to a language they already knew. The Indus script has no such bilingual key, and the language beneath it is a mystery, for no one knows what tongue its people spoke, so it may stay silent forever.

the-jet-stream-the-river-of-wind-that-st.context_blurb:
About seven miles up, near the ceiling of the weather layer, a narrow ribbon of wind races around the planet from west to east. It steers the storms that cross North America and Europe, sets the speed of transatlantic flights, and when it buckles it can pin heat waves or cold snaps in place for weeks.

This is the jet stream, flowing near the tropopause about 30,000 feet up, and an airliner flying east from New York to London can ride it and arrive over an hour ahead of schedule, while the flight home must fight it. Do not mix it up with the Gulf Stream, which is a warm ocean current.

The first person to record it was Wasaburo Oishi, a Japanese scientist who ran a weather lab near Mount Fuji. Between 1923 and 1925 he launched small pilot balloons filled with hydrogen and followed each one through a theodolite, a surveyor's telescope, reading the wind's speed and direction at every height. His 1,288 readings showed a fierce, permanent wind high over Japan. Yet the world ignored him for decades, because Oishi was a devoted Esperantist who wrote his 1926 report and the 18 that followed in Esperanto, an invented world language that few scientists could follow.

Japan then turned the jet into a weapon: it sent about 9,300 fu-go balloon bombs to ride the winter jet over the Pacific, a journey of some 6,000 miles, and each balloon was made of many sheets of mulberry paper, called washi, glued in layers with a paste of konjac potato. About 300 reached North America, the first weapon ever to cross between continents.

The jet roars hardest in winter and eases off in summer because it forms along the polar front, the sloping boundary between cold polar air and warm subtropical air, and the sharper the temperature contrast across that boundary, the faster it blows.

It rarely runs straight, but meanders in giant loops called Rossby waves, swinging north and south as it circles the hemisphere. A deep southward dip pulls Arctic air far below its usual range and brings a sudden cold snap, while a northward bulge lets warm air push up.

Sometimes a loop sticks. A ridge of high pressure stalls the eastward march of weather, a pattern called a blocking high. Its classic shape is the omega block, its loop curving like the Greek letter omega, Ω. In late June 2021 one trapped a dome of scorching air over western North America; the village of Lytton, British Columbia, reached 49.6 °C, a Canadian record, in one of the deadliest heat waves in North American history.

In February 2020 a powerful jet pushed a British Airways 747 across the Atlantic to London in 4 hours 56 minutes, touching 825 mph over the ground, faster than sound travels at sea level, and yet no sonic boom fell. A boom depends on speed through the air, not over the ground, and the plane's airspeed stayed below the sound barrier while the whole river of air raced east and carried it along.

Higher still, over the Arctic, spins the polar vortex, a ring of fast winds that usually keeps the coldest air on the planet penned near the pole. When a sudden warming high in the stratosphere weakens and splits it, the jet stream buckles and Arctic cold spills south, as in the February 2021 freeze that left much of Texas without power.

the-kalahari.context_blurb:
The Kalahari spreads over some 900,000 square kilometres of Botswana, Namibia and South Africa, a sea of red sand dotted with grass and camelthorn trees. It is not a true desert but a thirstland that catches 110 to over 500 millimetres of rain a year, with almost no water lying on the surface.

Its name comes from the Tswana word Kgala, meaning the great thirst, for a land of sand with no permanent rivers or lakes.

The sand is about 90 percent quartz, which is clear and colourless on its own. The red comes from a microscopically thin coat of iron oxide, the mineral hematite, which weathered out of the rocks, was carried in by groundwater and dried onto every grain, the same chemistry that turns iron rusty red.

The Okavango River flows in from the highlands of Angola and never reaches the sea. It fans out into the Kalahari as a vast green inland delta. Some 96 to 98 percent of its water rises back into the sky, lost to evaporation in the sun and to the thirsty plants that breathe it out, and almost none escapes. In the flood months of June to August the delta swells to about three times its usual size.

Farther out lie the Makgadikgadi salt pans, some 16,000 square kilometres of blinding white, dead-flat crust, one of the biggest salt flats in the world. They are the dried bed of Lake Makgadikgadi, an ancient inland sea that covered somewhere between 80,000 and 275,000 square kilometres, bigger than Switzerland, and lasted from about 2 million years ago until roughly 10,000 years ago.

Some 20,000 years back the lake brimmed over and its waters spilled out to the north-east, and that outflow helped cut the gorge of Victoria Falls on the Zambezi.

On the white pan rises Kubu Island, a crescent of granite over two billion years old, about a kilometre long and 10 metres high. Baobabs crown it, some reckoned to have lived over two thousand years, trees that stood on the lake's beach when it still held water. Kubu means hippopotamus in Setswana.

The central Kalahari has been the San people's home for many thousands of years, and they can draw water out of ground where an outsider would perish of thirst: they dig down to damp sand in a dry riverbed, push in a hollow grass stem and suck up the moisture. Then they pass it along a second straw into an ostrich eggshell, which is stoppered and buried as a secret water store.

the-karakoram.context_blurb:
North of the Himalaya, where Pakistan, India and China meet, the Karakoram packs the densest crowd of giant peaks on Earth into a range about 500 kilometres long. Its valleys are rivers of ice, and its summits include K2, one of the deadliest mountains to climb.

Its name is Turkic, from kara, black, and koram, gravel or rubble: traders first called the high Karakoram Pass black gravel for the dark, broken scree on its route, and European surveyors later stretched the name over the whole range.

Earth has only fourteen mountains over 8,000 metres; ten stand in the Himalaya, and the other four, K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I and Gasherbrum II, crowd into one small knot of Karakoram valleys on the border of Pakistan and China. Nowhere else are so many giants packed so close.

Trek for days up the ice to Concordia, about 4,600 metres up, where the Baltoro and Godwin-Austen glaciers meet, and all four stand around you at once. The photographer Galen Rowell, on the American K2 expedition of 1975, called that ring of peaks the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods, and he made it the title of his 1977 book.

Except at the poles, nowhere on Earth carries more ice: roughly a third of the range is frozen, against about a tenth of the Himalaya and 2 percent of the Alps. Its great artery is the Baltoro Glacier, about 63 kilometres long, which flows down from the flanks of K2 and feeds the Braldu River and then the Indus.

Mountain glaciers almost everywhere are shrinking, but many of the Karakoram's are not. In a 2005 paper the geographer Kenneth Hewitt named the Karakoram anomaly: between 1997 and 2002, 13 glaciers advanced, creeping forward over rock that had been bare, and 9 larger ones thickened by 5 to 15 metres. Some even rebuilt moraines that had been free of ice for over half a century.

The leading explanation is the Karakoram vortex, proposed by a Newcastle University team including Nathan Forsythe and Hayley Fowler: in summer a whirl of chilly upper air tightens over the range, bringing cloud and snowfall and holding temperatures down while the rest of the Himalaya warms. So the ice is fed rather than starved, though scientists are still testing the idea.

the-kathmandu-valley-city-of-a-thousand-.context_blurb:
In the foothills of the Himalayas in Nepal lies the Kathmandu Valley, a green bowl of terraced fields holding three old royal cities, Bhaktapur, Patan and Kathmandu, all crowded with Hindu and Buddhist temples. For centuries the valley stood on the trade road between India and Tibet, and its Newar craftsmen became famous for carved wood and stacked temple roofs.

Each of the three cities kept its own royal court, so the valley has three Durbar Squares, palace squares, not one, and around each king's palace generations of Newar craftsmen raised clusters of tiered temples.

On a hill above Kathmandu stands the Buddhist shrine of Swayambhunath, where troops of rhesus macaques rule the 365-step stairway and grab food from pilgrims, so travellers call it the Monkey Temple. A Buddhist legend says the bodhisattva Manjushri let his hair grow long while tending the hill, and its lice turned into the monkeys. Swayambhunath itself is a white dome, a stupa, under a golden spire, and on all four sides of the spire the Buddha's eyes are painted, a great pair of all-seeing eyes of wisdom watching every direction at once.

In Kathmandu's Durbar Square stands the carved wooden Kumari Ghar. It is the home of the Kumari, a small girl picked through a long, careful selection and worshipped until adolescence as a living goddess, the embodiment of the goddess Durga, known locally as Taleju. She is kept apart so that her feet do not touch the street, and on festival days she shows herself at a carved window to bless the crowds.

Just east of the city rises Boudhanath, a whitewashed dome some 36 metres high, among the biggest stupas in the world, where pilgrims walk clockwise all day spinning prayer wheels, a practice called kora.

The capital takes its very name from a wooden pavilion in its Durbar Square, Kasthamandap, from kastha, wood, and mandap, pavilion, a rest-house that gave shelter to traders on the road. Tradition says the whole building was raised from the timber of a single great sal tree. It stood for centuries until the 2015 Gorkha earthquake brought it down, and it has since been rebuilt.

The Swayambhu Purana, a Buddhist scripture, says the valley was once a great lake, at whose heart shone a lotus made of light. To reach the light and make the valley fit for people to live in, Manjushri struck the valley's rim with his flaming sword of wisdom and split the rock into the Chobar gorge, and the lake poured away. Geologists agree that the valley really was a lake for much of its past, drained through that same gorge.

In the 1270s a young Newar architect named Araniko took a team of eighty Nepali craftsmen across the mountains into the service of Kublai Khan. In the Khan's capital, Dadu, now Beijing, he built the White Stupa of the Miaoying Temple, over 50 metres tall, and the Khan made him Director of All Artisan Classes. Historians credit the valley's tradition of stacked temple roofs, carried east by Araniko, with helping to shape the pagoda across China and Japan.

the-lapita-pottery-trail.context_blurb:
Some 3,500 years ago, from the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea, a seafaring people sailed east into a Pacific no human had ever crossed. Archaeologists call them the Lapita. They left no writing, but island after island they left a trail that still shows up red in the sand.

Their signature is Lapita ware, stamped red-clay pots of reddish-brown clay pressed, before firing, with rows of tiny toothed geometric patterns from a comb-like tool, and wherever a shard turns up, the first seafarers had landed. That is how archaeologists know who reached each empty island first.

The whole culture is named after one dig on New Caledonia. An archaeologist digging there in 1952 asked a local man the name of the spot and wrote down Lapita, but the Haveke word was xapeta'a, meaning something like to dig a hole, so an entire ancient people ended up named after a word for the place where you dig.

Their pottery marks a line of finds stretching over 4,000 kilometres of open sea, eastward from New Guinea to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, and it records the first peopling of Remote Oceania, counted as the greatest ocean migration in all of prehistory.

Ancient DNA from the Teouma graves on Vanuatu, some three thousand years old, groups the earliest settlers with the native peoples of the northern Philippines and Taiwan, the cradle of the great Austronesian expansion, and these voyagers became the direct ancestors of the Polynesians.

They did not drift; they came prepared. Their double-hulled canoes were floating farms, loaded with pigs, chickens and dogs and with taro, yam, coconut and breadfruit to plant, so that each new island could be settled on purpose.

Teouma, on Efate island in Vanuatu, is the oldest cemetery yet found in the Pacific, and many of its Lapita skeletons have no skulls. Once the flesh had rotted, the living lifted the skulls out and laid them elsewhere. Three sat side by side on one old man's chest, three more lay between another person's legs, and a seventh was tucked inside a decorated Lapita pot. A bulldozer clearing land for a shrimp farm turned up the site by chance in 2003.

the-last-green-blink-of-the-sun-the-gree.context_blurb:
On a clear, still evening over the ocean, off Hawaii, the California coast or Key West, keep your eyes on the last sliver of the setting Sun. Sailors have told of what can happen next for centuries.

For a second or two, just before it vanishes, the Sun's top rim can flash green. The Sun itself does not turn green; only a thin rim of green light shows at its upper edge, and it is gone in a blink.

Why green? The dense air near the horizon bends sunlight like a weak prism and spreads its colours apart, so the top rim shows the colours that bend most. Blue should show there too. But on its long, slanting path the air scatters blue out of the beam, the same scattering that makes the daytime sky blue, and with the blue gone and the red already set, green is the last light left.

Near the poles the Sun moves almost sideways along the horizon, and then the flash can linger. On 16 October 1929 at Little America, Admiral Byrd's base near the Bay of Whales in Antarctica, a vivid green spot kept winking out and reappearing for about 35 minutes as the Sun crept along the ice.
