the-little-ice-age-written-on-the-land.context_blurb:
From about 1300 to 1850, much of Europe and North America lived through a long cold spell called the Little Ice Age. It was nothing like a true ice age, yet it froze rivers, pushed glaciers into villages, filled paintings with skaters and helped end a Norse colony on Greenland.

Despite its fearsome name it was a modest, patchy cooling, and the coldest winters ran only up to about 2 °C colder than today's, with no continental ice sheets at all.

In London the Thames froze hard enough for frost fairs, ice carnivals with tents, shops, taverns and even printing presses. The last great one came in February 1814, when an elephant was walked over the frozen river near Blackfriars Bridge, proof of how solid the ice was.

The river's shape helped as much as the cold. Old London Bridge stood on nineteen bulky piers, cased in timber starlings, that squeezed the tide through narrow arches, so drifting ice jammed against them and the slow, shallow river froze behind them as if dammed. The bridge was pulled down in 1831, embankments later narrowed the river, and the faster, deeper Thames has never frozen solid in London since.

In the Alps above Chamonix, glaciers from Mont Blanc crushed the hamlets of Le Châtelard, La Bonnenuit and La Bonneville between about 1600 and 1610. Around 1645 the frightened villagers called in the Bishop of Geneva, and he went up to the ice front and performed an exorcism on the glacier. It did not work; only the end of the Little Ice Age, two centuries later, halted the ice.

In the Netherlands the canals froze each winter. The painter Hendrick Avercamp, deaf and unable to speak and known as the mute of Kampen, filled his canvases with whole towns out skating on the ice, and skating is still a Dutch passion.

Erik the Red brought Norse settlers to Greenland around 985, and a few thousand people worked some 500 farms there with cattle and sheep. As the cold deepened, the summers grew too short to grow enough hay to feed the animals through the winter, and the seal hunt faltered too. The Western Settlement emptied around 1350 and the Eastern by the late 1400s. Climate was one thread among several: the colony also lived by selling walrus ivory to Europe, and that trade collapsed when African elephant ivory undercut it.

the-lut-desert-dasht-e-lut.context_blurb:
In southeastern Iran lies the Dasht-e Lut, a basin of black rock, sand seas and wind-carved ridges ringed by mountains. It is one of the most lifeless places on Earth, and from space it shows the hottest ground ever measured.

In 2018 NASA's MODIS satellite instrument clocked the Lut's bare ground at 80.8 °C, or 177 °F, the hottest land surface ever recorded on Earth. That is the temperature of the ground seen from orbit, not of the air; the hottest air ever reliably measured, in California's Death Valley, was far cooler.

The secret is the floor's colour: more than half of it is dark volcanic rock, blackened by ancient lava, and dark ground soaks up sunlight instead of reflecting it, like a black iron pan left out in the sun. The ring of mountains then traps the heat, with hardly any wind to carry it off.

The hottest patch of all is a dark plateau in the north of the Lut, Gandom Beryan, whose Persian name means Toasted Wheat. Legend says a load of wheat was once simply left lying on it, and within days the heat of the ground had scorched it black. The tale is folk legend, not measurement, but it suits the place.

Between June and October, fierce winds from the northwest blast sand against the Lut's rock and carve it into long, parallel ridges, kaluts to the locals and yardangs to geologists, up to 75 metres tall and running for more than 150 kilometres. Seen from above, their endless ranks of ridges and hollows look like the streets and towers of a ruined metropolis, and the region is nicknamed the abandoned city of ghosts.

When UNESCO listed the Lut as a World Heritage Site in July 2016, it was a first for Iran, for every Iranian site before it, from palaces and mosques to ancient cities such as Persepolis, had honoured human culture. The Lut became Iran's first natural site, chosen to protect the land itself.

the-maldives-and-coral-atolls-darwins-th.context_blurb:
Off the southwest tip of India, some 1,200 small coral islands make up the Maldives, strung on rings of reef across the Indian Ocean. A turquoise lagoon sits inside each ring, and the white sand barely clears the waves. How such rings of coral came to stand alone in the deep ocean was a puzzle that Charles Darwin set out to solve.

No nation on Earth sits lower: on average the Maldives stands only 1.5 metres higher than the sea, and its highest natural ground, on Addu Atoll, reaches only about 2.4 metres. A resort's 5.1-metre mound, sold as the country's highest peak, is an artificial dune. Each ring of reef around a lagoon is an atoll, and the English word comes from atholhu in Dhivehi, the language Maldivians speak.

Darwin gave his answer in 1842, in his first book, The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs. A volcanic island once rose where each atoll now lies, with a coral reef fringing its shore. Over ages the volcano gradually sank under the waves, while the coral kept building upward toward the sunlight it needs, until only a ring of living reef marked where the island had stood.

Coral reefs filled Darwin with awe. On the Keeling atoll in 1836 he marvelled that tiny, tender animals had heaped up the whole vast reef. Writing up the journey in his book The Voyage of the Beagle, Darwin said that travellers boast of the huge size of the Pyramids of Egypt and other great ruins, yet even the greatest of them looks trifling beside these mountains of stone.

Darwin had the theory before the proof. In November 1835, sailing on HMS Beagle, he studied the reef ringing the lush island of Tahiti and sketched the whole sinking-island idea there, and it was April 1836 before the ship came to a real atoll, the Keeling or Cocos Islands, where he could test it.

The proof waited more than a century. Drill holes at Funafuti in the 1890s and at Bikini in 1947 stopped short, still in coral. In 1952 at Enewetak Atoll, a drill bored through some 1,300 to 1,400 metres of coral, about 4,200 to 4,600 feet, and struck dark volcanic basalt: the drowned volcano Darwin had predicted.

A living atoll can grow upward only so fast, so the Maldives would be among the first nations to feel any rise in the sea. In October 2009 President Mohamed Nasheed and his ministers put on scuba gear and met as a cabinet about 5 metres underwater, signing a message for the Copenhagen climate summit, the first such stunt by any government.

the-mariana-trench-challenger-deep.context_blurb:
In the western Pacific, east of the Philippines, the seafloor drops into the Mariana Trench, the deepest gash on the planet. At its bottom lies the Challenger Deep, close to 11 kilometres down, a cold, black place under crushing water that only a handful of people have ever visited.

The Challenger Deep bottoms out at about 10,935 metres, while Mount Everest is 8,849 metres tall, so if you dropped the mountain in, its summit would still lie about 2 kilometres underwater. The deep lies roughly 300 kilometres southwest of Guam, the largest of the Mariana Islands and the nearest sizeable inhabited land.

The name comes from a ship. In 1872 the Royal Navy fitted out HMS Challenger as a floating laboratory and sent it on a four-year voyage to measure the depths of the world's oceans. On 23 March 1875, over this trench, the crew of HMS Challenger let down a weighted line about 8,184 metres to the bottom, the deepest reading of the voyage, and the deepest point on Earth was later named for the ship. The trench runs about 2,550 kilometres but is only about 69 kilometres wide, and seen from above it curves across the seafloor in a crescent.

For 85 years no one reached the bottom. Then on 23 January 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste, a small steel ball hung beneath a float of fuel, down through nearly five hours of darkness, and became the first people ever to reach the floor of the deepest place on the planet. For 52 years they were the only ones. On the way down a loud crack rang through the cabin, as the outer Plexiglas viewport window split under about 16,000 pounds per square inch, but the two men kept sinking anyway. The crack and the silt they stirred up held them to about 20 minutes on the bottom.

On 26 March 2012 the film director James Cameron, maker of Titanic and Avatar, dived alone in the Deepsea Challenger to about 10,908 metres, the deepest solo dive ever, and spent some three hours on the floor.

Down there the water presses at about 1,086 bar, some 1,072 times the pressure at sea level, or about 8 tons on every square inch, like balancing a full-grown elephant on your thumbnail. Sunlight never gets that far down, so no plant or alga can live there. Trench animals depend instead on marine snow, a slow, steady sprinkle of dead plankton and other leftovers drifting down from the bright surface waters.

Here the ancient Pacific Plate, old and chilled and heavy, dives under the smaller Mariana Plate and sinks back into the mantle, and geologists call this swallowing of one plate by another subduction. As the diving plate goes down, water is squeezed out of it and rises through cracks into the mantle rock above. That water turns the rock into serpentine mud, which oozes up through faults and has built at least 19 great mud volcanoes along the edge of the trench, erupting serpentine mud instead of lava. Microbes that live without sunlight feed on what they bring up.

the-matterhorn.context_blurb:
On the border of Switzerland and Italy, above the Swiss village of Zermatt, the Matterhorn rises to 4,478 metres as an almost perfect pyramid of rock. It is the most famous mountain shape in Europe, and the model for the Toblerone chocolate logo.

Its four steep faces point almost exactly north, east, south and west, each turned toward its own point of the compass, three on the Swiss side and the south face looking into Italy.

The peak was never pushed up as a spike: over millions of years, four glaciers gnawed bowl-shaped hollows into four sides of the mountain at once, grinding away everything around it until only its hard core stood, with knife-edge ridges meeting at a point. Geologists call a peak carved this way a horn, and a four-faced one is so typical that they speak of the Matterhorn type.

Stranger still, the summit is not European rock. Its top thousand metres or so is gneiss from a slice of the African plate, thrust across Europe as the two continents met and the ancient Tethys Ocean closed, so the top of this Swiss peak is a piece of Africa.

On 14 July 1865, on Edward Whymper's ninth attempt, his party of seven became the first to reach the summit. On the descent Douglas Hadow, the novice of the group, lost his footing and dragged three others off the ridge. The rope joining those four to the three above snapped, and the four fell about 4,000 feet down the north face. That rope was the oldest and weakest the party carried, brought along only as a reserve. Whymper and two guides, the Taugwalders, survived, and in his book Scrambles Amongst the Alps he warned that courage and strength are worth nothing without prudence.

In the heatwave of 2003, about 1,500 cubic metres of rock, as much as four houses, broke off the Hörnli ridge without warning, and helicopters lifted some 90 climbers to safety. The culprit was thawing permafrost: for thousands of years, ice frozen into the mountain's cracks had cemented the rock together, and in the heat it gave way.

Sensors show the summit is never still: it shakes far harder than the foot of the mountain, up to fourteen-fold, ringing like a slow tuning fork. Some of the shaking comes from earthquakes, but much of it is microseism, a faint, endless trembling of the ground made when ocean waves crash on distant coasts and send vibrations through the Earth.

the-meander-and-the-oxbow-lake.context_blurb:
Across a flat valley floor, a river rarely runs straight. The lower Mississippi, winding through the American South to the Gulf of Mexico, swings in great looping curves, and the same physics carves loops deep into solid rock in the canyons of Utah and Arizona.

On every bend the water runs fastest around the outside and gnaws at the bank, while on the inside it slows and drops sand, and so, bend by bend over centuries, a straight river grows into sweeping curves called meanders. The word comes from the Maiandros, today's Büyük Menderes in Turkey, a river famous for its bends.

A bend can loop so tightly that only a narrow neck of land divides its two arms, and when a flood bursts across that neck the river takes the shortcut, leaving the old loop behind as an oxbow lake. The name comes from the U-shaped wooden collar that curved around an ox's neck in a yoke.

The still lake slowly fills in, turning to swamp and at last to dry ground, and all that remains is a meander scar, a ghostly curve traced across the floodplain.

At Utah's Goosenecks, the San Juan River loops tightly 300 metres down between sheer stone walls, travelling more than six miles to advance just one and a half. Long ago it wandered across low, flat land; then the Monument Upwarp slowly lifted the region, and the river sawed straight down to keep pace. Bends engraved into bedrock this way are entrenched meanders, and the Goosenecks are the finest example on Earth.

Near the town of Page, Arizona, at Horseshoe Bend, the green Colorado River curls nearly all the way around a sandstone butte, 300 metres below the rim; uplift some 5 to 6 million years ago trapped it and forced it to cut down. One day the river will saw through the thin neck of rock and abandon the loop, leaving a natural rock bridge spanning the gap, the same shortcut that strands an oxbow lake, done in stone.

Beside today's Lake Powell in Utah, the Colorado has already done it. A few thousand years ago it cut through the neck of a loop, cutting 6 miles off its course, and left an empty stone moat circling a tall mesa. Geologists named such a stranded, dried-up loop in rock after this very place: a rincon. From space it looks like a doughnut dropped in the desert, an oxbow fossilised in rock.

the-mekong.context_blurb:
The Mekong is the great river of mainland Southeast Asia. It rises on the Tibetan Plateau and runs for thousands of kilometres through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam to the South China Sea, a highway, a frontier and a rice bowl all at once.

In the heart of Cambodia, a short river called the Tonlé Sap links the huge Tonlé Sap lake to the Mekong, and for half the year it drains the lake south-east into the big river, but then it turns around and runs backwards, filling the lake. It is one of the only rivers on Earth that switches direction twice a year.

The monsoon does it: from about June, heavy monsoon rains soak the whole Mekong basin, and the swollen river rises until its level tops the Tonlé Sap's mouth and the weight of water forces the smaller river backwards. Tides have nothing to do with it, and the flow turns again when the rains ease around October.

In southern Vietnam the Mekong splits into many arms on its way to the sea, and the Vietnamese call it Sông Cửu Long, the Nine Dragons River, for those winding arms. Upstream it has other names: in China it is the Lancang, and in Thailand and Laos Mae Nam Khong, Mother of Water.

In the dry months Tonlé Sap lake holds only about a metre of water over some 2,700 square kilometres. The reversed flood pours in for months, and at its peak the lake spreads to about 16,000 square kilometres, nearly six times bigger, and 9 to 14 metres deep, drowning the forest around its shore.

In southern Laos, near the Cambodian border, the Mekong spreads to about 14 kilometres across, its widest point, and braids around thousands of sandy and rocky islands that the Lao call Si Phan Don, the 4,000 Islands.

Just below them the river crashes through a cluster of rocky islets as Khone Phapheng Falls, barely 20 metres high but about 10.8 kilometres wide from one edge of their channels to the other, the widest falls in the world. That barrier of rapids means the Mekong can never be sailed all the way up into China.

In the 1890s the French kept failing to steam their boats up past the falls. So they built a railway over Don Det and Don Khon, two of the islands: boats were hauled out of the water, carried round the falls on rails and floated again above them. The line ran from 1893 to 1940, the first railway in Laos.

the-mid-atlantic-ridge-where-the-seafloo.context_blurb:
An enormous chain of underwater mountains, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, splits the Atlantic down its centre, from the far north almost to Antarctica. Along it new ocean floor is being born, and in one place, Iceland, the ridge climbs out of the sea so that you can walk across it.

The ridge is one stretch of Earth's longest mountain chain, a single volcanic seam some 65,000 kilometres long that circles nearly the whole globe, and almost all of it lies hidden underwater on the seafloor. Hardly any explorer has ever seen it.

The ridge mostly lies about 2.5 kilometres down, but in Iceland eruptions have stacked up rock until the boundary between the plates runs over dry land. At Thingvellir it opens into cliffs and fissures you can walk through, such as the great gorge Almannagjá. The plates on either side drift apart about 2.5 centimetres a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow, so the Atlantic widens at that crawl every year. As they part, molten rock rises from deep below to fill the opening and hardens into fresh crust, an endless manufacturing of ocean floor called seafloor spreading.

In Thingvellir lake, the flooded fissure of Silfra is filled with water of such clarity that divers appear to hang in the air as they glide through the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates. The boundary is really a broad zone of cracks, and Silfra is one of them. Its water starts as meltwater from Langjökull, Iceland's second-largest glacier, about 50 kilometres away, and seeps underground through porous lava for 30 to 100 years, filtered clean enough to drink.

In that same rift, in the year 930, Icelanders founded the Althing, an assembly that met there nearly every year until 1798, and it is among the oldest parliaments on Earth still going.

Just after 7 in the morning on 14 November 1963, the cook of the fishing boat Ísleifur II saw dark smoke rising off Iceland's south coast, where a volcano was erupting from the seafloor 130 metres down, and over the following days a brand-new island, Surtsey, rose out of the waves. Surtsey has been off limits since 1965 to everyone but a few scientists, and keeping boots off the raw rock lets them watch living things move onto brand-new land from the very start. The first plant, sea rocket, sprouted in 1965, and the island became a World Heritage Site in 2008.

The ridge's great secret was found on paper. In the 1950s the American geologist Marie Tharp, working with Bruce Heezen, built the first true map of the Atlantic floor out of ships' depth soundings, and along the ridge's crest she traced a deep rift valley running down its spine. It was a key clue that the plates were pulling apart, and a cornerstone of plate tectonics.

Why does Iceland alone rise into daylight? It gets a double dose of magma, because it sits on the spreading ridge and, at the same time, right over a deep-seated mantle hotspot, a plume of heat from far below. That double supply has piled the ridge into a plateau. Few places on Earth erupt so often: Iceland bursts out about every three or four years, and in recorded history it has poured out roughly a third of all the basalt lava erupted on the planet.

the-mississippi.context_blurb:
The Mississippi drains the heart of the United States, running 2,350 miles from the north woods of Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico. Its basin stretches from the Rockies to the Appalachians, and along the way the river loops, wanders, builds new land and sometimes rewrites the map.

It begins as a stream you can wade, a ribbon of water just a few strides across, trickling out of Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota. The explorer Henry Schoolcraft named the lake in 1832 by splicing two Latin words, veritas, truth, and caput, head, to mean true head.

Lower down, on the flat floodplain of the American South, it refuses the direct route to the sea and coils in great lazy loops called meanders, travelling miles sideways for every mile it gains toward the sea. The word comes from the winding Menderes River in Turkey.

A meander never sits still. The current runs fastest around the outer bank of each bend and cuts it away, while sand piles up on the slow inside, and that lopsided wear makes every loop crawl sideways across the plain. When a flood carves a straighter path across a loop's neck, the river abandons the old bend and leaves behind a quiet, curved oxbow lake beside the main channel. Louisiana and Arkansas are dotted with them.

The grandest is Lake Chicot in southeast Arkansas, a C-shaped ribbon of water about 22 miles long that marks the river's course of some 600 years ago, the largest oxbow lake in North America.

At Head of Passes, near its mouth, the river splits three ways, into Pass a Loutre, South Pass and Southwest Pass, each riding out into the Gulf on its own finger of mud, so instead of a neat triangle the delta splays like a bird's foot.

Rain falling on parts of 31 states and two provinces of Canada ends up in the Mississippi, a basin of about 1.2 million square miles, some 40 percent of the continental United States. Only the Amazon and the Congo drain bigger basins, which makes the Mississippi's the third-largest on Earth.

In the winter of 1811 and 1812, violent earthquakes struck near New Madrid, Missouri. In northwestern Tennessee the shaking sank a stretch of forest, the Mississippi rushed in, and Reelfoot Lake was born, where the stumps of drowned bald cypresses still rise from the water.

The quakes came as three huge shocks of about magnitude 7, and boatmen swore the river ran backward, upstream, for hours. They were right, for a while: the shaking heaved up the riverbed and set off great sloshing waves that pushed the current the wrong way for a few hours.

The river still jumps its banks. In an 1881 flood it tore a new channel past Kaskaskia, once the capital of Illinois. The town still belongs to Illinois, but it now sits on the river's west bank, and the only road in runs through Missouri.

the-monsoon-reversal-and-meghalayas-wett.context_blurb:
Every year the winds over India turn around. In summer they blow in from the warm sea, loaded with water, and soak the land for months; in winter they reverse and blow dry back out to sea. Nowhere does the summer rain fall harder than in Meghalaya's Khasi Hills, in India's far northeast near Bangladesh.

Up in those hills the village of Mawsynram, home to about 1,300 Khasi people, catches around 11,872 millimetres of rain a year, almost 39 feet, and since 1985 Guinness has named it the rainiest place on Earth where people live. A few rainforest towns in Colombia claim even more. Near Cherrapunji, that endless rain feeds Nohkalikai Falls, an unbroken column of water plunging 340 metres into a turquoise pool, the tallest plunge waterfall in India.

Why do the winds flip? Each summer the Indian landmass warms more quickly than the sea around it, so hot air rises over the land and leaves low pressure behind, and moist ocean air rushes in to fill it: the summer monsoon. In winter the land cools first, and dry air flows back out to sea. The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mawsim, season, because Arab sailors named the winds that changed with the time of year and rode them across the Indian Ocean and home again.

Cherrapunji holds the record for a single year: in the twelve months after August 1860 it received 26,470 millimetres, about 86 feet of rain, the most ever measured anywhere in one year. July 1861 alone brought some 9,300 millimetres, the wettest month on record.

Meghalaya is so wet because the Khasi Hills stand like an east-west wall across the path of the monsoon's Bay of Bengal branch, so moist air off the bay is forced up over the hills, cools and wrings out its water. Geographers call this relief rain. The British wrote the town's name as Cherrapunji, but its true Khasi name is Sohra, which officials heard as Cherra, with punji, a cluster of villages, tacked on by Bengali lowlanders. Meghalaya officially brought back the name Sohra in 2007.

Across India, farmers watch the sky for the burst, the day the monsoon rains finally arrive. They normally reach Kerala, at India's southern tip, around 1 June, then roll north to cover the whole country by mid-July. With over half of India's cropland fed only by rain, one governor of India's central bank called the monsoon the country's real finance minister.

Khasi villagers raise bridges that are alive. They guide the hanging aerial roots of the rubber fig across streams, season after season, until they twine together into a path, and unlike wood, a living root bridge keeps growing stronger, lasting by some accounts several hundred years.

Sohra has a cruel paradox: a town among the rainiest anywhere runs out of water to drink in each dry season. Its forests have been cut down, so the rain pours straight off the bare slopes and washes the soil away instead of soaking in, and in winter people must trek far to fetch water.

The most celebrated root bridge, the Umshiang below the village of Nongriat, some 180 to 200 years old and about 30 metres long, is a double-decker: its builders trained the roots along hollow trunks of betel-nut palm, then grew a second walkway of roots directly above the first.

To the Khasi a root bridge is a sacred inheritance, not just a path. They link it to an old legend of the jingkieng ksiar, a gleaming ladder of gold that, at the dawn of the world, connected heaven and earth.

the-mystery-eruptions-reading-earths-ash.context_blurb:
Some of the biggest volcanic eruptions in human history happened where no one wrote them down, or where the record was lost. Yet each one left a fingerprint in the ice at the poles, and scientists have learned to read that frozen archive layer by layer, like detectives working a cold case.

A great eruption hurls sulfur gas high into the sky, the winds spread it around the world, and it turns to sulfate and falls on the ice sheets, so each year's snow in Greenland and Antarctica locks in a sulfur spike for every big blast. The largest such spike in some 7,000 years sits near the year 1257.

Trekkers on Lombok, in Indonesia, spend days reaching Segara Anak, a crater lake about 200 metres deep in the hollow that remained after an earlier peak exploded in 1257, and beside it rises Mount Rinjani, Lombok's tallest peak and Indonesia's second-highest volcano.

For 750 years no one knew which volcano made the 1257 spike, until in 2013 the geographer Franck Lavigne and his team compared the chemistry of microscopic glass grains trapped in the polar ice with ash on Lombok and found the culprit: Mount Samalas.

The people of Lombok had known all along. The Babad Lombok, a chronicle written on palm leaves, records that when Samalas fell, its avalanches of hot rock swallowed Pamatan, the royal capital of the Lombok kingdom. The city's ruins have never been found, but the chronicle and the ice tell the same story.

For about a year and a half from AD 536, a weird haze darkened the sun over Europe and Asia. The Byzantine writer Procopius said the sun shone dimly, like the moon, and snow fell in summer as famine spread. Ice cores now show that a colossal volcanic eruption caused it, though which volcano is still argued over: a northern one at high latitude, perhaps in Iceland, is a leading suspect.

Far older and larger was Lake Toba on Sumatra, which erupted about 74,000 years ago in the biggest blast in nearly 2 million years. Stanley Ambrose and others proposed the Toba bottleneck, the idea that the disaster crashed the human population to just a few thousand people. It is hotly debated, since stone tools at Jwalapuram in India look almost unchanged above and below the Toba ash, a hint that people there survived.

the-named-winds-mistral-sirocco-harmatta.context_blurb:
Some winds are so strong, so regular or so strange that the people who live with them gave them names, like characters in a story. Around the Mediterranean and the Sahara, these named winds shape farming, painting, war and even the health of the Amazon.

In Provence, in southern France, the mistral pours cold and dry through the Rhône valley toward the sea, averaging about 50 kilometres an hour on 100 to 150 days a year, and its name means masterly in Provençal, the master wind.

At Arles in 1888, Vincent van Gogh worked in the open air while the mistral howled. To stop it from carrying off his work, he hammered iron pegs into the earth and tied his easel's legs to them with rope. He loved the clean, clear light the wind left behind once it had scoured every cloud from the sky.

From the south comes the sirocco, a hot, dusty wind off the Sahara that gathers moisture over the Mediterranean and drops the desert dust as red blood rain on southern Italy, sometimes tinting Alpine snow orange. In Venice it helps pile up the acqua alta floods.

Across West Africa the harmattan blows from late November until March, dry and from the north-east, carrying Saharan dust as far as the coast of the Gulf of Guinea, and after the sticky tropical heat it feels so refreshing that people nickname it the Doctor. Its haze can ground flights, and its humidity can fall below 15 percent, cracking lips.

In Egypt the khamsin roars up from the south each spring, scorching and full of sand, and its name is Arabic for fifty, for the roughly fifty days of March, April and May when it keeps returning. It can push the thermometer up by 20 °C within a couple of hours, and it has choked whole armies, Napoleon's in 1798 among them.

Near Trieste and along the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, cold air heaps up behind the mountains until it pours over and tumbles down onto the warm Adriatic, and this is the bora, named for Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind. It is a katabatic wind, dense air sliding downhill under its own weight, and in December 1998 one gust hit 248 kilometres an hour on the Maslenica Bridge.

Winds carry Saharan dust to astonishing places. The dustiest spot on Earth is the Bodélé Depression in the southern Sahara, the dry bed of ancient Mega-Lake Chad, whose floor is made of the silica skeletons of long-dead microorganisms. Winds funnelled between the Tibesti and Ennedi mountains loft over 700,000 tons of it on a single day.

Some of that dust crosses the Atlantic and feeds the Amazon. The rainforest's soil is poor in phosphorus, and its rivers carry it off more quickly than fallen leaves can put it back. NASA satellites found that about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust settle on the Amazon each year, bringing some 22,000 tons of phosphorus, close to what the forest loses.

the-namib.context_blurb:
The Namib runs nearly 2,000 kilometres down the Atlantic coast of Namibia in southern Africa: red dunes, gravel plains, fog banks and a shore of shipwrecks. A cold ocean current offshore keeps it almost rainless, and its plants and animals survive by tricks found nowhere else.

The cold Benguela current chills the sea air and wrings out its moisture before it reaches land, and the Namib has been arid for 55 million years at the very least, which makes it the oldest desert on Earth. The Nama people, who have herded goats along its edges for centuries, named it in their click language, and Namib means a vast place, or a place where there is nothing.

At Sossusvlei, star-shaped dunes rise past 300 metres, and the tallest, about 325 metres, is nicknamed Big Daddy, among the highest dunes on Earth. Climbers sink to their ankles all the way up. The dunes glow orange-red at sunrise because every grain wears a coat of iron oxide, rust, which deepens with age, so the oldest dunes are the reddest. Dune 45, the famous ridge beside the road, is built of sand some 5 million years old.

The western Namib gets almost no true rain, only 5 to 10 millimetres a year, but the cold current breeds thick sea fog that rolls inland on over 180 days in a year, and the whole web of desert life drinks from it.

In Deadvlei, a white clay pan ringed by orange dunes, stands a grove of black, twisted camelthorn trees that died some 600 to 900 years ago after moving dunes blocked the water that reached the pan. They are not petrified: the wood has simply dried out, scorched dark by the sun, and the air is far too dry for anything to rot it.

In 1908 the railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond in the sand and showed his inspector, August Stauch, setting off a rush. A showy German town, Kolmanskop, grew up among the dunes, with a ballroom, a tram and the first X-ray station in the southern hemisphere. The diamonds ran out, the town was abandoned by 1956, and today sand pours through its doorways.

The Namib's northern shore, the Skeleton Coast, is littered with whale and seal bones and the rusting hulls of ships wrecked in cold fog on hidden reefs, and the San people called it the Land God Made in Anger. Portuguese sailors called it the Gates of Hell. In thick fog on 5 September 1909 the German steamer Eduard Bohlen ran aground there. Since then blowing sand has buried the beach and the shoreline has crept out to sea, so her rusting hull now sits some 400 metres inland, a ship marooned among the dunes.

On the gravel plains grows the Welwitschia, found only in the Namib, which can live 1,000 to 2,000 years. In all that time it grows only two leaves, leathery straps up to 4 metres long that keep growing from the base while the wind shreds their ends into ribbons.

Thousands of bare rings dot the Namib's grassy plains, fairy circles a few metres wide, each fringed with taller grass and living out a cycle of 30 to 60 years. Scientists have argued over them for more than a decade: Norbert Juergens blames sand termites eating the grass roots, while Stephan Getzin argues that the grasses arrange themselves to share scarce water. Neither camp has yet proven its case, and the question remains open.

the-nile.context_blurb:
Egypt is nearly all desert, yet a thin green ribbon of farmland runs the length of the country, hugging the banks of a single river. The Nile rises in the lakes and highlands of east Africa and flows thousands of kilometres north to a vast delta on the Mediterranean, and Egyptian life always followed its rhythm.

The Greek historian Herodotus, writing around 450 BC, argued that without the river's water and mud there would be no Egypt at all, only Sahara, and he called Egypt the gift of the Nile.

The Nile is one of the few great rivers that flows north, from the highlands of the south down to the Mediterranean, so Egyptians called the upstream south Upper Egypt and the downstream north Lower Egypt. It is the reverse of what a map suggests. Before the dams, each summer the flood laid a new layer of dark silt across the fields, and the Egyptians named their fertile valley Kemet, the Black Land, after that mud. The dead desert beyond was Deshret, the Red Land. The water itself fell as rain far away: the steady, year-round White Nile pours out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, far to the south, deep inside Africa.

The Egyptians counted not four seasons but three, each named for what the river was doing, and the first and most important was Akhet, the flood, from about mid-June to mid-October, when water and fresh silt buried the fields. After it came a season of growing and a season of harvest.

The flood was never the same twice, so priests built nilometers, stone steps, pillars or shafts reaching the water, marked in cubits. Reading the flood's height early in the year let them forecast how big the coming harvest would be, plenty or famine. South of Aswan, boats met six cataracts, stretches of whitewater over hard rock, shallow and choked with boulders, which stopped boats and formed the ancient border between Egypt and Nubia. The second now lies drowned under Lake Nasser.

The Nile begins as two rivers. The clear White Nile runs steady all year; the muddy Blue Nile comes crashing out of highlands drenched by the monsoon, bringing the summer flood. They meet at Khartoum, capital of Sudan, and flow side by side, unmixed, for a stretch below the city. Together, the Atbara and the Blue Nile bring most of the flood's water and about 97 to 98 percent of its silt, stripped from the Ethiopian highlands, so Egypt's famous farmland is really soil washed down from Ethiopia.

Near the sea the river splits into a web of channels and marshes and builds a wide triangle of fresh land, which the Greeks named after the triangular capital letter of their alphabet, delta, and every river mouth built that way has carried the name since.

For over two thousand years the Nile was crowned the longest river on Earth, at about 6,650 kilometres, but a 2014 Brazilian study measured the Amazon at about 6,992 kilometres, depending on which far headwater counts as the source. So the title is now genuinely disputed, though by volume there is no contest: the Nile carries only about 1 percent of the Amazon's water.

The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, ended the flood. Lake Nasser behind it traps about 98 percent of the Nile's silt, some 100 million tons a year, so farmers must buy fertilizer instead. Starved of new mud, the delta is eroding and sinking: sea currents wear its coast away faster than the river can rebuild it, while its old clay soils settle and the sea rises.

the-norwegian-maelstroms-saltstraumen-an.context_blurb:
Along Norway's Arctic coast, the Atlantic tide is squeezed through narrow gaps between islands and whipped into some of the fiercest currents and whirlpools on Earth. Sailors feared them for centuries, and they gave English one of its most dramatic words.

Near the town of Bodø lies Saltstraumen, measured as the strongest tidal current anywhere in the world: as the tide turns, four times daily, the sea is forced through a gap barely 150 metres across at up to 40 kilometres an hour.

The racing water coils into whirlpools as wide as 10 metres and as deep as 5, big enough to swallow a small boat, so local boaters cross only at slack water, when the current briefly rests. Whirlpools like these gave English the word maelstrom, from Dutch and Norse malen, to grind, and straum, stream: a grinding stream.

The strait looks modest, but as much as 400 million cubic metres of seawater pours through it in each six-hour run of the tide. All that water has to pass the narrow gap in the same span of time, so it must speed up, and that is what turns an ordinary tide into Saltstraumen's ferocious flow.

Farther north, off the southern tip of the Lofoten Islands, churns the Moskstraumen. In 1841 Edgar Allan Poe made it the setting of A Descent into the Maelström, the tale of a fisherman dragged down its spinning funnel who barely escapes, and the story carried the word maelstrom into English. Jules Verne used it again in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas.

Unlike most great whirlpools, the Moskstraumen forms out in the open sea, between the islands of Mosken and Moskenesøya, not in a narrow channel, which made it all the more baffling to sailors. Modern surveys put its current at 3 to 5 metres a second; older accounts wildly exaggerated its power.

the-nubian-pyramids-of-mero.context_blurb:
Far up the Nile, in the desert of Sudan, steep little pyramids crowd the skyline at Meroe, royal burial ground of the Kingdom of Kush. Kush was a great African civilization in its own right, a rival and sometimes a ruler of Egypt, with its own gods, its own script and its own way of building for the dead.

The country with the most pyramids is not Egypt: about 255 ancient pyramids stand along the Nile in Sudan, more than double the roughly 120 in Egypt, in three great royal fields, El-Kurru, Nuri and Meroe.

Their builders were the Kingdom of Kush, also called Nubia, and earlier Kushite kings from Napata even conquered Egypt and ruled it as its 25th Dynasty, the Black Pharaohs, beginning with King Piye around 727 BC. Around 590 BC the capital moved south to Meroe, which became Kush's greatest royal cemetery.

Nubian pyramids look nothing like the giants of Giza: their sides rise at about 70 degrees, far steeper than Egypt's 40 to 50, from small bases, so they stand only 6 to 30 metres high, tall and narrow like needles packed close together. They worked differently too. A Kushite king lay in a set of chambers carved into the rock below ground, reached by a stairway. The pyramid was built right on the ground above that tomb, a marker standing over the grave rather than a container holding it.

Many of Meroe's grandest pyramids covered women, for Kush was ruled at times by powerful queens who held the throne themselves. One of them, Amanishakheto, a queen ruling in her own name, was buried early in the 1st century AD under her own steep pyramid, N6, with a hoard of gold jewellery. King Piye loved his horses so dearly that at El-Kurru he was buried beside four of his favourites, standing upright, the first royal horse burial in the Nile valley in more than 500 years.

Kushite monuments carry the word kandake, the royal title of a ruling queen, borne by many women over the centuries. Greek and Roman writers mistook it for one woman's personal name, which is why Acts, in the Bible, calls the Kushite ruler whose treasurer Philip baptized Candace.

Today dozens of Meroe's pyramids stand oddly flat-topped. In 1834 the Italian Giuseppe Ferlini blasted about forty of them with explosives, tearing each down from the summit, hunting for gold hidden deep inside. At Queen Amanishakheto's pyramid he found it: a royal hoard of bracelets, rings and amulets, now in museums in Berlin and Munich.

In 1910 archaeologists at Meroe dug up a bronze head of the Roman emperor Augustus. Kushite forces under Queen Amanirenas had hacked it off a statue when they raided Roman Aswan around 25 BC, then buried it under a temple step so that worshippers would trample Rome underfoot. Its inlaid eyes of glass and calcite survived, and after 2,000 years in the ground they still gaze out with a startlingly lifelike stare. The head is now in the British Museum.

At Naqa the Kushite kings built a Lion Temple to Apedemak, their own lion-headed war god, who has no counterpart in Egypt; its carvings show him lion-headed, and one gives him three heads and four arms.

Meroe was also one of the ancient world's great ironworking centres, and centuries of furnaces left huge black mounds of slag around the city. Struck by them, the scholar A. H. Sayce called Meroe the Birmingham of Africa, after the English industrial city.

Kush even had a script of its own, Meroitic, about two dozen signs used from the 3rd century BC. Around 1909 Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out the sound of every sign, so today a scholar can read any inscription aloud, letter by letter. Yet texts pairing Meroitic with a known language are so rare that the language itself is still only partly understood.

the-pacific-ocean-and-point-nemo.context_blurb:
The Pacific is the giant among the planet's oceans, stretching from the Arctic to the Antarctic and from Asia to the Americas. Somewhere in its empty south lies the loneliest spot on Earth, and along its edges the ground shakes and the mountains smoke.

The Pacific Ocean covers about 165 million square kilometres, while every continent and island together covers only about 149 million, so all of Earth's dry land would fit inside it with room to spare. It is crowded with islands too, coral rings and volcanic peaks from the Aleutians to New Zealand, more than 25,000 of them, a greater number than every other ocean put together.

Its gentle name came from Ferdinand Magellan: in 1520, on the first voyage around the world, after a brutal passage past the stormy southern tip of South America, he broke out onto calm water and called it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea. The calm was partly luck.

Far out in the South Pacific lies the oceanic pole of inaccessibility, the point farthest from any land, called Point Nemo, and its nearest shores are about 1,670 miles off: Ducie Island in the Pitcairn group, Motu Nui near Easter Island, and Maher Island off Antarctica. Ships and planes rarely pass by. But the International Space Station orbits only about 250 miles up, so when it crosses overhead, the astronauts on board are the nearest people to Point Nemo.

The spot is named for Captain Nemo, the submarine commander of Jules Verne's famous novel, and in Latin nemo means nobody, just what the captain chose to be. The Croatian survey engineer Hrvoje Lukatela pinpointed it by computer in 1992.

Because it is so far from people, space agencies use the sea around Point Nemo as a deliberate crash zone. Close to 300 dead satellites, supply ships and even whole stations have been guided down there since 1971, and engineers call it the spacecraft cemetery. The most famous was the Mir space station, Russia's 130-ton outpost, steered into a blazing re-entry in March 2001 until it came down in flaming pieces near Point Nemo.

Around the ocean's rim runs the Ring of Fire, a horseshoe of trenches and volcanoes about 25,000 miles around, where the ocean floor dives beneath the surrounding continents. It holds about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes, and about 90 percent of all earthquakes strike along it. The Pacific also holds the deepest place in all the oceans, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, about 10,911 metres down, deeper than Everest is tall, and named for HMS Challenger, whose crew first sounded these depths in the 1870s.

the-panama-hat-actually-from-ecuador.context_blurb:
The best-known straw hat on Earth is called the Panama, yet not one has ever been woven in Panama. It is light, fine and cool in the sun, and its true home lies farther south.

Weavers on Ecuador's coast have made these hats by hand for some four centuries, especially in Montecristi and Cuenca, from toquilla straw, the split fibre of a palm-like plant native to that coast.

How did the wrong country get the credit? In the 1800s Panama was a booming crossroads of trade, and Ecuador's hats were sent out through its busy ports to buyers everywhere, so the world named them after the place they came from last. Gold Rush prospectors crossing the isthmus wore them home, and in 1906 a photograph of President Theodore Roosevelt in one at the Panama Canal works made the name stick.

The finest grade is the Montecristi superfino, with up to 3,000 weaves per square inch, which can take a master weaver eight months. Its weave is so fine that a true superfino can be rolled up small enough to pass through a wedding ring. It is said to hold water without leaking, and in 2012 UNESCO honoured the weaving of these hats as living heritage.

the-pantheon-romes-unbeaten-concrete-dom.context_blurb:
In the heart of Rome stands the Pantheon, a temple finished under the emperor Hadrian around AD 128 and still roofed by its original dome. Walk in through its porch and you enter a vast round hall, lit from above, that has amazed architects for nearly 1,900 years.

Nobody has ever beaten its dome: it is still the largest dome of plain concrete, with no steel inside, ever built, and modern domes go bigger only by hiding steel bars in the concrete. The hall has no windows at all, and its only daylight pours in through the oculus, Latin for eye, a round hole about 9 metres across at the very top of the dome, open to the sky.

Rain falls straight through the oculus onto the marble, yet the hall never floods, because the floor rises very slightly in the middle and slopes about 30 centimetres down to small drain holes. That 2nd-century Roman drainage still carries the rain away. The hall also hides a perfect geometry: its height from floor to crown and its width are both 43.3 metres, so a sphere 43.3 metres across would fit exactly inside it.

The porch stands on 16 granite columns, each almost 12 metres tall and weighing 50 to 60 tonnes, and every shaft is one solid piece of stone. The grey ones came from the Mons Claudianus quarry in Egypt's eastern desert and the pink ones from Aswan, floated down the Nile and shipped across the Mediterranean. Inside, the dome is carved with 140 coffers, sunken panels in five rings of 28, and they scoop material out of the ceiling, making the dome far lighter than a solid one would be.

The builders changed the concrete mix with height: heavy travertine chips at the base, then lighter terracotta and tufa, and finally pumice, the lightest volcanic rock, near the oculus. Engineers estimate that a dome of solid heavy concrete would have carried about 80 percent more stress, probably too much to stand.

As Rome fell, popes and princes stripped its temples for stone, and nearly all of them vanished. The Pantheon survived because in AD 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated it as a Christian church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, so it was cared for instead of quarried.

The dome has no steel, no keystone and no central column; where a keystone would sit there is only the open oculus. Its half-sphere shape channels the weight down into the rotunda's own walls, which swell to as much as 6.4 metres thick to carry it.

In the 1600s Pope Urban VIII, a Barberini, had the porch's bronze torn off, and Romans joked that what the barbarians had not done, the Barberini did. Some of it went into cannons, and most famously it became Bernini's baldachin, the towering bronze canopy above the high altar of St Peter's Basilica.

the-pink-fire-on-the-mountains-alpenglow.context_blurb:
On a clear evening in the Alps, the valleys sink into cold blue shade while the highest snows still burn pink. The peaks and the sky opposite the sunset glow with colours that last only minutes, made by the low sun's light travelling a long path through the air.

Above Chamonix, when the sun slips behind the mountains, the top snowfields of Mont Blanc blush pink and orange while the villages are already dark, and climbers call this rosy light on the highest peaks alpenglow, from the German Alpenglühen. Because only the summits catch it, they seem to float.

Turn away from the sunset and look at the sky opposite: a soft pink band glows there, between 10 and 20 degrees up from the horizon, and it is called the Belt of Venus, after the girdle of the goddess Aphrodite, whom the Romans called Venus.

Below the pink lies a darker blue-grey band that climbs as the dusk deepens, and it is the shadow of the Earth itself, rising through the atmosphere as the sun sinks. Astronomers call it the twilight wedge.

In the Dolomites the glow is called enrosadira, the turning-rosy, as the pale crags burn red, then purple. A Ladin legend says the peaks are the rose garden of King Laurin; after his capture, the dwarf king cursed his garden so that no one should see its roses by day or by night. But his curse forgot the twilight, which is neither day nor night, so in the brief glow of every sunrise and sunset the roses still blaze.

the-pink-lakes-hillier-and-retba.context_blurb:
Some lakes are pink, truly pink, and not by any trick of the light. Lake Hillier, on an island off the coast of Western Australia, is a 600-metre pool of bubblegum pink, kept apart from the dark blue Southern Ocean by a thin strip of sand.

Fill a glass from it and the water is still pink, because the colour is alive: tiny microbes that love salt, the alga Dunaliella salina along with pink bacteria and archaea, tint the whole lake.

The alga lives in brine some eight times as salty as seawater, and it shields itself from salt and sun by packing its cells with beta-carotene, the orange pigment of carrots, so richly that no natural source on Earth holds more.

In Senegal, Lake Retba, the Lac Rose, owes its colour to the same alga. Its brine is as much as ten times saltier than seawater, and up to 3,000 workers wade in each day to harvest salt by hand. Before they go in, they rub their skin with shea butter, the fat of the West African shea nut, so the searing brine cannot burn them. When floods diluted the lake in 2022, it briefly turned green.

the-polar-lights-aurora-borealis-and-aus.context_blurb:
On clear, dark winter nights in the far north, curtains of green light ripple and fold across the sky over Yellowknife in Canada, Fairbanks in Alaska and Tromsø in Norway. The aurora borealis, the northern lights, has a southern twin, the aurora australis, and the Sun paints them both.

The light comes from the solar wind, a stream of charged particles blown off the Sun: Earth's magnetic field funnels those particles toward the poles, where they crash into atoms high in the air and make them glow. In Finland the lights are called revontulet, fox fires, after a folk tale of an Arctic fox racing over the snowy fells and flicking sparks into the sky with its tail. In the bone-dry Arctic air, a fox's fur really can throw off tiny static sparks.

The aurora is not scattered at random but rides a ring about 6 degrees of latitude wide around the geomagnetic pole, called the auroral oval, and those three towns sit almost right under it. Stand at the pole itself and you would be inside the ring, seeing less. Most of the aurora glows a soft green about 100 kilometres up, and that green comes from atoms of oxygen struck by the incoming particles. Fairbanks logs over 200 possible aurora nights a year, and on a clear, dark night in season the lights appear about four nights in every five.

During violent solar storms a rare blue-purple fringe can glow along the bottom edge of the aurora, below the green, and that light comes from molecules of nitrogen lower down. High above, beyond 150 to 200 kilometres, a deep red crown may top the display. It is oxygen again, but there the air is so thin that an atom can sit undisturbed for as long as roughly two minutes before it releases its red light. Lower down, collisions snuff the glow before it can appear.

Often the aurora hangs as a quiet green arc for hours, then around local midnight it explodes into twisting curtains for an hour or two. Energy from the Sun has been building up in Earth's magnetic tail and dumps into the upper air all at once, an outburst called an auroral substorm.

In Abisko, a tiny village in Swedish Lapland beside Lake Torneträsk, a patch of clear sky called the blue hole often opens while cloud smothers the region. Abisko sits in the rain shadow of the mountains around it: air rising over the peaks drops its moisture, then sinks dry down the sheltered side and tears a hole in the clouds.

In September 1859 came the Carrington Event, the most powerful geomagnetic storm on record, when the aurora shone so far south that people in Boston could read newspapers outdoors around 1 a.m. The same flood of particles drove electric currents through the long telegraph wires, so some operators unhooked their batteries and went on tapping out messages for a couple of hours, running on electricity from the aurora alone.

While Norway's sky is ablaze with the northern lights, Tasmania's may light up with a southern twin at that very instant, sometimes swirl for swirl. Earth's magnetic field lines arc from the far south to the far north, and one burst of particles slides down both ends of the same line at once, painting twin displays called conjugate auroras.

In about 2016, Albertan sky-watchers in Canada began snapping a mauve band across the sky above a green picket fence of light, and they gave it the name Steve, borrowed from the animated film Over the Hedge. Scientists later turned the name into Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement. A 2018 NASA-led study found that STEVE is not an aurora at all but a river of superheated gas, near 3,000 °C, only about 25 kilometres wide yet hundreds long, streaming west to east at some 6 kilometres a second.

the-red-sea-a-new-ocean-being-born.context_blurb:
The Red Sea runs like a slender finger of ocean between Africa and Arabia, ringed by hot desert and linked to the Indian Ocean by a slim strait in the south. It looks like an ordinary sea, but it is something rarer: a young ocean in the act of being born.

Africa and Arabia are splitting apart along a rift down its middle at about a centimetre a year, a little more in the south, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. Slow as that is, over millions of years it is enough to build an ocean.

Its water is among the saltiest of any sea, around 40 parts per thousand against about 35 for normal seawater, because the desert sun evaporates it fiercely and almost no rivers flow in to replace what is lost.

The Red Sea began opening less than about 45 million years ago, and if the spreading goes on for many millions of years it could widen into a full ocean, just as the Atlantic opened when the supercontinent Pangaea split apart. Geologists call it a baby ocean, one of the few places where you can watch a continent tear into ocean floor.

Its water is usually bright turquoise, so why red? The leading but unsettled answer is blooms of reddish algae, the cyanobacterium Trichodesmium erythraeum, which can stain the water a rusty red-brown as a bloom dies. Another theory holds that red simply meant south in an old way of naming directions by colour.

In Ethiopia's Afar Depression three rifts meet, the Red Sea's, the Gulf of Aden's and the great rift of East Africa, and there, as Arabia pulls away, the African plate itself is cracking into two, the Nubian and Somali plates. That rift runs more than 6,000 kilometres south through Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania.

Two kilometres down, submersibles have found something eerie: lakes on the seabed. These brine pools hold water 3 to 8 times saltier and denser than the sea above, so heavy that it never mixes, with its own shores and slow waves, and with no oxygen it kills any animal that strays in. Mussels and microbial mats crowd their rims, and the Red Sea has about 25 of them.

The richest is the Atlantis II Deep, about 2,000 metres down and close to 68 °C, whose mud holds the largest known metal deposit on any seabed, with copper, cobalt and zinc concentrated about a thousand times beyond ordinary seawater.

As oceans warm, many reefs bleach when the sea gets only slightly warmer than its usual summer high. The reefs of the Gulf of Aqaba, at the Red Sea's northern tip, tolerate water 5 to 7 degrees above their summer maximum and rode out recent record heatwaves without mass bleaching. Scientists think their ancestors came in from the Arabian Sea through the hot southern Red Sea, a natural filter that let only heat-tolerant corals pass.

the-ring-of-fire-a-rim-of-subduction-vol.context_blurb:
A great horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones, some 40,000 kilometres long, wraps around the rim of the Pacific. It runs up through Chile and Peru, along the western edge of North America to Alaska, across the Aleutians, and down past Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia to New Zealand.

This fiery belt is the Ring of Fire. Some 450 volcanoes stand along it, about three-quarters of the planet's active ones. Nine in every ten of the planet's earthquakes happen on this belt as well, including most of the biggest ever recorded, because all around the Pacific, plates of ocean floor are diving and grinding down under the land.

Japan's Mount Fuji, a near-perfect snowy cone 3,776 metres high not far from Tokyo, is a Ring of Fire volcano, rising near where the Pacific Plate dives under Japan, and it is the country's most sacred peak. It last erupted in 1707. High on the frontier between Argentina and Chile, where the Nazca Plate slides under South America and lifts the Andes, stands Ojos del Salado, 6,893 metres high, and since nearby Aconcagua is not a volcano, no volcano on Earth stands higher.

Near its summit, at about 6,480 metres, a small crater lake fed by snowmelt is the highest lake on the planet, higher even than Lake Titicaca. In the Pacific Northwest the Cascade volcanoes, Rainier, Hood and St. Helens among them, are fed by the small Juan de Fuca Plate, which sinks under North America along the Cascadia subduction zone.

When a magnitude-5.1 quake struck Mount St. Helens on 18 May 1980, the mountain's swollen north side broke away in the largest landslide ever recorded, and the volcano blew out sideways, flattening forest across a fan 19 miles long. The summit dropped by about 400 metres.

In April 1815 Mount Tambora, on Sumbawa in Indonesia, produced the mightiest eruption ever recorded, and it cut the mountain down from about 4,300 metres to 2,851, blasting away roughly a third of its height and leaving a crater 6 to 7 kilometres wide. The explosions were heard 2,600 kilometres off. Its ash and sulfur veiled the sun and dropped global temperatures some 0.5 °C, so in 1816 frost and snow struck the Northern Hemisphere in midsummer, and people called it the Year Without a Summer.

Why do subduction zones build volcanoes at all? The diving plate carries seawater and water-bearing minerals down with it, and kilometres below, heat and pressure drive that water out and into the hot mantle rock above. The water lowers that rock's melting point, so solid rock begins to melt, a process called flux melting. The sticky, gassy magma it makes builds the steep, explosive cones of the Ring of Fire.

Hawaii's Mauna Loa is not on the ring at all: it sits over a hotspot in mid-ocean, and its runny basalt oozes out without big explosions, building a broad, gentle shield that makes it the largest volcano anywhere by volume, about 75,000 cubic kilometres.

the-rub-al-khali-empty-quarter.context_blurb:
Across southern Arabia, over parts of Oman, Yemen, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, stretches a desert as big as France, wave after wave of dunes. Almost no one has ever lived there, and even the Bedouin mostly kept to its edges.

Arab travellers named it the Rub' al Khali, the Empty Quarter, the emptiest corner of Arabia. The Sahara is far bigger overall, but it is broken up by rock, gravel and mountains, while the Rub' al Khali is one unbroken expanse of some 650,000 square kilometres, the largest continuous sea of sand on Earth.

From the air its dunes, some nearly 250 metres high, glow a deep red-orange to the horizon, because each grain of sand wears a thin coat of iron oxide.

Above ground it is lifeless, yet the rocks below hold the opposite of emptiness. In 1948 American engineers drilling for the Saudi king found Ghawar, the largest oil field ever found, with some 170 billion barrels, and in 1981 it pumped 5.7 million barrels a day. A second giant, Shaybah, found in 1968, lies deep in the dunes of the Empty Quarter itself.

It was not always dry. In old lakebeds scientists have found hippopotamus teeth, the bones of long-horned cattle and even clam shells. Between about 11,000 and 5,500 years ago, stronger monsoon rains filled the Rub' al Khali with lakes and rivers, a time scientists call Green Arabia. One lake filled a basin of about 1,100 square kilometres, then burst and carved a valley 150 kilometres long.

Harry St John Philby, a British explorer who advised the Saudi king, set off in 1932 to find Wabar, a lost city that legend said God had destroyed for its wickedness. He found no city, but instead a cluster of craters blasted out by a meteorite, the largest about 116 metres wide, strewn with black glass beads fused from the sand by the heat of the impact.

Arabian legend also speaks of Ubar, also called Iram, a wealthy city of the frankincense trade that the sands swallowed. In the 1980s and 1990s the filmmaker Nicholas Clapp and the NASA scientists Ronald Blom and Charles Elachi hunted it from space, using Space Shuttle radar and satellite images to trace old caravan tracks, packed hard by countless camels, that converged on Shisr in Oman. A dig there in 1992 found a fortress that had collapsed into a limestone sinkhole, though whether it is the real Ubar is still disputed.

the-sahara.context_blurb:
The Sahara spreads over some 9.2 million square kilometres of northern Africa, from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. The whole continental United States would fit inside it. It looks timelessly dry, yet its rocks remember lakes, hippos and herds of cattle, and much of it is not sand at all.

It is the biggest hot desert in the world, though not the biggest desert of all, since a desert simply means a place with very little rain, and the frozen deserts of Antarctica and the Arctic are larger still. At midday its sand can heat beyond 80 °C, and a reading of 83.5 °C was once taken on the sand near Port Sudan. An egg white sets at about 70 °C, so the old traveller's saying is true: that sand could fry an egg.

It was not always dry. Beneath the sand lie old lakebeds and the bones of hippos and crocodiles. During the African Humid Period, monsoon rains reached far north and filled the Sahara with lakes and rivers, and it was still green as recently as about 6,000 years ago.

On the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in southeastern Algeria, now bare rock and sand, around fifteen thousand rock paintings and engravings record that green world. The most striking show people driving great herds of cattle, alongside hippos and crocodiles, where only rock and sand survive today. Camels appear only in later scenes, after the land had dried. At Erg Chebbi, near Merzouga in Morocco, visitors ride out to dunes some 150 metres tall and watch them change through the day, glowing from rose pink to deep apricot as the light shifts.

Near Ouadane in Mauritania, a target of concentric rings about 40 kilometres across is visible from orbit, and astronauts use this Eye of the Sahara as a landmark. It is no meteorite crater: about 100 million years ago magma pushed layers of rock up into a dome, and slow erosion later stripped the dome down into rings.

Far in Egypt's southwest lies the Gilf Kebir, a bone-dry plateau. In 1933 the explorer László Almásy came upon a cave there whose walls had been painted some eight thousand years before, crowded with tiny figures who seem to be swimming, a startling sight hundreds of kilometres from any water. Some scholars question that reading, but the cave became famous through The English Patient.

Each year the wind lifts enormous loads of dust off the Sahara and carries them high over the Atlantic. NASA's CALIPSO satellite found about 27.7 million tons crossing each year, carrying some 22,000 tons of phosphorus, and much of it settles on the Amazon rainforest, replacing about as much as the forest loses to rain and floods. The dustiest spot of all is the Bodélé Depression in northern Chad, the dried floor of a once-huge lake, packed with the fossil shells of diatoms, tiny lake plankton rich in phosphorus.

Under the western Sahara lies a buried river, the Tamanrasset, which once ran some 2,600 kilometres from the highlands of Algeria to the Atlantic, and in 2015 radar satellites, whose beams can see through dry sand, traced its hidden path.

Sand seas, the ergs, make up just one part in four of the Sahara, and most of the rest is bare rock plateaus, called hamada, and gravel plains, called reg, with dry riverbeds, salt flats and mountains between. Its highest point is not a dune but Emi Koussi in the Tibesti Mountains of northern Chad, a giant shield volcano about 3,415 metres high, capped by nested collapse craters.

the-sargasso-sea-a-sea-with-no-shores.context_blurb:
Far out in the North Atlantic lies a sea unlike any other: calm, deep blue and warm, with golden-brown seaweed floating across it for miles. Bermuda, near its western edge, is the closest land.

This is the Sargasso Sea, the only sea on Earth with no shore, bounded not by coasts like every other sea but only by open ocean.

Its walls are four currents of the North Atlantic Gyre, turning clockwise around it in one slow loop that traps anything adrift in the calm centre. The western wall is the Gulf Stream, warm enough to carry Caribbean water north past America and out toward Europe. The North Atlantic Current runs along the north, the Canary Current down the east, and the North Equatorial Current along the south.

The seaweed is sargassum, and it never touches the seafloor. It stays afloat on hundreds of tiny gas-filled bladders, berry-like floats called pneumatocysts that dot its fronds. It even reproduces simply by breaking apart.

In September 1492 the ships of Christopher Columbus sailed into the weed, giving the first written account of the Sargasso. His crews feared that so much weed meant shallows and hidden rocks. But when they let down a weighted line it touched no bottom, only deep, open water, for the weed drifts on an ocean miles deep, hundreds of kilometres from any shore.

The Sargasso is also a nursery. European eels leave their rivers and swim 5,000 to 10,000 kilometres across the Atlantic to spawn there and die. The same sea is the birthplace of a second species, the American eel, from the rivers of eastern North America, which makes a shorter crossing of up to about 4,000 kilometres.

For thousands of years no one found an eel egg or a baby eel, because the young drift back from the Sargasso as clear, leaf-shaped larvae that look nothing like eels. Aristotle dissected eel after eel without finding any young and decided that eels simply grew out of the mud, with no parents at all, an idea the world believed for some 2,000 years.

The riddle fell to the Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt, who spent nearly twenty years towing fine nets across the Atlantic and measuring every eel larva he caught. He reasoned that the smallest larvae must lie closest to where they hatched, chased ever-tinier ones across the ocean, and found the very smallest of all in the Sargasso Sea, which he named the eels' birthplace in 1923. Direct proof came only in 2022, when satellite tags followed 26 eels all the way there.

the-savanna-grassland-kept-open-by-fire.context_blurb:
In East Africa the grassland rolls on and on beneath a vast sky, and herds of zebra and wildebeest graze it while lions stalk them. Savannas like this also spread across South America and Australia, and they look like a stable, natural landscape. In fact they are held open, year after year, by flame and grazing.

On Tanzania's Serengeti, said to take its name from the Maasai word for endless plains, the signature tree is the umbrella-thorn acacia, its flat, spreading crown a black silhouette at sunset.

The Serengeti gets about 500 to 1,200 millimetres of rain a year, easily enough to grow forest, yet it stays grassland because fire sweeps across it every dry season, killing young tree seedlings while the grass simply grows back. Grass survives fire and grazing because it keeps its growing tissue, the meristem, down at the base of every blade near the soil, so when the top is grazed, burned or mown, the blade simply pushes up fresh and green. A tree carries its buds up in its branches, right where teeth and flames can reach them.

Half a world away, the Cerrado spreads over roughly one-fifth of Brazil, some 1.9 million square kilometres, and with roughly 10,000 plant species it is the richest savanna on Earth. Corky bark and deep roots carry its trees through the fires.

Across tens of millennia, Aboriginal Australians in the tropical north have set gentle, low fires, burning a mosaic of old and fresh patches so that a wildfire finds too little fuel to grow, and in 1969 the archaeologist Rhys Jones named the practice firestick farming. Reviving it on a large scale has sharply cut the land lost to wildfires.

Across the African savanna rise termite mounds, some over 5 metres tall, and rings of trees and shrubs crowd around them while bare grass stretches between. The colony works and enriches the mound's soil until it holds more water and nutrients than the ground around it, and trees take root there.

Ecologists long assumed that rainfall decides everything: enough rain makes forest, too little makes savanna. But when they mapped how much of Africa south of the Sahara is wooded, they found that over a wide band of rainfall, roughly a metre to two and a half metres a year, the same climate can hold either closed forest or open savanna. Fire and grazing tip the balance: grass feeds the fires that kill tree seedlings, so a burned, grazed patch stays savanna while its unburned neighbour under the same rain closes into forest. Ecologists call these alternative stable states.

the-sea-that-glows-blue-bioluminescent-b.context_blurb:
In a few warm, sheltered bays around the world, the sea comes alive at night. Dip a hand or a paddle and the water lights up blue-green around it in a spreading spray of sparks. Puerto Rico has more of these glowing bays than any other country, and the brightest lies on the island of Vieques.

The glow is alive: Mosquito Bay on Vieques is crowded with billions of dinoflagellates, single-celled plankton that drift in the water and flash the instant they are disturbed. Each one flashes for only about a tenth of a second when jostled, then goes dark, so the light traces your moving hand exactly and dies away just behind it, like a glowing wake.

In 2006 Guinness World Records named Mosquito Bay the brightest glowing bay on the planet. After Hurricane Maria in 2017 the plankton crashed and the bay went dark for months, but within about eight months the glow was back.

Puerto Rico's three glowing bays are Mosquito Bay, Laguna Grande at Fajardo and La Parguera at Lajas, and since swimming is banned in the first two to protect the plankton, La Parguera is the one bay where visitors can still wade into the glow.

Mosquito Bay packs up to 700,000 of these plankton into a single gallon, far more than the open coast outside. Its narrow, twisting S-shaped mouth lets them in but keeps them from washing back out to sea, while the mangroves around the shore feed them.

On the Maldivian island of Vaadhoo, glowing plankton wash ashore after dark, each wave leaves a scatter of blue sparks on the sand, and footprints glow for a moment underfoot, so visitors call the beach the Sea of Stars. It is cold light: inside the plankton a molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen to glow with almost no heat.

Each spring Taiwan's Matsu Islands shine with blue tears, the work of a plankton called Noctiluca scintillans. Researchers keep a wary eye on the blooms, for if the plankton multiply too far they form red tides that strip the oxygen from the water and leave dead zones where fish suffocate. Coastal pollution is making the blooms bigger.

the-sonoran-desert.context_blurb:
The Sonoran Desert spreads over southern Arizona and northwest Mexico, down into Baja California and around the Gulf of California. It is the land of the coyote, the roadrunner and the rattlesnake, and of the giant cacti that have come to stand for the whole American West.

Its emblem is the saguaro, the many-armed giant of postcards and cowboy films, found growing wild in this desert and in no other place on the planet.

A young saguaro is a single column with no arms at all, and it sprouts its first arm only at about 50 to 70 years old, when it may stand three to five metres tall. It can live on to 150 or 200 years. The record saguaro, almost 79 feet tall, grew near Cave Creek, Arizona, until a windstorm brought it down in 1986. Shallow roots and heavy arms leave even giants open to a hard blow.

Where most deserts see a single brief rainy spell or none, the Sonoran is watered twice a year, by gentle Pacific storms from December to March and violent monsoon thunderstorms from July to September, and that double soaking makes it green and crowded with life.

After a downpour a big saguaro drinks in a huge load of water within hours. Its trunk is pleated with 12 to 24 vertical ribs that fan open like an accordion as it swells, so it can hold some 3,000 litres, and water then makes up some 85 to 90 percent of the whole plant's weight.

On the coasts of the Gulf of California grows the cardón, the tallest species of cactus on Earth, its columns reaching nearly 20 metres. With mild winters and two rainy seasons, the Sonoran is also the richest desert in the world for plants, with more than 2,000 kinds.

In Baja California grows the boojum tree, a tall, thin, prickly trunk shaped like a carrot turned upside down. Godfrey Sykes, a botanist from Tucson, gave it its name in 1922, borrowing it from the boojum, a monster in Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem The Hunting of the Snark, the creature that makes people vanish.

Baja's Magdalena plain is home to the creeping devil, a cactus that lies flat and wanders. Its front tip keeps growing forward while the old back end of the plant dies and rots away, so over the years the whole plant travels slowly across the sand.

the-steel-pan-trinidad.context_blurb:
On the Caribbean island of Trinidad, at Carnival, whole orchestras of gleaming steel pans ring out, sweet and bright as bells. The steelpan, national instrument of Trinidad and Tobago, is one of the very few new acoustic instruments invented in the 20th century, and poor young Trinidadians built it out of scrap.

Every pan begins as a discarded 55-gallon oil drum: the maker hammers its top into a shallow dish, then dents and tunes a grid of oval notes, the larger ovals ringing lower and the smaller ones higher.

Its roots lie in a ban. In the 1880s Trinidad's colonial rulers banned the hand drums of African tradition, along with stick-fighting. Trinidadians answered by cutting bamboo stalks to different lengths and stamping them on the ground for a deep, tuned boom, and these tamboo bamboo bands, from the French tambour, drum, kept the rhythm going until the pan arrived.

The pan's home music was calypso, also called kaiso, Trinidad's witty storytelling street song, full of scandal, humour and current events, and the first pan players arranged tunes by calypsonians such as Lord Kitchener.

At the Carnival of 1946, the first since the wartime ban, Winston 'Spree' Simon played his hand-built 14-note pan with the British Governor looking on, and alongside calypso he played Schubert's Ave Maria. He even played the British national anthem, proving that an oil-drum instrument could play anything.

Bands of up to a hundred players each spend weeks polishing a single tune and then battle through the night on the Queen's Park Savannah in Port of Spain, in a contest called Panorama, first held in 1963 and the largest steelband competition in the world.

The first pans of the 1940s clanged like tin cans. Ellie Mannette, later hailed as the Father of the Modern Steel Drum, found the cure in 1946: he wound rubber around the tips of his sticks, which softened each strike and gave the pan the warm, mellow voice every pannist has used since. He also sank the drum's top into a deep bowl, making room for many more notes.

Britain first heard the pan in 1951, when TASPO, short for Trinidad All-Steel Percussion Orchestra, the first band made entirely of oil drums to play abroad, performed at the Festival of Britain on London's South Bank. It silenced critics who had sneered at pan as dustbin noise, and some players, such as Sterling Betancourt, stayed and planted steelpan in Britain.
