the-sundarbans-mangrove-coast.context_blurb:
At the mouth of the Ganges and Brahmaputra, on the Bay of Bengal, where India meets Bangladesh, the land dissolves into a maze of muddy islands and tidal channels lined with tangled trees that grow in salt water. This forest floods and drains twice every day.

Its name, Sundarbans, is Bengali, from sundar, beautiful, and ban, forest: the beautiful forest. The name is also tied to the sundari, the mangrove tree that once carpeted the delta. Spread over about 10,000 square kilometres of trees rooted in salt water, it is listed by Guinness World Records as the largest mangrove forest anywhere.

The mud here is so soaked that it holds almost no oxygen, yet roots must breathe. So mangroves grow breathing roots, pneumatophores, that stick straight up out of the mud like snorkels, and tiny pores on them take in air at low tide.

The Sundarbans is a patchwork of about 102 islands laced by some 400 tidal rivers and creeks. The tide averages about 2 metres and can reach 5.7, so every day roughly a third of the land disappears under the sea and then reappears.

Mangroves also shield the coast. When a super-cyclone struck India's Odisha coast in 1999, its surge drowned most of the nearly 10,000 dead. Researchers who studied village after village found that the width of the mangrove belt between a village and the sea best predicted survival, and villages behind wider belts lost far fewer lives.

Mangrove coasts are among the world's great carbon traps. A mangrove buries most of its carbon in the deep, waterlogged mud around its roots, roughly three to five times more per acre than an ordinary tropical forest, locked away in airless mud metres deep. Scientists call it blue carbon.

Mangroves fringe warm coasts from Florida to Indonesia, but only in the Sundarbans do tigers live in them: some 180 to 200 Royal Bengal tigers, paddling across the channels between islands in search of prey.

the-taiga-the-great-northern-forest.context_blurb:
Across the top of the world runs a single, nearly unbroken band of dark conifer forest, through Alaska and northern Canada, across Scandinavia and the whole width of Russia. Its trees are built for long, brutal winters, their pointed shapes shedding snow and their dark needles soaking up the thin northern sun.

This great ring of trees is the taiga, and it is the largest land biome on Earth. Its other name comes from Greek myth: Boreas was the god of the freezing north wind that brought winter, his name passed into Latin as borealis, northern, and so the taiga is also the boreal forest.

Most people picture the world's trees crowding the warm tropics, but about one tree in every three on Earth grows in this cold northern ring, the largest forest belt on the planet. Each of them grows slowly in the short summers.

Eastern Siberia's forest belongs to a strange conifer, the larch: it carries cones, yet every autumn it goes gold and lets all its needles fall, spending winters colder than minus 60 °C bare before it grows a fresh coat in spring. The Dahurian larch is the most cold-hardy tree on Earth.

Much of the taiga grows over permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year and reaches down hundreds of metres, so roots can use only the thin layer of soil that thaws each summer. That is why the trees spread their roots wide and shallow; larch roots seldom go deeper than about 20 centimetres.

Cold slows rotting to a crawl. So the boreal forest's trees, soils and peat bogs store nearly twice as much carbon per unit of area as tropical rainforests, more than those famous jungles hold. The frozen ground of the far north alone holds an estimated 1,460 to 1,600 billion tonnes of carbon, about twice the amount in the whole atmosphere.

the-taklamakan.context_blurb:
In the far west of China lies the Taklamakan, a desert of restless dunes filling the vast Tarim Basin. For centuries Silk Road caravans hugged its edges, hopping from oasis to oasis, rather than risk its heart, and its dry sands have kept some strange secrets.

Its name is popularly read as a warning, that whoever goes in will not come out, though scholars still debate its true origin. Caravans gave it a darker nickname still: the Sea of Death.

It is one of the driest places on Earth because it lies in a giant bowl walled by some of the highest mountains anywhere, whose frozen summits wring the moisture out of clouds before they arrive. The Tian Shan, the Celestial Mountains, wall its northern side, with the Kunlun to the south and the Pamir to the west.

The dunes never stop moving, and along the desert's edge the shifting sands buried whole Silk Road towns. Loulan, abandoned around 330 CE after its lake dried up, lay lost until Sven Hedin stumbled on it in 1900, and at Niya in 1901 Aurel Stein dug out about a hundred wooden tablets left where they fell.

The salty, rainless sand also mummified the dead. The Tarim mummies, up to about 4,000 years old, have their skin, red-blond hair and woollen clothing all still intact. One of them, the Chärchän Man, was buried in leggings of tartan, a checked weave strikingly like the ancient Celtic cloth of Europe.

Their Western-looking features started a long argument over whether they had wandered in from far away. In 2021 scientists sequenced the oldest mummies' DNA and found they were no migrants at all but a genetically isolated local population, people native to the region, whose ancestry reached back to Ice Age hunters of northern Eurasia.

The Yarkand, the Hotan and the Tarim rush down from the peaks, feed oasis farms, then soak into the sand and evaporate, never reaching any ocean. A basin like this, with no outlet to the sea, is called endorheic, from the Greek for flowing within.

To reach oilfields in its heart, China built the Tarim Desert Highway between 1993 and 1995, about 552 kilometres long and some 446 of them over live dunes, the longest road across moving sand in the world. To keep the sand from burying it, engineers planted a living green belt beside it some 436 kilometres long, over 20 million saplings watered by drip pipes fed from salty groundwater.

the-tango-the-r-o-de-la-plata-buenos-air.context_blurb:
In the 1880s, tango rose out of the rough port neighbourhoods of two cities that face each other across a vast, muddy estuary: Montevideo in Uruguay and Buenos Aires in Argentina. It grew up among poor immigrants in dockside dance halls, scandalised polite society, and became the passionate soul of a whole region.

The two cities face each other across the Río de la Plata, a broad estuary where the Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet the Atlantic, and both countries have argued ever since over who owns tango.

The immigrant docklands held far more men than women, so the young toughs called compadritos practised the hard new steps with other young men, almost a mock duel between rivals, before they ever danced with a woman.

Around 1870 German sailors and immigrants carried the bandoneón, a square, button-covered cousin of the accordion, to the docks, and its deep, sobbing cry became the voice of tango. Yet it was never meant for dancing: in the 1840s the German instrument dealer Heinrich Band designed it as a cheap, portable stand-in for the pipe organ in small, poor churches that could not afford one.

The heart of the dance is the abrazo, the close embrace danced chest to chest, and the old milongueros boasted that from that first embrace they could read a partner's musicality, his respect, his whole character.

Tango's first great singing star, Carlos Gardel, is claimed by both countries. In 1920 he signed papers claiming Tacuarembó in Uruguay as his birthplace, probably to dodge French military service. But his French birth certificate, confirmed genuine in 2012, shows he was born in Toulouse, France, on 11 December 1890.

The most famous tango of all, La Cumparsita, was the work of Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, a Montevideo student of twenty, and it premiered on 19 April 1917 at the city's Café La Giralda, where the audience called for it six times that night.

At a milonga, a tango dance, you invite a partner across the hall without a word. You catch the other dancer's eye and give a tiny nod, the cabeceo, from cabeza, head: a held gaze means yes, a glance away is a gentle no, and nobody is ever turned down in public.

Ástor Piazzolla, a master of the bandoneón, began in the 1950s to blend jazz and classical music into tango, and he called his style nuevo tango. Purists were so enraged that some sent him death threats, but works such as Libertango carried his sound around the world. In Paris his teacher Nadia Boulanger had urged him to stop imitating Europeans and write tango.

After more than a century of rivalry, Argentina and Uruguay put tango forward together, and in 2009 UNESCO inscribed it as Intangible Cultural Heritage, one shared treasure belonging to both nations.

the-terracotta-army.context_blurb:
Outside Xi'an in central China, under the slopes of Mount Li, lies the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, who united the warring states of China in 221 BC and made himself its first emperor. Beside it, in great underground pits, stands one of the wonders of the ancient world: an army made of clay.

It was found by accident. On 29 March 1974, in a time of drought, farmers led by Yang Zhifa were digging a well in Xiyang village when, about a metre down, they struck the head of a clay soldier and broke into a pit holding thousands more. The archaeologist Zhao Kangmin pieced the first warriors together from fragments, some no bigger than a fingernail.

Once the pits were mapped, they turned out to hold not a small honour guard but a whole army drawn up for battle: more than 8,000 life-size warriors, with about 130 wooden chariots and hundreds of clay horses. The emperor had them made to guard him for all eternity in the afterlife, a bodyguard that would never stand down. And no two soldiers share a face: sculptors started from about ten basic face shapes, then changed each by hand, adding hair, ears, moustaches and expressions, so the army looks like a crowd of thousands of real, different men.

Today the warriors look plain grey, but they were once painted in bold, bright colours, including a man-made pigment called Chinese purple that the Qin craftsmen produced. On newly dug figures the paint can curl and flake within minutes of meeting the air. The soldiers also held real bronze weapons, and more than 40,000 bronze arrowheads, blades and crossbow triggers have come out of the pits. Some of the swords emerged after more than 2,000 years underground with edges still sharp enough to cut, several inscribed with dates between 245 and 228 BC.

The historian Sima Qian, writing about a century after the emperor's death, described the sealed tomb itself. He said it held a model of the entire realm, with rivers and seas of flowing mercury beneath a ceiling of stars, and in 2020 scientists aimed a laser at the air above the mound and measured mercury several times higher than the local background. He also wrote that the tomb defends itself, with hidden crossbows rigged to fire on their own at any robber who breaks in. Whether they survive, no one knows.

Work on the tomb began in 246 BC, the very year the future emperor became king of the Qin state, when he was only about 13 years old. Some 700,000 conscripted workers laboured on it for about 38 years.

After fifty years of digging in the pits, the emperor's own burial chamber, under the grassy mound at the centre, has never been opened. Archaeologists leave it sealed on purpose, fearing for any paint inside and wary of the mercury, so what lies within remains unseen.

The pits lie about 1.5 kilometres east of the mound, and the ranks of warriors in Pit 1 all face east, toward the rival states the emperor had conquered, the direction his old enemies had come from. They stand there still, an eternal vanguard.

the-theremin-russias-untouchable-instrum.context_blurb:
In October 1920 a young Russian physicist, Lev Termen, known in the West as Leon Theremin, unveiled an electronic instrument unlike any before it. He had been working on early sensors that used radio waves, and he turned that research into music.

His invention, the theremin, was the first musical instrument played without ever being touched. It has two metal antennas. As the player's hands move through the air near them, one hand sets the pitch and the other sets the volume, so the music seems to be pulled out of empty space.

The sound is an eerie, swooping, wavering wail. One critic compared it to a cello lost in a thick fog, weeping because it cannot find its way home. That ghostly voice later haunted the science-fiction and horror films of the 1950s.

Termen's own story turned dark. Back in the Soviet Union he spent years as a prisoner, made to design secret listening devices for the state.

the-three-ways-plates-meet-a-plate-bound.context_blurb:
Earth's rocky shell is broken into great slabs called tectonic plates, and they never stop moving. Where two plates meet they can do only three things: pull apart, push together, or slide past each other. Each kind of meeting builds its own landscape, and you can visit all three.

At Thingvellir in Iceland a path drops into a deep canyon, with the North American plate rising as a cliff on one side and the Eurasian plate as the other wall. The two plates are pulling apart here, and a place where plates spread away from each other is called a divergent boundary. Over the 10,000 years since lava flowed there, the ground has widened some 70 metres. Nearby at Silfra, divers slip into a water-filled fissure in the same rift, its glacier meltwater so clear they can see about 100 metres, and by stretching out both arms a diver can touch both plates at once, one hand on each.

Along South America's Pacific shore the Nazca plate dives under the South American plate at the Peru-Chile Trench, and melting rock above it feeds the volcanoes of the Andes, for where one plate sinks beneath another the boundary is convergent. The Andes, about 8,900 kilometres long, are the longest continental range on Earth, and in Argentina they rise to Aconcagua, 6,961 metres, the highest summit outside Asia.

In California the plates do the third thing: along the San Andreas Fault, some 750 miles long, they grind sideways past each other, neither building new crust nor swallowing old, which makes it a transform boundary. Fences and creek beds that cross it are jogged out of line, and a sudden slip on its northern stretch caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Because the Pacific plate creeps northwest, Los Angeles, which rides on it, is slowly sliding toward San Francisco, which lies chiefly on the neighbouring plate, and in several million years the two cities should end up side by side.

The whole shell is split into some seven or eight big plates plus about fifteen small ones, and the biggest is the Pacific plate, about 103 million square kilometres, more than any continent covers. Most plates move only a few centimetres a year, and at Thingvellir they part by about 2 centimetres, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

Sometimes the ground moves in a rush. At Dabbahu, a volcano in the Afar region of Ethiopia, a fissure stretching 60 kilometres and gaping as wide as 8 metres tore open in 2005 in roughly two weeks, releasing some 400 years of built-up strain almost at once. Afar is where three rifts meet, and the East African Rift runs on south from there into Kenya and Tanzania. Geologists expect that some ten million years from now a narrow sliver of eastern Africa will tear away and the sea will flood into the gap, forming a whole new ocean, just as the Red Sea opened long ago.

the-tides-and-the-record-breaking-bay-of.context_blurb:
Twice a day, almost everywhere on Earth, the sea slowly climbs the shore and then slides back again. In most places it rises only a metre or two, but on Canada's Atlantic coast, in the Bay of Fundy, it climbs higher than anywhere else on the planet.

The Moon does most of the lifting: its tide-raising pull is more than twice the Sun's, and twice a day the whole ocean answers it and rises. In the Bay of Fundy, a long, tapering inlet lying between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the sea rises and falls by about 16 metres twice a day, the highest tides on Earth. Ungava Bay in northern Quebec runs so close that some call the record a tie.

Each flood tide carries some hundred billion tonnes of sea water into the bay, and each ebb carries it out again, roughly twice the combined flow of every river on the planet over the same hours. Far from land, the lunar pull raises the water a mere 54 centimetres or so, too gently for a ship to notice. Tides grow into giants only where a coastline's shape funnels them, and Fundy's long, narrowing funnel stacks the water ever higher as it squeezes in.

At Mont-Saint-Michel, the abbey island off Normandy in France, where the tide range reaches about 14 metres, a saying usually pinned on Victor Hugo claims the sea rushes in as fast as a galloping horse. That is lore, not a measurement, but walkers really are stranded by the rising water and quicksand.

Why two high tides a day? The Moon pulls hardest on the ocean facing it and least on the water on the far side, which is left behind. So the Moon raises a bulge of water on the near and far sides of the Earth at the same time, and as the planet turns through both, most coasts get two highs about twelve hours apart.

Twice a month, at new and full Moon, the Sun and the Moon fall into a straight line and pull together, and the tides leap to their highest, which are called spring tides, from springing up, not from the season. Fundy's greatest water came in October 1869 at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia, when the Saxby Gale's fierce winds and low pressure drove a storm surge ashore on top of a tide already running high, and the sea reached 21.6 metres. That record has never been beaten.

On the Rance estuary in Brittany, France, in 1966, President Charles de Gaulle opened the world's first power station to make electricity from the tides, using 24 turbines to harness a tide of about 8 metres. For 45 years no tidal station anywhere grew larger.

Seven days or so later, at the quarter Moon, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel, and these weakest tides are neap tides, from an old Anglo-Saxon word meaning something like without the power. Even Fundy runs slack then.

Many bays are funnels, so why is Fundy the champion? The water in the bay naturally rocks from end to end in about the same twelve and a half hours as the tide's own rhythm, so each new tide pushes at just the right moment, like well-timed shoves on a swing. This lucky match is called tidal resonance.

In the city of Saint John the river spills seaward over a sunken ledge of rock in a foaming rapid, but twice a day the Fundy flood overpowers it, and the whole rapid turns around and runs backward, upstream and uphill, over the same ledge. It is called the Reversing Falls.

On the Petitcodiac, close to Moncton, the incoming tide turns into a bore, a single wave that marches upriver against the flow. In July 2013 the surfers Mark Whitbread and Colin Wessels rode it for about 29 kilometres over two and a half hours, the longest wave ever ridden in North America.

the-trade-winds-and-the-doldrums-the-hig.context_blurb:
On either side of the equator, steady winds blow across the tropical oceans day after day. For centuries they were the highways of sail, carrying explorers, merchants, colonists and treasure between the continents.

In the Northern Hemisphere these trade winds blow from the northeast and in the Southern from the southeast, both curving toward the equator, and a ship leaving Europe could ride them west across the tropical Atlantic to the Americas. That same reliable highway carried crops and ideas between continents, and it also carried colonists and the ships of the transatlantic slave trade.

The name began with no thought of commerce: in the 14th century trade meant a track or course, and sailors said the wind blew trade when it held steadily one way. Only later, because these winds carried England's merchant fleets, did the money meaning stick.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus let the northeast trades carry him west from the Canary Islands. Going home, that same wind would only have pushed him farther west. So in January 1493 he climbed north into cooler latitudes to catch the westerlies, which blow back toward Europe. Trades out and westerlies home make a great clockwise wheel of wind around the North Atlantic.

Right at the equator the trades of both hemispheres collide, cancel out and rise, leaving a belt of breathless calm that sailors called the doldrums, where a sailing ship could lie still for weeks. Scientists call it the Intertropical Convergence Zone.

In the Pacific the trades drove the Manila galleon route: between 1565 and 1815, Spanish treasure ships sailed between Manila in the Philippines and Acapulco in Mexico, carrying silver to Asia and silk and porcelain back, riding the trades one way and the Kuroshio current the other.

Portuguese captains homeward-bound along Africa's western shore met winds and currents running steadily against them. Their answer was the volta do mar, the turn of the sea: sail the wrong way first, westward across the Atlantic toward Brazil, then swing round to catch the westerlies home. Historians say Europe's sea empires could hardly have arisen without this trick.

Air flows toward the low pressure along the equator, so you might expect the trades to blow due south in the north and due north in the south. Instead both lean westward, because the Coriolis effect of Earth's spin deflects moving air to the right north of the equator and to the left south of it. If the planet stopped spinning, the slant would vanish.

the-wallace-line-an-invisible-border.context_blurb:
Between Asia and Australia lies a scatter of thousands of islands, and through them runs an invisible border. On one side live Asia's animals, such as tigers, monkeys and orangutans; on the other, Australia's marsupials and cockatoos. In places the two worlds are divided by only a narrow strait.

The sharpest crossing is the Lombok Strait, barely 35 kilometres wide: from Bali you can see Lombok, yet the wild animals on the far shore belong to a different world. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace mapped this frontier in 1859, and in 1868 Thomas Henry Huxley named it Wallace's Line.

When ice-age glaciers locked up water and sea level dropped by some 120 metres, dry land linked many of the islands together. But the channel of the Lombok Strait plunges at least 250 metres, far deeper than the seas ever fell, so its floor never came up as land, and the animals on either side never mixed.

On the western side, Borneo, Sumatra, Java and Bali rest on the Sunda Shelf, a broad underwater platform rarely more than 50 metres deep, which became dry land at low sea, a peninsula of Asia called Sundaland. On the eastern side, the falling seas uncovered the Sahul Shelf, the shallow rim of Australia, and fused New Guinea with Australia into a single landmass, Sahul, which a person could once have crossed on foot.

Between the two shelves lie islands such as Sulawesi, Lombok, Flores and Timor, cut off by deep water on every side and never joined to either continent, and this in-between zone of about 347,000 square kilometres is called Wallacea. Its wildlife is a mix of Asian and Australian types found nowhere else.

One line was not enough for so blended a zone. In 1896 Richard Lydekker drew another along the eastern rim of Wallacea, hugging the edge of the Sahul Shelf, and it is known as Lydekker's Line. Between it and Wallace's Line runs Weber's Line, where Asian and Australian life balance equally.

Far to the north, the Wallace Line passes between Borneo and Sulawesi through the Makassar Strait, which is 130 to 370 kilometres across yet plunges to about 2,500 metres. It divides the animals just as sharply as the narrow gap at Bali, proof that the real barrier is deep water, not distance.

the-waltz-vienna.context_blurb:
Few sounds are as Viennese as a waltz: couples whirling round and round a ballroom floor to music in three-four time. Vienna, the capital of Austria, made the dance its own in the 1800s, but the waltz began far from palaces, and it arrived as a scandal.

When the waltz reached Vienna's ballrooms in the early 1800s, critics were outraged that the partners turned in a closed hold, man and woman face to face, his hand resting on her waist. Older ballroom dances had kept couples apart in group figures, and in 1816 The Times of London called the waltz an indecent foreign dance.

It grew out of the Ländler, a heavy-footed country dance in three-four time from the farming villages of Bavaria and Austria, sped up and polished for the city. Some scholars now see the two as sibling dances rather than parent and child. The name comes from the German walzen, to roll or turn, for the dance's whirling spin, and the word first appears in print in 1748, in the text of an order banning the dance.

In 1863 the Habsburg emperor Franz Joseph gave Johann Strauss the Younger, who wrote more than 500 dance pieces, a salaried post as Music Director of the Royal Court Balls. His father, Johann Strauss the Elder, had wanted the boy to become a banker.

His most famous waltz, By the Beautiful Blue Danube, named for the broad river that flows through Vienna, was written in 1866 and is now the city's unofficial anthem. It began as a choral piece and became a triumph only in its orchestral version at the Paris World's Fair of 1867.

The city was mad for dancing even earlier. In 1814 and 1815 the Congress of Vienna gathered Europe's kings and diplomats to reshape the continent once Napoleon was beaten. An endless round of balls and dancing swallowed their time, so that Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne joked that the Congress danced a great deal but did not move forward.

the-worlds-great-rivers.context_blurb:
The world's great rivers are the arteries of civilization, where people have farmed, traded and built cities for thousands of years. Each holds its own records, and ranking them is trickier than it looks: the longest, the biggest, the deepest and the most international are all different rivers.

In Egypt, in the heart of the desert, the Nile flows northward to the Mediterranean, about 6,650 kilometres in all, and each summer its flood once laid down fresh black mud over the fields, feeding Egypt's farms for thousands of years.

By volume nothing rivals the Amazon, draining the South American rainforest: every second it pours some 215,000 to 230,000 cubic metres of water into the Atlantic, roughly one-fifth of what all rivers together deliver, outpouring the seven rivers that rank below it put together. Even where it first enters Brazil, it already carries more water than any other river. Asia's longest river is the Yangtze, about 6,300 kilometres, flowing wholly within China from the Tibetan Plateau east to the Pacific and carving dramatic gorges on the way. North America's biggest river, the Mississippi, begins as a small stream flowing out of Lake Itasca in Minnesota and gathers water from roughly 40 percent of the continental United States before it reaches the Gulf of Mexico. The Danube, rising in Germany's Black Forest and flowing to the Black Sea, touches ten countries, a record no other river matches, and passes four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

The Nile is really two rivers joined. Each summer, heavy rains on the Ethiopian Highlands send the Blue Nile surging out of Lake Tana, and it brings about 70 percent of the Nile's flood. The White Nile is the smaller in volume, but it gives the Nile its great length, for its farthest streams gather in the hills around Lake Victoria in East Africa. The two meet at Khartoum, capital of Sudan, the pale, milky White Nile running beside the darker Blue with a visible line between them before they merge.

The Congo, in central Africa, holds a different record: in its canyons the riverbed drops some 220 metres into lightless water, the deepest of any river, and down there a blind, colourless fish has evolved. Its huge arc through the rainforest also makes it the only major river to cross the equator twice, dipping south and swinging back north before it hurls itself through Livingstone Falls toward the Atlantic.

Near Manaus in Brazil two great tributaries meet, the Rio Negro, black as coffee, and the pale, silty Rio Solimões, as Brazilians call the upper Amazon, milky with mud from the Andes. At this Meeting of the Waters they refuse to blend for about 6 kilometres, because they differ in warmth, in speed and in density: the Rio Negro is warmer, about 28 °C, slow and almost free of sediment, while the Solimões is cooler, about 22 °C, fast and heavy with silt.

the-yangtze.context_blurb:
The Yangtze is Asia's longest river, flowing some 6,300 kilometres across China from the high west to the sea beside Shanghai. For thousands of years it has been China's great highway, and along one stretch it squeezes through canyons that poets have praised for fifteen centuries.

Below the town of Baidicheng, boats travel for about 193 miles between cliffs hundreds of metres high until the river opens out at Yichang, and this run of three canyons, Qutang, Wu and Xiling, is the Three Gorges. Qutang is the shortest and Xiling the longest, but the best loved is Wu Gorge, a 45-kilometre canyon famed for its twelve peaks, above all the needle known as Fairy Peak.

Near Yichang, at Sandouping, stands the Three Gorges Dam, a concrete wall 185 metres tall and more than 2 kilometres wide, completed in 2012, whose 32 main turbines make it the largest power station on the planet.

Behind the dam lies a reservoir about 600 kilometres long, holding some 40 billion tonnes of water raised high above the old riverbed. In 2005 the NASA geophysicist Benjamin Fong Chao calculated that lifting so much mass slowed Earth's spin very slightly, lengthening the day by about 0.06 microseconds, far too little to feel. The rising water drowned towns and farmland along the valley, and about 1.3 million people were forced from their homes. Plans showed 13 cities, 140 towns and 1,350 villages partly or wholly flooded.

How can a reservoir slow a planet? Think of a spinning figure skater: when she stretches her arms out wide she turns more slowly, because moving mass farther from the axis slows a turning body. Raising the water lifts mass away from Earth's axis in the same way.

Poets have praised these gorges for some fifteen centuries, and travellers carved verse into the cliffs. The Tang poet Li Bai wrote of his small boat shooting downstream past thousands of mountains while howling monkeys called without pause from both banks. Much of the carved poetry now lies beneath the reservoir.

The river begins far to the west, high on the Tibetan Plateau, where its first trickle is meltwater from the glaciers of Geladaindong Peak, 6,621 metres high in the Tanggula Mountains. That melt feeds the Tuotuo, the headwater stream of the great river.

the-yellow-river-huang-he.context_blurb:
From the Tibetan Plateau to the Bohai Sea, some 5,464 kilometres across northern China, flows the Huang He, the Yellow River. Its water runs yellow-brown for almost its whole course, and over the centuries it has both fed Chinese civilization and drowned it.

The colour is the fine mud the river carries in its water: as it cuts through soft, pale soil it picks up enormous loads of silt, and that suspended mud tints it for nearly its whole length.

Most of the mud comes from one place, the Loess Plateau, which the river saws through in its middle course, an upland of wind-blown dust piled 50 to 80 metres thick and more than 90 in places. Winds carried that dust off deserts such as the Gobi over some 2.6 million years, every summer's rains sluice it down into the river by the ton, and more than 90 percent of the river's silt comes from here.

For two thousand years the silt has settled in the river's bed, so people walled it in with ever-higher levees. At Kaifeng, an ancient capital in Henan province, the riverbed now lies about 10 metres above the streets, so the river flows higher than the rooftops, held in only by its banks. Geographers call it a hanging river.

On the Loess Plateau the soft earth is easy to dig, and for hundreds of years farming families carved their homes straight into its cliffs, cave dwellings called yaodong. They are made from the very soil the river washes away downstream.

The raised bed is always ready to burst free, and since about 595 BC the river has flooded some 1,500 times and changed its course 26 times. Its flood of 1931 killed an estimated 1 to 4 million people, among the deadliest disasters ever recorded, and for such floods the Chinese call the river China's Sorrow.

Yet the same silt spread a soft, fertile yellow soil that simple tools could till, China's earliest villages clustered along the river, and so this valley is honoured as the cradle in which Chinese civilization grew. For that, the river is also called China's Pride.

the-yucatan-cenotes-and-the-dinosaur-cra.context_blurb:
The Yucatán Peninsula of southern Mexico is a low plain of soft limestone covered in jungle. It has almost no rivers on its surface, yet it is full of water hidden underground, and beneath it lies the scar of the most famous disaster in Earth's history.

Rainwater sinks right through the porous stone, and the only open water lies in round, flooded sinkholes scattered through the forest, the cenotes, from the Yucatec Maya word ts'ono'ot, a well. Some 6,000 to 10,000 of them dot the peninsula, and the Maya drank from them. Their water is famously clear because it is rain that has seeped slowly down through the limestone for years, leaving its sediment behind, so divers hover as if in air above the cavern floor.

Map the cenotes of the northwest Yucatán and the thickest line up in a great curve about 180 kilometres across, from Celestún on the west coast round to Dzilam, and that Ring of Cenotes traces the buried rim of a giant crater blasted out by an asteroid. Off the peninsula's Caribbean shore, where its underground rivers reach the sea, more than 1,000 kilometres of coral run along the coasts of Honduras, Guatemala, Belize and Mexico: the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

The crater is Chicxulub: some 66 million years ago a space rock about 10 kilometres wide struck here, filling the air with dust and soot that blotted out the sun. The darkness that followed ended the long reign of the dinosaurs, all but the birds, and wiped out about three-quarters of all species.

The cenotes are dissolved, not dug: rainwater carries a little acid that eats the limestone slowly, across many thousands of years, hollowing out caves until a roof collapses, and a landscape shaped this way, riddled with caves, sinkholes and underground rivers, is called karst. To the Maya, cenotes were holy doors to Xibalba, the underworld, and above all they belonged to Chaac, the hook-nosed god of rain and lightning. In a land whose water hid underground, the god who filled the wells mattered most.

Beneath the surface the cenotes link up into flooded mazes, the longest submerged cave systems known anywhere. Sistema Sac Actun, the White Cave, has about 378 kilometres of mapped passages, and nearby Sistema Ox Bel Ha more than 435.

At Chichén Itzá one great cenote stood apart, the Sacred Cenote, about 60 metres across and connected to the temples by a causeway of stone. Between 1904 and 1910 Edward Thompson dredged it and dived into it, bringing up thousands of offerings, gold, jade, incense and copper bells, along with the bones of people sacrificed to Chaac.

In 2007 cave divers reached a pitch-black flooded chamber and called it Hoyo Negro, meaning Black Hole. Beside the remains of Ice Age beasts such as sabre-toothed cats lay a girl of 15 or 16, her skeleton almost whole, who fell into the then-dry cave some 12,000 to 13,000 years ago. Nicknamed Naia, she is one of the oldest and most complete humans ever found in the Americas.

throat-singing-tuva-and-mongolia.context_blurb:
Across the grassy steppe of Tuva, a small Russian republic in southern Siberia, and of neighbouring Mongolia, a lone herder can sing two notes together, a low, steady drone with a bright pitch floating above it, as if one man were a whole choir.

This is throat-singing, which Tuvans and Mongolians call khöömei, a Turkic word meaning throat.

Singers say their sounds are not invented but borrowed from the steppe's own wild voices: the deep growl is the howling winter wind, and a rolling trill is a bubbling brook. So a song becomes a map of the homeland, rooted in an old belief that a place's spirits live in its sounds as much as in its shape.

Each style has a name, and the highest is sygyt, a shrill whistle like a flute's that hovers far above the drone, made by pressing the tongue against the gums. The lowest is kargyraa, a deep growl. A throat-singer is often joined by the igil, Tuva's two-string fiddle, its neck topped by a carved horse's head, whose low bowing falls like hoofbeats under the voice. Mongolia plays a larger cousin, the morin khuur.

One Tuvan style, ezengileer, has a bouncing beat made by the soft palate flicking open and shut, and its name comes from ezengi, the Tuvan word for stirrup, for it copies the sway of a rider trotting in the stirrups.

The upper note seems like magic, yet it is pure physics. A low drone already contains fainter overtones, called harmonics, ringing above it. Holding the drone, the singer reshapes mouth and throat to focus a narrow band of those harmonics into one sharp peak while hushing the rest, so a faint overtone hidden inside the drone rings out loud as a separate note. UNESCO calls it a melody of harmonics.

tidal-bores-rivers-that-run-backwards.context_blurb:
Twice a day, in a few special rivers, the incoming sea does something startling: it rears up into a single wall of water that rolls upstream, the wrong way, sometimes for many kilometres. It happens only where a big rising tide is squeezed into a shallow, narrowing river mouth.

On England's River Severn, which has one of the greatest tidal ranges on Earth, about 13 metres, the flood tide rears into a wave about 2 metres tall that races inland against the current, and such an upstream wave is called a tidal bore. Surfers chase it for miles.

On the Amazon the bore is heard before it is seen, a distant rumble that gave it its name, the pororoca, which may come from a Tupi word meaning great roar. The wave stands as tall as 4 metres and can surge some 800 kilometres inland. Because a bore is one long wave that keeps re-forming instead of breaking, a rider can stay on it far longer than on any ocean wave, and in 2003 the Brazilian surfer Picuruta Salazar rode the pororoca on the Guamá River for 12.5 kilometres and 37 minutes.

The pororoca's pounding also reshapes the land, and between 1845 and 1850 it wore through low, flat Caviana Island near the Amazon's mouth and split it into two.

The biggest bore on Earth races up China's Qiantang River near Hangzhou, a roaring wall up to 9 metres tall moving at about 40 kilometres an hour, and it is nicknamed the Silver Dragon. People have gathered to watch it for over a thousand years; the Southern Song court held a Tide Watching Festival in its honour, and the world's oldest known tide table, from AD 1056, was made for this river.

A bore can also be lost. For centuries the Seine in France had one, the mascaret, which locals called la barre, but by the 1960s it was gone. Engineers had dredged the river deeper for shipping, erasing the shallow, narrowing funnel that a bore needs. The reverse can happen too: Canada's Petitcodiac bore, choked by a causeway in 1968, came back after its gates were reopened in 2010.

tikal.context_blurb:
Deep in the rainforest of northern Guatemala rise the pale limestone pyramids of Tikal, one of the greatest cities of the Classic Maya, which flourished from about 200 to 900 AD. Howler monkeys roar at dawn among its temples, and its story runs from royal tombs and great rivalries to a city that ran out of clean water.

Its tallest pyramid is Temple IV, about 70 metres high, and from the top you break out above the rainforest canopy, the endless sea of treetops that buries the rest of the city from view. That view became an alien world on film: in Star Wars: A New Hope, from 1977, the jungle seen from Temple IV stands in for the forest moon Yavin 4, home of the rebel base.

Across the Great Plaza two pyramids face each other, and the taller, eastern one, Temple I, a royal tomb, is known as the Temple of the Great Jaguar, after a carved lintel showing a king seated on a jaguar throne. Its shorter twin, Temple II, is the Temple of the Masks.

Around 900 AD Tikal's people walked away, and across the Maya lowlands most researchers now blame a drought lasting decades, made worse by the Maya's own clearing of forest and loss of soil, though the exact trigger is still argued over. The jungle then hid the city for nearly a thousand years. Temple I climbs to its shrine in nine great stepped terraces, chosen on purpose, since they are widely thought to stand for the nine levels of the Maya underworld.

Its kings probably knew the city as Yax Mutal, but its name today, Tikal, was given much later by Yucatec Maya speakers and means roughly at the waterhole, fitting for a city with no rivers or lakes that lived on stored rain.

Tikal's fiercest rival lay to the north: Calakmul, in what is now Campeche, Mexico, seat of the Kaan, or Snake, dynasty, whose emblem was a snake's head.

King Jasaw Chan K'awiil I lay buried deep inside Temple I, and archaeologists tunnelled to him in 1962. On his skeleton lay the greatest prize Tikal has yielded, a necklace of 114 carved jade beads weighing 3.9 kilograms. Beside him were a jade mosaic vessel bearing his portrait, jaguar pelts, shells and pearls.

The city drank only rain, caught off its broad paved plazas and kept in huge lined reservoirs. A 2020 study found that the Corriental reservoir stayed clean for centuries because the Maya filtered its water through minerals, zeolite and coarse quartz sand hauled some 30 kilometres, which strained out microbes and even toxins. It is the oldest known water filter in the Americas, about 2,000 years old.

Yet the reservoirs may have turned on the city in the end. Mud from the bottoms of the biggest ones, dating from Tikal's last years, is poisoned with mercury, washed in from cinnabar, the bright red paint the Maya loved for walls and tombs. Together with blooms of toxic blue-green algae, it would have made the water undrinkable.

timbuktu.context_blurb:
Timbuktu is a dusty desert city where the Sahara gives way to the grasslands, in what is now Mali, home today to about 85,000 people. Between the 1300s and the 1500s it was one of the richest and most learned cities on Earth, built on gold, salt and books.

To English speakers its name became a byword for the farthest place imaginable, as in the saying from here to Timbuktu, because for centuries Europeans pictured it as a place of mythical riches at the edge of the world. It lies about 20 kilometres north of the Niger River, exactly where camel caravans out of the Sahara met the river boats that carried goods on into West Africa.

The lands to the south were rich in gold but short of salt, so caravans hauled salt cut in great blocks from the desert mines of Taghaza and Taoudenni, and traders liked to say that the two changed hands weight for weight. That was an exaggeration, but salt worth pennies in the desert could sell for gold at its edge. The domed tombs of Sufi saints, called marabouts, stand all through the town, and because 333 of these saints lie buried there as its guardians, Timbuktu is called the City of 333 Saints. Militants smashed several tombs in 2012, and local masons rebuilt them.

Timbuktu's families guarded, for centuries, up to an estimated 700,000 handwritten manuscripts in home libraries, and though they cover medicine, law and poetry, they are most famous for astronomy and mathematics, with star charts and tables of the planets. They prove a literate, scientific West Africa long before the colonial era. Three great mosques rise over the town, Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahya, built not of stone but of sun-dried mud. Djingareyber, the oldest, was raised in 1327 for the emperor Mansa Musa by the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. Around 1510 the traveller Leo Africanus found that of everything sold in Timbuktu's markets, books brought the richest profit, more than any other merchandise.

The city's greatest scholar, Ahmed Baba, chancellor of the Sankore madrasa, wrote more than forty books and kept some 1,600 at home, but when a Moroccan army stormed Timbuktu in 1591 the invaders marched him away into exile, and he lost his library. The city's manuscript institute now bears his name.

Several European adventurers lost their lives trying to reach the fabled golden city. In 1828 the Frenchman René Caillié became the first to get there and back alive, winning a 10,000-franc prize, but instead of gold he found only a huddle of plain houses built of mud and earth.

The toron, beams of palm wood sticking out of the mosques' walls, are permanent scaffolding, so that every year the whole town can climb them to re-plaster the mosques with fresh mud. Without that yearly coat, the rains would slowly dissolve the buildings.

In 2012 armed militants seized Timbuktu and began destroying whatever they judged un-Islamic. The librarian Abdel Kader Haidara and a network of helpers smuggled some 350,000 manuscripts out in metal trunks and footlockers, past checkpoints and down the Niger by boat to Bamako. When the militants retreated in January 2013 they burned about 4,200 manuscripts, only a fraction, because most were already safe.

tiwanaku-and-pumapunku.context_blurb:
High on a vast plain near Lake Titicaca in Bolivia lie the ruins of Tiwanaku, with its sunken courtyards, its carved gateways, its giant statues and blocks of stone cut so precisely they look machine-made. Its people built one of the great civilizations of the Andes without wheels, iron or strong beasts of burden.

Tiwanaku flourished from about AD 500 to 1000 and had collapsed centuries before the Inca rose in the 1400s, so it was already an old, abandoned city when the Inca found it. The two are often confused because both centred on the Andes near Lake Titicaca.

The city stands about 3,850 metres up on the altiplano, Spanish for high plain, the widest high plateau on Earth outside Tibet, stretching across Bolivia and Peru. Its most famous monument is the Gate of the Sun, a doorway carved from one block of andesite weighing about 10 tons, crowned by a figure holding a staff in each hand, his head ringed with rays, usually identified as the creator god Viracocha.

Next to the city is Pumapunku, a temple whose blocks are so sharp-edged and evenly matched that they look machine-made. Many were cut to the same H-shaped pattern, locking together like puzzle pieces into rows of miniature doorways. Such precision has drawn ancient-alien claims, but archaeologists such as Alexei Vranich credit skilled Tiwanaku masons, pointing to earlier stonework around the Titicaca basin. The builders used no mortar: in notches carved at the joints, Tiwanaku metalworkers poured molten metal, an unusual bronze of copper, arsenic and nickel, which hardened in place into I-shaped clamps binding block to block.

The largest stone, a red sandstone slab, is estimated at about 131 tonnes and came from a quarry some 10 kilometres away. The harder andesite blocks were quarried on the Copacabana Peninsula, about 90 kilometres off, and moved across or around Lake Titicaca.

Nights on the high plain freeze hard, yet Tiwanaku's farmers fed perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 townspeople. Their secret was waru waru, strips of earth heaped up between ditches of water: the water soaked up the day's sun and gave off warmth at night, and the coldest air pooled down in the channels rather than around the plants. When a long drought struck around AD 1000, the system faltered and the city declined.

tokyo-the-endless-city.context_blurb:
Tokyo spreads along Tokyo Bay on the eastern coast of Honshu, Japan's main island, a seemingly endless city of glass towers, neon crossings and quiet shrines. Twice in the 20th century it was flattened, by earthquake in 1923 and by bombing in 1945, and each time it rose again.

Its most famous crossing is in Shibuya: when every traffic light turns red together, up to about 3,000 people surge across from all sides, cutting straight through the middle. The Shibuya Scramble opened in 1973, and on its busiest days up to 500,000 people cross it. Greater Tokyo, joined with Yokohama, holds some 37 million people, about as many as California, which makes it the most populous urban area on the planet and the biggest in human history. Where you draw the boundary changes the count.

For over 250 years the Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan from this city. Its name then was Edo, and in 1868, when the shogunate fell, Emperor Meiji, still a young man, shifted his residence from Kyoto to the city and renamed it Tokyo, the Eastern Capital. In 2012 the Tokyo Skytree was completed on the city's east side, a slender white broadcasting spire 634 metres tall and the tallest tower in the world. Around the centre runs the Yamanote Line, a loop with no last stop, linking the great hubs of Tokyo, Shinjuku, Shibuya and Ikebukuro, and one full circle takes about an hour.

Shinjuku Station holds the Guinness record as the busiest railway station on Earth, with about 3.5 million passengers a day before the pandemic, roughly six times the crowd at Paris's Gare du Nord, the runner-up. It has well over 200 exits. At the very centre of the city, behind wide moats and stone ramparts, lies an island of woods and lawns, the Imperial Palace, home of the Emperor of Japan, on the grounds of old Edo Castle. Out in Tokyo Bay, Odaiba, with its malls, giant Ferris wheel and life-size Gundam robot, stands on a man-made island. Its name recalls the gun batteries, daiba, raised there in 1853 against Commodore Perry's Black Ships, and some 249 square kilometres of new land have been made from the bay.

In its heyday Edo Castle was the largest castle anywhere in the world, its outer defences running some 16 kilometres around and covering about 230 hectares. Today's palace grounds are only about a third of it.

Earthquakes have levelled Tokyo more than once because three tectonic plates collide beneath the Kanto plain: both the Philippine Sea plate and the Pacific plate dive beneath the continental plate there. That double subduction makes it one of the most quake-prone cities on Earth. When the Great Kanto earthquake, magnitude 7.9, hit just before noon on 1 September 1923, thousands of charcoal cooking fires were burning in a city of wooden houses. Whipped by typhoon winds, those fires merged into a firestorm that raced across the city and caused about 90 percent of some 105,000 deaths.

The Skytree's height is a pun: in a traditional way of reading numbers aloud, the digits six, three and four can be said as mu, sa and shi, spelling Musashi, the ancient name of the province and plain on which Tokyo stands.

tornado-alley-and-the-supercell.context_blurb:
In spring the flat plains of the central United States, from Texas north through Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska, breed more tornadoes than anywhere else on Earth. Most are born from supercells, towering thunderstorms that rotate as they climb.

Weather experts call this belt of plains Tornado Alley, a nickname rather than a line on any official map.

From April to June two air masses meet here: dry, cool air spilling east off the Rocky Mountains rides up over warm, wet air streaming north from the Gulf of Mexico, and the trapped moist layer bursts upward into supercells. Over the Texas Panhandle the edge between hot, dry desert air and moist Gulf air is called a dryline, and storm chasers wait along it because great rotating storms often fire right there. Cross it and the humidity drops off a cliff; the dry air is denser and wedges underneath, shoving the moist air up.

On 31 May 2013 a monster tornado crossed the farmland near El Reno, Oklahoma, measuring 2.6 miles across, the widest ever measured. Mobile radar clocked its winds past 300 miles an hour, yet it was rated only EF3, because it churned mostly over open country. It killed eight people, among them the storm researcher Tim Samaras, his son Paul and Carl Young.

Tornadoes are ranked by the damage they leave behind. In 1971 Ted Fujita of the University of Chicago introduced the Fujita scale, running from 0, which snaps branches, to 5, which can lift a well-built house off its foundations. Since 2007 the United States has used an updated version, the Enhanced Fujita scale.

The Plains have the greatest number of twisters, yet the southern states of Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee and Georgia, a region the meteorologist Allen Pearson named Dixie Alley in 1971, lose many more lives in each storm. There about 29 percent of tornadoes strike after dark, against 19 percent on the Plains, often hidden by rain and forest, and night tornadoes kill about two and a half times as many people because they catch families asleep.

tower-karst-stone-forests-and-drowned-dr.context_blurb:
Across southern China and Southeast Asia rise some of the strangest landscapes on Earth: steep grey towers of limestone standing alone on flat plains or rising straight out of the sea. They look as if something pushed them up, but the opposite is true.

Beside the Li River, around the city of Guilin, hundreds of these stone thumbs rise from the paddies, and this kind of land is called tower karst, limestone slowly dissolved by rain over millions of years. The word karst comes from the Kras Plateau in Slovenia, where such landscapes were first studied.

The most famous view on the river, printed on China's 20-yuan banknote, is Yellow Cloth Shoal near Xingping, named for a flat beige slab on the riverbed that looks like yellow cloth spread underwater. Seven karst hills stand around it, doubled in the still water. The city of Guilin, at the head of the river, takes its name from the osmanthus trees that perfume it each autumn, for Guilin means forest of sweet osmanthus. Fan Chengda, a poet of the Song dynasty, judged its scenery the finest under heaven.

How did the towers get so tall? Chinese geographers sort them into fenglin, separate spires on a plain, and fengcong, clusters of cones on a shared base. Both were carved downward, not pushed up: over millions of years rain dissolved away the softer limestone around them, leaving the hard towers standing. The dissolving agent is carbonic acid, which forms when rainwater soaks up carbon dioxide from the air and soil, and this weak acid slowly eats the calcium carbonate that limestone is made of.

In Vietnam's Gulf of Tonkin the same towers stand in the sea, for Ha Long Bay is a drowned karst landscape: after the last ice age the rising sea flooded the valleys between the towers, leaving some 1,600 islands. Ha Long means descending dragon, from a legend that a mother dragon and her young spat out jewels and jade that became a wall of islands against invaders.

In Yunnan, the Stone Forest of Shilin is karst at ground level, a maze of grey blades up to 50 metres high. Its limestone is more than 270 million years old, laid down as shell and seafloor mud when the region lay under an ancient sea.

Not every stone tower is karst. In Hunan, the thousands of sheer pillars of Zhangjiajie, the model for Avatar's floating Hallelujah Mountains, are quartz sandstone, shaped by freezing ice and running water rather than dissolved by acid.

transform-faults-the-plates-that-grind-p.context_blurb:
Not every plate boundary builds or breaks the crust. Along a transform fault, two plates simply grind sideways past each other, making no new crust and destroying none, but storing up strain that is let go in sudden, violent earthquakes.

The most famous runs some 1,200 kilometres up California: the San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific plate slides northwest past the North American plate.

On the dry Carrizo Plain, Wallace Creek crosses the fault, and its lower half has been dragged about 130 metres to the northwest. Most of that shift built up over thousands of years, but about 23 feet of it happened in an instant during the Fort Tejon earthquake of 1857. When San Francisco was shaken in 1906, the fault tore open along some 477 kilometres, about 296 miles, more than a third of its whole length, and fences and roads that crossed it were jogged up to 6 metres out of line.

Los Angeles rides the Pacific plate and San Francisco the North American, sliding past each other by an inch or two a year, so in about 20 million years Los Angeles, now some 350 miles south, would sit right beside San Francisco. The tiny town of Parkfield, astride the fault, has had a magnitude-6 quake about every 22 years since 1857, so regularly that it calls itself the Earthquake Capital of the World. The US Geological Survey wired its ground for a long earthquake-prediction experiment.

Turkey's North Anatolian Fault closely resembles the San Andreas. Since the Erzincan earthquake of 1939 it has broken in an orderly chain, each rupture loading the next section like a zipper, across more than 1,000 kilometres. The 1999 Izmit quake struck less than 100 kilometres east of Istanbul, so the march of ruptures has reached the edge of that great city, and the last unbroken gap lies right beneath it.

Where a sliding fault steps sideways, the crust between the steps stretches and drops into a pull-apart basin. Along the Dead Sea Transform, where the Arabian plate has slid about 105 kilometres north past the African plate, such basins hold the Sea of Galilee, the Dead Sea and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Dead Sea's shore, about 430 metres below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth.

troy-the-mound-of-hisarlik.context_blurb:
On a plain in the northwest of Turkey, close to the Aegean and the straits of the Dardanelles, rises a grassy mound called Hisarlik. For centuries readers thought Homer's Troy, the city of the Trojan War in the Iliad, was pure legend. Then, in the 1870s, the digging began, and the mound turned out to hold a real city, many times over.

Inside the mound are at least nine cities, each raised on the levelled rubble of the one before, labelled from Troy I at the bottom to Troy IX at the top and spanning roughly 3000 BC to AD 500. Visitors today can climb Troy's real stone walls and gate, but the most famous object in the story of its fall, the wooden horse, was never dug up and belongs wholly to legend. It is not even in the Iliad; it appears later, in the Odyssey.

The mound stands some 15 metres high, yet nature did not build it. Over thirty centuries, town after town of mud brick was built there, fell into ruin and was built over, and archaeologists of the Near East call a mound raised this way a tell. Most of the Troys were mud brick and slumped into the mound, but Troy VI built great sloping walls of cut limestone, laid without mortar, that still rise 9 to 10 metres in places.

Heinrich Schliemann, a wealthy German amateur, dug up a gold hoard he named Priam's Treasure, after Troy's king in Homer, and he called its golden diadems the Jewels of Helen, after the queen whose flight began the war. The hoard also held some 8,750 tiny gold rings, goblets and silver vases. In his rush to reach Homer's city, Schliemann cut a trench about 40 metres wide straight down to bedrock through the middle of the mound, wrecking priceless layers, and visitors still call that scar Schliemann's Trench.

In fact the gold came from the Troy II layer, about 2400 to 2200 BC, while the Troy of King Priam's war belongs to around 1250 BC, so Priam's Treasure is roughly a thousand years older than any Priam. For a century Troy was imagined as nothing more than the little citadel on the mound, but excavations led by Manfred Korfmann from the late 1980s revealed a lower city of about 30 hectares spread around it, making the real Troy more than sixteen times the size of the fort.

In the houses of Troy VIIa, huge storage jars called pithoi, some taller than a man, stood sunk in the floors to hoard grain, oil and water, while rooms were split into cramped quarters, like a town bracing for a siege. And that layer ends in violence. A layer of black ash caps it, its streets are littered with sling-stones and bronze arrowheads of Greek type, and bodies were left unburied. So Troy VIIa, from about 1300 to 1180 BC, excavated by Carl Blegen, matches better than any other layer the stormed and burning city of Homer's poem. Most scholars therefore place Homer's war in Troy VII.

tsunamis-the-wave-that-empties-the-sea-f.context_blurb:
A tsunami is no ordinary wave whipped up by wind. When an undersea earthquake, a volcano or a landslide suddenly shoves the seafloor, the whole depth of the ocean above is set moving, and a pulse of water races outward across the sea.

People used to call it a tidal wave, but tides play no part in it; its name is Japanese, from tsu, harbour, and nami, wave, a harbour wave, because a swell that seemed slight at sea reared up to wreck Japan's harbours. Out on the deep ocean it may be only a small bump that a passing ship hardly feels, yet it is racing along at more than 800 kilometres an hour, about as fast as a jet airliner.

On 26 December 2004 a quake of about magnitude 9.1 off Sumatra sent tsunamis over the whole Indian Ocean, killing some 228,000 people, and the toll was so high because that ocean had no tsunami warning system at all, no buoys and no alerts. The disaster spurred the world to build one. Most tsunami-making megaquakes strike off Alaska, Chile, Japan and the Cascadia coast, along the Ring of Fire around the Pacific, which is why the oldest warning centre on Earth stands in Hawaii.

On All Saints' Day in 1755 an earthquake shook Lisbon, and then the harbour drained; curious crowds walked out onto the mud, and some 40 minutes later the tsunami rolled over them. The sea pulls back like that when the wave's trough reaches the shore before its crest, which happens often but not always. In open water the 2004 wave was only about a metre tall, its crests up to 200 kilometres apart. In the shallows its front slowed from about 800 to under 80 kilometres an hour, the faster water behind crowded into it, and at Banda Aceh the wave rose to between 15 and 30 metres, a piling-up called shoaling.

At Maikhao Beach in Thailand's Phuket, ten-year-old Tilly Smith saw the sea froth and pull back, and she recognised the signs because, two weeks earlier, her teacher Andrew Kearney had taught them during a geography class at school. She raised the alarm, the beach was cleared, and about 100 people were saved. Krakatoa's 1883 explosion in the Sunda Strait was heard some 4,500 kilometres away, yet of about 36,000 dead, more than 34,000 were killed by the towering tsunami it raised.

High over the little Japanese settlement of Aneyoshi, an ancestors' stone warns people not to build homes below it, and in 2011 the wave climbed the valley and stopped about 100 metres short of the stone, so every household that had stayed above it survived.

In 1958 an earthquake shook loose a rockfall of some 30 million cubic metres into Lituya Bay in Alaska, and the water it threw up climbed 524 metres up the opposite mountainside, the tallest wave ever recorded, yet because the inlet is so remote only about five people died. On 11 March 2011 a quake of about magnitude 9.0 off Japan's Oshika Peninsula raised a tsunami up to 40 metres high that flooded the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant and caused three reactor meltdowns.

tulum.context_blurb:
Almost every great Maya city lies deep inland under the jungle, but Tulum is different. It stands on a cliff about 12 metres high on the east coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, the only major Maya city built on the shore, its stone temples gazing out over the turquoise Caribbean Sea.

The Maya called it Zama, meaning dawn, and the name fits, because the cliff faces due east and the temples catch the first light rising over the sea each morning. The name Tulum is much newer; it comes from the Yucatec Maya word for wall, after the rampart that ringed the city on three sides.

Tulum was a busy port, trading obsidian, jade and salt by canoe. Its tallest temple, El Castillo, lines up with the one natural gap in the offshore reef. So archaeologists think it doubled as a navigation beacon: lights in its windows could have guided trading canoes through the channel into the sheltered cove. That role is an interpretation, not a proven fact.

tundra-and-permafrost-the-frozen-ground.context_blurb:
Far to the north, in Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada, the forests run out and give way to the tundra, a treeless plain of moss, grass and dwarf shrubs. Similar treeless land caps high mountains, and beneath the far northern tundra lies a hidden world of ice.

Under the thin summer carpet the deeper ground never thaws. Only a top layer, averaging about 1.5 metres, softens each summer, and below it the soil stays frozen year after year, in parts of Siberia to nearly 1,500 metres down. Ground that stays frozen for at least two years running is called permafrost, and it lies under about 15 percent of the Northern Hemisphere's land.

In Oymyakon, a village in Siberia, some 500 people live through winters so harsh that drivers leave their engines running so the fuel will not freeze, and on 6 February 1933 it reached minus 67.7 °C, making it the coldest place on Earth where people live all year. Yakutsk, home to about 355,000 people, is the largest city built on permafrost, and builders there raise each block on a grid of concrete piles driven deep into the frozen ground, leaving an air gap so the building's warmth cannot reach and melt the ice.

When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground slumps into a lumpy maze of sinkholes and dips where meltwater pools, and geologists call this thermokarst, after karst, the pitted landscape of dissolving limestone. In Siberia's thaw lakes, ancient mud from long-dead plants releases methane, a potent greenhouse gas, which bubbles up and, when winter seals the lake, freezes into stacks of pale white discs in the ice.

Once loggers stripped the trees from a slope in Sakha in the 1960s, the exposed frozen ground started to melt and slump. The scar became the Batagaika crater, now roughly a kilometre in length and as much as 100 metres deep, and still widening by more than 10 metres a year, and locals call it the Gateway to the Underworld. Its crumbling walls lay bare hundreds of thousands of years of frozen history, buried forests and mammoth bones among it.

Permafrost is also a natural deep-freezer. Siberian reindeer herders on the Yuribei River came upon Lyuba in 2007, a baby woolly mammoth. Her skin, organs and last meal were intact after about 42,000 years, because the frozen ground had kept her as if in ice.

Tundra is not only a polar thing. Climb a tall tropical mountain, such as Ecuador's Andean volcanoes or Kilimanjaro, and above a certain height the forest ends, giving way to alpine tundra, bare of trees for the same reasons as the Arctic: too much cold and too brief a growing season. Journey away from the equator toward either pole and that treeline sinks lower and lower, until near the poles it reaches sea level and the mountain tundra meets the polar tundra at the coast.

u-shaped-valleys-and-hanging-valley-wate.context_blurb:
A river and a glacier carve valleys of very different shapes. In Yosemite in California's Sierra Nevada, in the Swiss Alps and along the coast of Norway, the ice of past ages left deep, flat-floored troughs with sheer walls, and waterfalls that leap from far above.

At the entrance to Yosemite Valley stands El Capitan, a wall of pale granite about 100 million years old that rises some 3,000 feet without a break, often called the largest exposed granite monolith on Earth. Climbers need days to scale it. The first waterfall a visitor meets is Bridalveil Fall, a thin, year-round ribbon of water that falls 620 feet. The Ahwahneechee called it Pohono, spirit of the puffing wind, because gusts blow the water sideways.

Bridalveil leaps from a hanging valley. While the great main glacier gouged Yosemite's deep trough, the smaller glacier in the side valley could not grind nearly as deep, so when the ice melted the side valley was left stranded high on the wall. Its stream now free-falls off the lip. J.R.R. Tolkien walked through the Lauterbrunnen Valley in Switzerland as a young man in 1911, a glacial cleft walled by cliffs nearly 1,000 metres high and laced with some 72 waterfalls, and it became his picture of Rivendell, the elven refuge of Middle-earth.

Ice alone is too soft to scratch granite, yet on Pothole Dome and Lembert Dome in Yosemite the rock is buffed so glassy that hikers slip. The polishing was done by grit and boulders frozen into the glacier's base, which turned the moving ice into a vast sheet of sandpaper. In Montana's Glacier National Park, the lakes shine turquoise because melting ice pours in rock ground so fine that it never settles, called glacial flour, which hangs in the water and scatters sunlight. In the Lauterbrunnen Valley, Staubbach Falls drops 297 metres from a hanging valley, the longest unbroken plunge of any Swiss waterfall, and the wind tears it to spray before it lands, so the Swiss named it the dust brook, for Staub means dust. Goethe visited it in 1779 and wrote a poem about its spirit-like mist.

The stones frozen into a glacier's base also gouge the bedrock with long straight grooves called striations, and since they run the way the ice moved, geologists read them like arrows to find the direction a vanished glacier once flowed.

Norway's Sognefjord reaches over 200 kilometres into the land and plunges some 1,300 metres deep, while a shallow ridge of rock, a sill, lies across its entrance. A fjord is simply a glacier-carved U-valley that the sea has flooded, and the sill is the ridge the glacier left at its end.

Why a U at all? A river cuts along one narrow line on its bed and leaves a sharp V. A glacier instead grinds and plucks along its whole width and base at the same time, shaving the walls into a smooth, rounded U over 10,000 to 100,000 years. That shape is the fingerprint that tells geologists ice, not water, made a valley.

uluru-and-kata-tjuta.context_blurb:
Near the very centre of Australia, in a flat red desert, rise two of the world's most famous rocks: Uluru, a single huge rounded mass of stone, and, about 25 kilometres to its west, Kata Tjuta, a cluster of great domes. Both are deeply sacred to the Aṇangu, the Aboriginal people whose land this is.

Uluru stands 348 metres above the plain, taller than the Eiffel Tower, and a lone, tough mass of rock rising abruptly from flat land like this is called an inselberg, German for island mountain. Its summit is 863 metres above sea level. It is no rock to stroll around in a minute: the track that loops its base runs 9.4 kilometres, close to six miles, around one unbroken hump of stone.

Kata Tjuta means many heads in Pitjantjatjara, a perfect name for its 36 separate rounded domes. Europeans long called it the Olgas, after its tallest dome, Mount Olga.

Morning and evening light turns Uluru a burning red-orange before it dims to violet. Break a piece open and it is grey, for the rock is arkose, a sandstone rich in feldspar. Only its outer skin glows, because the iron in that skin has oxidised, literally rusted.

Uluru's layers stand almost on end, tilted to about 85 degrees, and they plunge into the earth for at least 2,400 metres, so most of the rock lies buried underground, like the hidden bulk of an iceberg. The less famous neighbour is actually the taller: Mount Olga rises about 546 metres above the plain, roughly 200 metres higher than Uluru. The explorer Ernest Giles named it in 1872 for Queen Olga of Württemberg.

At the foot of Uluru lies Mutitjulu, a permanent waterhole, precious in the desert, and a sacred Aṇangu site tied to the ancestral story of Liru, a venomous snake, and Kuniya, a python. Uluru was handed back to the Aṇangu on 26 October 1985, and exactly 34 years later, by the Aṇangu's own decision and out of respect for their sacred rock, the climb to the summit closed for good.

The rock itself is staggeringly old: Uluru's sandstone formed some 550 to 530 million years ago, when the first animals were only just appearing on Earth, about 300 million years before the dinosaurs.

Why do the two look so different? Uluru is fine, even arkose that wore down into one smooth block. Kata Tjuta is conglomerate, cobbles and boulders of many kinds of rock cemented together in a sandstone paste like natural concrete, and that coarse, uneven rock weathered into 36 separate heads.

uluru-and-the-red-centre.context_blurb:
Uluru rears out of the dead-level desert at the centre of Australia, with nothing but plain around it as far as the eye can see. To the Aṇangu, its Aboriginal keepers, it is a living, sacred place; to geologists, it is a giant that shows only its tip.

The word for such a solitary rock mountain standing over a plain is inselberg, German for island mountain, a mass of tough rock left standing when the softer land around it wore away. Uluru rises 348 metres above the plain and measures 9.4 kilometres around.

The Aṇangu law and stories called Tjukurpa, the Dreaming, memorised and handed down over tens of millennia, map ancestral events onto Uluru's caves and gullies, and they also carry survival knowledge: how to travel, where water and food can be found, and when. The red dome is only the tip, for its rock layers continue down below the sand for about 2.4 to 2.5 kilometres, so most of Uluru's bulk is hidden underground, like an iceberg.

Sunrise and sunset set the rock ablaze, yet that red goes no deeper than its surface: inside the caves at its base the same stone is plain grey. Iron in the outer rock has rusted, and that oxidised skin is what glows red.

At Uluru's base lies Mutitjulu, the only waterhole there that holds water all year, for centuries the most trusted Aṇangu campsite. In Tjukurpa it is the home of Wanampi, an ancestral water serpent that guards the pool.

The Aṇangu closed the climb on 26 October 2019, the 34th anniversary of the land's return to them. Outsiders assumed the main reason was the rock's sacredness, but the sign at the base stressed something else: as custodians, the Aṇangu felt responsible for the safety of visitors, and they worried about the climbers and their families.

The rock started out as level beds of sand, over half a billion years old. Then the Alice Springs Orogeny, a mountain-building squeeze some 400 to 300 million years ago, tipped those once-flat layers up to about 85 degrees, almost straight up and down.

Some 25 to 30 kilometres west rises Kata Tjuta, many heads, a cluster of 36 domes, and its tallest, Mount Olga, stands about 546 metres above the plain, roughly 200 metres higher than Uluru. It is built of a quite different rock, conglomerate, cobbles and boulders of granite and basalt cemented together.

ushuaia.context_blurb:
On Tierra del Fuego, the large island where South America ends, the Argentine port of Ushuaia looks across a narrow strait to snowy peaks and glaciers. Its motto calls it the end of the world and the beginning of everything, and more than 90 percent of all visitors to Antarctica, about 1,000 kilometres away, set sail from its docks.

With more than 82,000 people, Ushuaia is billed as the southernmost city on Earth. A smaller Chilean town, Puerto Williams, lies a little farther south across the water, so Ushuaia is really the southernmost city of any real size.

The island's name, Land of Fire, dates from 1520, as Magellan's fleet sailed by and the crew saw flames and smoke dotting the shore. They were the campfires of the native Yamana people, who kept fires burning against the cold all along the coast, even on hearths inside their bark canoes. A colourful tale says the land was first called the Land of Smoke until the king of Spain renamed it.

The strait before the town takes its name from HMS Beagle, the British survey ship that charted these waters between 1826 and 1830. On the ship's second voyage, Charles Darwin sailed through in 1833 and marvelled at the blue of its glaciers.

valparaiso.context_blurb:
Valparaíso is a Pacific port on the central coast of Chile, its houses stacked up dozens of hills so steep that ordinary streets give up. In the 1800s it was one of the great harbours of the world.

To climb those slopes, people have ridden ascensores since 1883, small cars hauled up the cliffs on cables, really funiculars balanced against each other on steep tracks. The first, Ascensor Concepción, still runs, and about 16 survive as National Monuments of Chile.

The hillside houses form a patchwork of clashing colours, and the reason is thrift. Families who could not afford new metal clad their homes in corrugated iron rescued from old ship hulls and painted it with leftover marine paint from the shipyards.

Before any canal existed, every ship between the Atlantic and the Pacific had to battle round Cape Horn through its storms, and Valparaíso was where weary crews rested and restocked after the passage. Its banks, brothels and saloons boomed so wildly that sailors called it Little San Francisco, after the California gold-rush port.

Then in 1914 the Panama Canal opened, thousands of kilometres up the coast, giving ships a shortcut between the oceans, and almost overnight they stopped coming. The boomtown fell quiet, already shaken by a great earthquake in 1906.

The poet Pablo Neruda, who filled his homes with ships' figureheads, in 1959 took over a half-built house on a hilltop for its view of the harbour and made it a writing hideaway called La Sebastiana, after Sebastián Collado, the Spaniard who began building it. It is now a museum.
