varanasi-the-eternal-city-on-the-ganges.context_blurb:
Varanasi, on the River Ganges in northern India, is the holiest city in Hinduism. Pilgrims come from all over India to bathe in the river at dawn, and families bring their dead here to be cremated at the water's edge, for to die in Varanasi is believed to bring the greatest blessing of all.

Along its riverfront, long flights of stone steps called ghats lead down into the Ganges, traditionally counted as 84, an almost unbroken stairway where the city bathes, prays and floats little lamps each morning.

Babylon and Ur crumbled to dust long ago, but people have lived in Varanasi for some three thousand years without a break, so it ranks among the oldest cities in the world that are still lived in today. Mark Twain called it older than history, tradition and legend put together.

Its great cremation ground is Manikarnika Ghat, where some 200 to 300 bodies are burned every day beside the river, so its fires never go out, burning day and night all year round. To Hindus this is a place of hope, not horror. Every evening at Dashashwamedh Ghat, a row of robed young priests swing tall brass lamps while conch shells sound and bells ring, in the Ganga Aarti, an offering to the river Ganges herself, which Hindus revere as a living goddess.

Hindus believe the soul is caught in samsara, an endless cycle of death and rebirth, and that cremation here breaks that cycle and frees the soul for ever, a release called moksha.

The city's older name is Kashi, from a Sanskrit root meaning to shine, so Varanasi is honoured as the City of Light. Hindus hold it to be Shiva's own city, founded by him at the dawn of the world. Above the oldest lanes rises its holiest shrine, the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, sacred to Shiva, its tall spire and dome plated with gold so that it shines out over the old city.

At Manikarnika only one family may light the funeral pyres, an office handed down the male line for as long as anyone remembers. They are the Dom, placed outside the traditional caste order yet holding a duty no cremation can do without, and their hereditary head bears the title Dom Raja, king of the burning ground.

vatnajokull-iceland.context_blurb:
In southeastern Iceland lies Vatnajökull, the largest glacier in Europe outside the Arctic, a dome of ice covering about 8 percent of the country. Beneath it hide whole mountain ranges and active volcanoes, so this is a land where fire and ice meet.

Vatnajökull is an ice cap, a mound of glacier ice that buries the land beneath it but covers less than 50,000 square kilometres; anything bigger, like the ice over Greenland or Antarctica, counts as a full ice sheet. Its ice averages about 380 metres thick and reaches some 950 metres at its deepest.

At the foot of its outlet glaciers, guides lead people into caves of blue ice carved by meltwater, and strangely they are safe only in winter, from about mid-November to March, when the ice is frozen hard. In the warmer months they melt and collapse, and each year the meltwater carves new ones. Icebergs break off one outlet glacier into the lagoon of Jökulsárlón, drift out to sea where the surf polishes them smooth, and are thrown back by the tide onto black volcanic sand, where they glitter like gems on a shore travellers call Diamond Beach.

The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs right through Iceland, and along it the Eurasian plate and the North American plate are slowly pulling apart, by about 1.8 to 1.9 centimetres a year, while magma rises to fill the gap. A mantle hotspot beneath adds even more heat, which is why volcanoes burn under Vatnajökull's ice. The busiest of them is Grímsvötn, which erupts every few years in its active spells, more often than any other volcano in Iceland, and its heat keeps a lake in its caldera liquid even under the ice. Its 2011 eruption threw ash some 20 kilometres high and grounded about 900 European flights.

When a volcano erupts under the glacier, its heat can fill a secret lake of meltwater beneath the ice, held in until the pressure bursts it free in one rush, a flood Icelanders call a jökulhlaup, glacier run. In 1996 one released some three cubic kilometres of meltwater across the plain south of the glacier and swept away a 376-metre bridge on the Ring Road, yet no one was killed.

Several of Iceland's oddest peaks, Herðubreið among them, were born from eruptions sealed under thick ice. The lava stacked into steep walls, hemmed in by ice, until it broke through into open air and spread into a flat cap. Such a flat-topped, steep-sided peak is called a tuya, and its height shows the thickness of the ice that has since melted away. The geologist Bill Mathews named the form in 1947, after Tuya Butte in British Columbia.

venice-the-city-on-a-sunken-forest.context_blurb:
Venice rises from a shallow saltwater lagoon on the Adriatic Sea in northeastern Italy. Over a millennium ago, refugees from the mainland settled its scattered sand islands, and they raised a city of marble palaces on ground that is nothing but mud.

Venice spreads over some 118 little islands, laced together by about 400 bridges across some 150 canals, and its old centre has no cars at all, for Venetians have always travelled and carried their goods by boat on the canals. There is no bedrock beneath the lagoon, only soft mud, so every stone palace stands on a forest of wooden piles hammered deep into the lagoon floor. The marble city rests on drowned tree trunks.

Those piles should have rotted long ago, but sealed in airless mud, out of reach of the microbes that rot wood, they have soaked up minerals over the centuries and hardened until they are almost stone. The builders' favourite pile wood was alder, which barely rots under water, and the trunks came floating down from distant forests in Croatia, Slovenia and Montenegro, perhaps 8 to 16 million piles in all.

Venice floods at high tide, an event called acqua alta, high water, and it turns dangerous when the tide is joined by the sirocco, a warm wind blowing up the Adriatic from Africa that piles the sea into the lagoon. Low-lying St Mark's Square goes under first, now more than 60 times a year. The worst flood of all came on 4 November 1966, when the water reached 194 centimetres, the highest ever recorded there, and about 90 percent of the old city went under. That disaster pushed Italy to build MOSE, movable barriers that can close the three mouths of the lagoon.

Santa Maria della Salute, the domed church at the mouth of the Grand Canal, stands by a 17th-century count on 1,106,657 wooden piles, over a million tree trunks beneath one church.

Switched on in 2020, MOSE is made of rows of separate hollow steel gates, 78 in all, lying flat on the seabed at the three inlets, Lido, Malamocco and Chioggia. Venice also sinks while the sea creeps higher, and in the 20th century factories at Marghera on the mainland made it much worse by pumping groundwater out from beneath the lagoon, dropping the city 5 to 10 millimetres a year in the 1960s.

Normally the gates sit full of water in their housings, out of sight. When forecasters warn of a dangerous tide, compressed air is pumped into each hollow gate to drive the water out, and the buoyant gates swing up on their hinges to wall off the sea. They can seal the lagoon in about half an hour, and MOSE first held back a flood on 3 October 2020.

Fire was another danger to a city built on wood. In 1291 Venice's rulers ordered every glassmaker out of the main city to the island of Murano, so that furnaces roaring past 1,500 °C could not set the city ablaze and the secrets of Venetian glass could be kept on one guarded island. The masters were honoured, but they were almost prisoners.

vesuvius-and-the-burial-of-pompeii.context_blurb:
On the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, about 9 kilometres east of the city of Naples, rises the only active volcano on the European mainland. In the year 79 it entombed the Roman towns at its feet so suddenly that they became the best window we have on everyday Roman life.

That volcano is Mount Vesuvius, and its eruption in AD 79 froze Pompeii in mid-step under a deep blanket of ash and pumice. Herculaneum, a smaller and wealthier seaside resort even closer to the volcano, vanished at the same time under some 20 metres of hot volcanic debris, and it lies beneath the modern town of Ercolano.

Almost no one died from lava. At least eight scorching clouds of gas and ash, each about 300 °C, rushed down the slopes at up to 100 kilometres an hour and killed in seconds, and volcanologists call such a ground-hugging cloud a pyroclastic surge. Vesuvius is far from dead, and scientists expect another violent eruption, yet about 3 million people live around its base, some 600,000 of them in the red zone that would have to flee first.

Across the bay at Misenum, the 17-year-old Pliny the Younger watched the eruption and left the one surviving eyewitness description, comparing the cloud to an umbrella pine, the Mediterranean stone pine, rising high on a trunk and then spreading into branches. The blast hurled about a million and a half tons of rock into the air each second, and its column shot about 33 kilometres up into the stratosphere, the layer that begins around 12 kilometres high.

Volcanologists call this most violent style, a narrow column racing many kilometres up before it spreads into a canopy, a Plinian eruption, after Pliny the Younger. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, Rome's great naturalist, commanded the navy at Misenum, and he ordered his galleys to row across the bay toward the volcano to rescue friends trapped near the mountain. When his helmsman begged him to turn back, he answered that fortune favours the bold; he died on the beach at Stabiae, probably overcome by fumes.

Pompeii's famous bodies are not petrified corpses: the victims decayed and left hollows in the hardened ash, and in the 1860s the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured wet plaster into those hollows, recapturing poses, faces and even the folds of clothes. About 1,044 casts have been made. One cast showed an adult wearing a gold bracelet and holding a child, long labelled a mother and baby, but DNA studied in 2024 showed that the adult was a man, unrelated to the child.

At Herculaneum, in the seaside Villa of the Papyri, a whole library of scrolls was charred into brittle black lumps, and the Vesuvius Challenge reads them with X-ray scans and AI, so that in 2023 the 21-year-old Luke Farritor made out the first whole word, porphyras, Greek for purple.

Vesuvius itself is a cone within a ruin: its young cone grows inside the broken rim of an older, larger crater, Monte Somma, which collapsed about 17,000 years ago, and geologists name such a volcano after it, a somma volcano.

victoria-falls.context_blurb:
Where Zimbabwe meets Zambia, the Zambezi River drops without warning over a sheer cliff of black basalt more than 1.7 kilometres wide into a narrow gorge. You can hear the roar and see the spray long before you reach Victoria Falls.

Long before any European arrived, the falls had a name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders, for the plume you see and the roar you hear from far away. David Livingstone, the Scottish explorer, reached them on 16 November 1855 and renamed them for Queen Victoria, but the old name is still used. That smoke is spray, thrown upward as the river falls: the 108-metre drop shatters the river into fine mist that jets more than 400 metres high, visible 50 kilometres away.

Victoria Falls is neither the tallest waterfall nor the widest, but at 108 metres high and 1,708 metres wide it forms the greatest unbroken sheet of falling water anywhere. Below the drop the river churns in a cauldron that the local Tonga people named Shungu Namutitima, boiling water.

At the very lip of the drop, in the low-water months from about mid-August to mid-January, a rock rim holds back the current enough for daring swimmers to float at the cliff edge in the Devil's Pool, which you can get to only by way of Livingstone Island, in Zambia. On clear nights around the full moon, moonlight shining through the endless spray paints a faint arc called a moonbow, and the falls are one of the most reliable places on Earth to see one.

Kololo boatmen paddled Livingstone to the island that now bears his name. There he cut his initials and the year into the bark of a tree, the only mark he ever let himself leave, which he later called this piece of vanity.

His famous line about scenes so lovely that angels must have gazed on them in their flight is widely engraved on plaques as if it described the falls, but in his diary he wrote it about the calm, palm-studded river upstream of them.

Below the falls the Zambezi snakes through a chain of sharp zigzag gorges, and each one is a spot where the falls used to be, for at least seven earlier falls of similar size were left behind as the river cut its way backward. The 100-kilometre Batoka Gorge is a stone record of every former lip. The falls pour over a vast sheet of basalt, once molten lava, which shrank as it cooled and split into a grid of straight cracks, and the river tears its falls backward along one crack, reaches a junction and jumps to the next. It has been carving those zigzags for some 1.4 to 2.5 million years.

vienna.context_blurb:
Vienna, on the Danube in Austria, was for centuries the capital of the Habsburg emperors who ruled much of Central Europe. It became the music capital of the world, and it is still a city of palaces, ballrooms and long, unhurried afternoons.

At the edge of the Prater fairground turns the Riesenrad, a red wheel built in 1897 for Emperor Franz Joseph's golden jubilee, 64.75 metres tall and one of the oldest Ferris wheels still turning anywhere. Vienna's other great institution is the coffee house, where the price of a single small coffee rents you a marble-topped table for hours, with bentwood chairs and newspapers clipped into wooden frames, and nobody rushes you.

In the ballrooms of the 1800s, couples whirled close together in the waltz until some collapsed, and moralists called it indecent, until the glittering balls held for the diplomats at the great Congress of 1814 and 1815 made it respectable. When Paris scrapped its bigger wheel in 1920, the Riesenrad became the tallest Ferris wheel on Earth, and it kept that crown for 65 years, until Japan's Technostar wheel opened in 1985. In 2011 UNESCO placed Viennese coffee-house culture on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, the list for living traditions rather than buildings, praising the coffee houses as places where you spend hours and take up space, yet pay only for the coffee.

Every New Year, Austria greets the year with The Blue Danube by Johann Strauss II, the Waltz King, a tune the city treats as its unofficial anthem. Viennese balls still open with the cry Alles Walzer, everyone waltz. Napoleon's occupations of 1805 and 1809 had proved the old city walls useless. In 1857 Franz Joseph decreed their removal, and on their line he laid out the Ringstrasse, a boulevard 5.3 kilometres long, soon lined with grand palaces, museums, the parliament and the opera.

At the Central Cemetery, Brahms, Schubert, Beethoven and Johann Strauss lie in a place of honour, but Mozart has only a monument there: he was buried in 1791 in a plain grave at St. Marx Cemetery whose exact spot was lost, and even his widow could not find it. The tale that he went into a pauper's mass grave is a myth.

Within the imperial palace, the Spanish Riding School has taught white Lipizzaner stallions since 1572 to perform the soaring leaps called the airs above the ground, and it is the oldest classical riding academy still at work. That palace is the Hofburg, the winter seat of the Habsburgs for over six centuries until the empire collapsed in 1918, a maze of some 2,600 rooms and 19 courtyards that is today home to the office of the Austrian president.

Vienna became the City of Music because three masters of the classical style worked there, Beethoven, Mozart and Haydn, the young Beethoven even taking lessons from Haydn, and in 1834 the musicologist R. G. Kiesewetter grouped them as the First Viennese School.

volcanic-lightning-the-ash-clouds-dirty-.context_blurb:
Sometimes a volcano makes its own storm. As a great eruption hurls ash miles into the sky, bright bolts of lightning can crackle through the dark plume, even with no rain cloud anywhere near.

When Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull erupted in 2010, cameras caught lightning deep inside its ash cloud, charged by the ash itself, its tiny grains colliding by the countless billion, not by any storm. The same ash choked jet engines and grounded flights across Europe for nearly a week.

Japan's Sakurajima, on Kagoshima Bay, goes off several times every year, and because the storms of bolts in its plumes rage inside churning ash and grit rather than clean rain, scientists nicknamed them dirty thunderstorms.

How does ash charge up? In 2020 the plume of Taal, a volcano in the Philippines, flashed with dozens of bolts a minute. The grains charge by triboelectric charging, the same static you make by rubbing a balloon against your hair, only titanic. Corrado Cimarelli's team proved it by firing real ash through a shock tube in the laboratory and making tiny bolts.

In 2008 the photographer Carlos Gutiérrez caught lightning inside the ash cloud of Chile's Chaitén volcano glowing a vivid green, and the physicist Arthur Few explained that the colour came from excited oxygen atoms, the same element that paints the aurora green.

On 15 January 2022 Hunga Tonga, an undersea volcano in the South Pacific, produced the most intense lightning ever measured, some 192,000 flashes, over two and a half thousand a minute, and the bolts arranged themselves in huge rings rippling outward up to 250 kilometres across. Today satellites watch for such bursts to warn airliners of invisible ash clouds.

washington-d-c.context_blurb:
The American capital, Washington, D.C., was built from nothing on swampy ground beside the Potomac River in the 1790s. Its white Capitol dome, its marble memorials and its long green Mall make it one of the most deliberately planned cities on Earth.

Most cities grow street by street, but Washington was designed whole before it existed. In 1791 the French-born engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant drew the whole city on paper before a single building went up, with avenues slanting across a grid and bearing the names of the states, circles where they meet, and a central Mall. After he was dismissed in 1792, the surveyor Andrew Ellicott finished the drawing.

On the Washington Monument, a clear colour line partway up records a halt of some two decades: work stopped in 1854 when money ran out, the stump stood through the Civil War, and when building resumed in 1879 the new marble came from a different quarry.

From the Capitol steps, the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial, almost two miles off, line up perfectly, and that is no accident, because the plan placed them on one sightline deliberately, with the Mall as a central axis, first in L'Enfant's design and later in the McMillan Plan. The city also stays low, because the Height of Buildings Act of 1910 limits each building to the width of the street it faces plus 20 feet. The popular belief that nothing may top the Capitol is a myth.

The ground under the Lincoln Memorial did not exist on 1800s maps: it is fill, mud the Army Corps of Engineers dredged from the Potomac between 1882 and 1911 and heaped onto the river's tidal flats, about 628 acres of new land. The western Mall and the Tidal Basin rose from the river the same way.

On 6 December 1884 workers crowned the monument with a little pyramid, some nine inches high, cast of aluminum, a metal then so hard to free from its ore that it cost nearly as much as silver. A few years later a new process made it cheap, the same stuff as kitchen foil.

water-that-isnt-there-and-cities-in-the-.context_blurb:
Air can play tricks with light. When layers of hot and cold air lie one over another, they bend light rays as they pass, and the eye is fooled into seeing water where there is none, or castles and mountains hanging in empty sky.

Drive across the Sahara and the track ahead shimmers with a silver pool that slides away as you approach. The scorching air just above the ground bends light from the sky upward into your eye, so what you really see is a patch of the blue sky above, which your brain reads as water. This is an inferior mirage.

In Greenland's frozen waters the trick runs the other way: icy air lies beneath warmer air, light bends downward, and a distant island or shoreline seems to rise and hang above the horizon. This superior mirage can even lift into view things hidden beyond the curve of the Earth.

In the narrow strait that separates Sicily from mainland Italy, sailors for centuries saw the far coast tower up into battlements that hovered over the water and then melted away, and they called the sight the Fata Morgana. The name is Italian for the fairy Morgana, Morgan le Fay of the King Arthur legends. A Sicilian tale says she raised a crystal palace in the air and pulled the far shore close, and when a barbarian king dived in to swim over and take the island, the vision broke and he drowned far from land.

A Fata Morgana can also stretch a real ship on the horizon into a tall, twisted phantom that appears to float clear of the water, and such sightings are often suggested as one source of the Flying Dutchman, the 17th-century legend of a doomed phantom ship. That is a proposed explanation, not proof.

Looking for the Northwest Passage in 1818, the British captain John Ross entered Lancaster Sound, saw a range of mountains blocking it, named them the Croker Mountains and sailed home in defeat. A year later his officer William Parry steered on through empty water where the range had seemed to stand, because the peaks had been a mirage, phantom mountains raised from distant ice.

In 1914 Donald MacMillan's expedition trekked some 125 miles over the Arctic sea ice toward Crocker Land, a country Robert Peary had reported in 1906. At last Piugaattoq, an Inuit hunter with the party, looked hard at its shining hills and said they were poo-jok, mist: a thin sea mist that a Fata Morgana had lifted into phantom mountains. No such land exists.

waterfalls-the-rivers-great-leaps.context_blurb:
A waterfall forms wherever a river meets a sudden step in its bed. The world's greatest falls pour off flat-topped mountains, over long cliffs of lava rock, or down chains of rapids, and every one of them is slowly eating its way upstream.

In Venezuela's Canaima wilderness, Angel Falls drops from the summit of Auyán-tepui about 979 metres in all, including a single unbroken plunge of some 807 metres, the tallest uninterrupted fall on Earth. The water often turns to drifting mist before it reaches the bottom. Victoria Falls, where the Zambezi divides Zambia from Zimbabwe, joins a width of 1.7 kilometres to a height of 108 metres, making it the largest single curtain of falling water on the planet.

David Livingstone reached it in 1855 and named it for his queen, but the Kololo and Lozi peoples already called it Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders, for its towering plume of spray and its roar.

On the border of Argentina and Brazil the Iguazú River spreads into roughly 275 individual falls around a vast curve of rock, and one narrow U-shaped chasm, the Devil's Throat, Garganta del Diablo in Spanish, swallows about half the river in one plunge. By volume the heavyweight is Boyoma Falls on the Congo River, seven stepped cataracts spread along more than 100 kilometres that pass about 17,000 cubic metres of water a second, more than Niagara and Iguazú together.

Auyán-tepui is a tepui, a lone sandstone tabletop with sheer walls that stands over the forest like an island, and such mountains are what remains after rivers and rain wore away the softer rock around them over tens of millions of years. Below Victoria Falls the Zambezi zigzags through a chain of narrow gorges in the basalt, because the river tore backward along cracks and fault lines in the rock, opening a new gorge each time it found a fresh line of weakness.

Niagara Falls is the clearest lesson in how falls move. A hard caprock of dolostone sits on soft shale. The soft shale crumbles and washes out from underneath, so the hard rock lip above keeps breaking off in slabs, and the falls retreat upstream. Niagara has crept back nearly 11 kilometres in some 10,900 years, though today it moves only about 30 centimetres a year, because much of its water is diverted for power.

wave-rock.context_blurb:
Near Hyden in Western Australia, some 300 kilometres inland among the wheat fields, a cliff about 15 metres high curls forward like an ocean wave frozen just before it breaks. Walk beneath its crest and you almost duck.

Wave Rock is the north face of Hyden Rock, a dome of granite rising alone from the plain, and its granite, about 2.63 billion years old, is some of the oldest crust in Australia.

No sea ever shaped it; the curl formed in the dark. Long ago, while the foot of the rock lay buried, groundwater soaking the soil slowly dissolved a hollow into the granite, perhaps 100 to 130 million years ago, and only when the surrounding soil wore away did the finished wave emerge into daylight.

Its vertical stripes, grey, yellow, brown and red, look like foam racing down the wave, but the weather painted them. Rain and seasonal springs run down the bare rock carrying dissolved iron and carbonate minerals, which stain the granite as they dry.

wellington.context_blurb:
Wellington, the capital of New Zealand, clings to steep hills around a deep harbour at the southern tip of the North Island, looking across a stormy strait to the South Island. It is a city of wind, earthquakes and film studios.

Its sea wind hardly ever drops, averaging about 27 kilometres an hour, and by average wind speed Wellington is reckoned the windiest city on Earth, so New Zealanders call it Windy Welly.

The cause is Cook Strait: the Roaring Forties, the strong westerlies of the Southern Ocean, are squeezed between the mountains of the two main islands into this one narrow channel, and like water through a pinched hose they speed up and hit the city.

At 41 degrees 17 minutes south, Wellington is the southernmost capital of any sovereign country, the capital nearest to Antarctica. Santiago, Montevideo and even Canberra all lie farther north. The Wellington Fault runs right through the city, marking where the Pacific and Australian plates slide past one another by 6 to 7.6 millimetres a year, building strain for the next great quake. In Upper Hutt one road was laid out extra wide just to keep houses back from the fault beneath it.

The director Peter Jackson made Wellington a film town, nicknamed Wellywood: in the suburb of Miramar, in an old paint factory turned studio, his Weta teams built creatures, armour and digital worlds, and New Zealand became Middle-earth for The Lord of the Rings.

The great Wairarapa earthquake of 1855, magnitude 8.2, heaved the harbour floor up by two to three metres, turning it into dry land, and much of today's central business district stands on that raised ground, later reclaimed. At Turakirae Head the coast jumped 6.4 metres in an instant.

where-the-sun-forgets-to-set-midnight-su.context_blurb:
Far enough north or south, the day stops behaving. In summer the Sun circles the sky without ever setting, and in winter it can vanish for weeks or months. All of it comes from the tilt of the spinning Earth.

At North Cape, the cliff at the top of Norway near 71 degrees north, the Sun never sets from about mid-May to late July, and near the June solstice it dips toward the sea around midnight, seems to pause, and climbs again: the midnight sun. The cause is Earth's axis, tipped about 23.5 degrees, for in the northern summer that tilt leans the North Pole toward the Sun, so at high latitudes the Sun never drops below the horizon. Earth is not any closer to the Sun then; the tilt alone does it.

The Arctic Circle, at about 66 degrees 33 minutes north, marks the southern edge of the midnight sun: on that line the Sun stays up for 24 hours on just one day a year, the June solstice. Its mirror in the south is the Antarctic Circle. The longest midnight sun in any real town belongs to Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago at about 78 degrees north, some 1,300 kilometres from the Pole, where Longyearbyen's endless day runs from about 19 April to 23 August.

The biggest city in the midnight-sun world is Murmansk, on Russia's Kola Peninsula, home to several hundred thousand people, where the Sun stays up for about 62 days, from late May to late July. Its dark mirror is the polar night: in Utqiagvik, Alaska, at 71 degrees north, the Sun sets in mid-November and stays below the horizon for about 65 days, until late January. The town still gets a few hours of pale twilight, snow-glow and aurora.

Strangely, in early January, in the depths of that sunless season, Earth is at its nearest to the Sun all year, a point called perihelion, while it is farthest away in early July, under the midnight sun. That proves the tilt, not distance, makes the seasons. At the North Pole in midsummer the Sun neither rises nor sets, nor does it arc overhead: it circles round the horizon sideways, in level loops, climbing in flat spirals to only about 23.5 degrees at the June solstice.

So the Pole's whole year is one long day and one long night, and the Sun rises there just once a year, around 18 March, and sets once, around 24 September. The halves are not equal, because the atmosphere refracts light over the horizon and keeps the Sun visible a few extra days, so the polar day lasts about 186 days and the night about 179, and the daylight wins by about a week.

The southern twin is McMurdo Station on Ross Island, at about 78 degrees south, Antarctica's largest research base, where the Sun never sets from about late October to late February. In winter its polar night runs from late April to mid-August.

wieliczka-salt-mine.context_blurb:
Under Wieliczka, a town just outside Kraków in southern Poland, miners cut salt for some seven centuries, until 1996, back when salt was precious enough to help fill a royal treasury. They left a labyrinth of tunnels and chambers, and some of the most surprising carvings anywhere underground.

The tour ends more than 100 metres down in a chapel of salt, often called the largest underground church in the world, some 54 metres long and 12 metres high, where altar, statues, stairs, floor tiles and even the glittering chandeliers were all cut by miners from grey rock salt. About 1.2 million people come to see it each year.

The miners' patron is Saint Kinga, a Hungarian princess promised to a Polish prince. Legend says that before her wedding she threw her engagement ring into a salt mine in Hungary, and the first block of salt cut at Wieliczka held the ring, shining inside it.

The salt itself is a gift from a vanished sea: some 13 to 14 million years ago an arm of an ancient sea in the Carpathian foothills slowly dried out under a warm climate and left a thick bed of rock salt behind. Following that one bed, miners dug more than 287 kilometres of passages, down to 327 metres, on nine levels.

xian-the-walled-city-at-the-end-of-the-s.context_blurb:
Xi'an, in central China, is one of the oldest cities in the country and once stood at the eastern end of the Silk Road. It was the capital of dynasty after dynasty, and in its golden age it was one of the largest cities on Earth.

A wall built under the Ming dynasty still encircles the old city, some 14 kilometres in circumference, its top broad enough to be a road along the sky, and visitors rent bicycles at the gate towers and pedal the whole circuit high above the streets.

For around ten centuries, silk-laden camel trains set out from this city toward the Persian and Roman worlds, and in those days it was called Chang'an, meaning perpetual peace, the eastern end of the overland Silk Road.

The old city kept time by morning bell and evening drum. At dawn the great bell in the Bell Tower, built in 1384, rang to open the day. At dusk the Drum Tower's huge drum sounded to warn everyone inside the walls that the gates were closing for the night curfew.

The monk Xuanzang walked the Silk Road to India and came home to Chang'an in 645 after about sixteen years, bringing 657 Buddhist scriptures, and around 652 the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, a brick tower of five storeys, was built to keep them safe. He spent the rest of his life translating them, and his journey later inspired the novel Journey to the West.

Silk Road traders founded Xi'an's Great Mosque around 742, and its keeper still goes up the minaret to call the faithful to prayer. But that minaret is no slender tower topped by a crescent: it is a Chinese pagoda, the Introspection Tower, and the whole mosque spreads across five courtyards under sweeping tiled roofs like a Chinese temple.

The great wall, which the first Ming emperor, Hongwu, started in 1370, looks wholly Ming, but along the west and south his builders raised it straight on top of the rammed-earth walls of the older Sui and Tang imperial city. So it still follows the outline of ancient Chang'an.

At its Tang peak, around 750, Chang'an held close to a million people on a planned grid of some 80 square kilometres, and in that age only Constantinople and Baghdad matched it.

yellowstone.context_blurb:
Yellowstone, mostly in Wyoming, became the world's first national park in 1872, and it sits on top of one of the biggest volcanic systems on Earth. Its ground steams, boils, spouts and glows with colour, holding more than 10,000 hot springs, mudpots, steam vents and geysers.

Its most famous geyser is Old Faithful, in the Upper Geyser Basin, the first in Yellowstone to be named, in 1870, and it shoots a boiling column some 106 to 185 feet high about every 90 minutes, reliable enough to plan a day around. In the Midway Geyser Basin lies Grand Prismatic Spring, named by the 1871 Hayden survey for its prism-like rings of red, orange, yellow, green and blue, and at about 370 feet across it is the largest hot spring in the United States.

Of the roughly 1,000 active geysers on Earth, more than half, over 500, erupt inside Yellowstone, more than in all the rest of the world together. Early visitors thought minerals had stained Grand Prismatic's rings, but the colours are alive: mats of heat-loving microbes, each colour band a different kind suited to its own water temperature, the coolest at the edge. The deep-blue centre is too hot for them; its blue is simply the colour of deep, clear water. In the Norris Geyser Basin waits Steamboat Geyser, the highest-shooting active geyser in the world, which reached 403 feet in 2019, about twice Old Faithful's height, but it keeps no schedule at all.

All of this lies inside one oval basin about 30 by 45 miles, a caldera left by the collapse of the ground above an emptied magma chamber, because Yellowstone is a supervolcano. Its floor still rises and falls as magma shifts below. At the park's north end, hot water rises through buried limestone, dissolves it, and lays it down again as white travertine, building a staircase of terraces that adds over two tons of new stone every day: Mammoth Hot Springs. In the park's own grand canyon, the Yellowstone River makes two great leaps, and the taller is the Lower Falls, plunging 308 feet, almost double Niagara's drop. The falls just upstream drop about 109 feet.

Yellowstone has erupted catastrophically at least three times, about 2.1 million, 1.3 million and 640,000 years ago. The oldest, the Huckleberry Ridge eruption, threw out some 2,450 cubic kilometres of rock and ash, thousands of times more than Mount St. Helens did in 1980. The canyon's walls blaze yellow, orange and red because hot, mineral-rich water has altered the volcanic rhyolite and the iron in it has oxidised, so in effect the canyon is rusting.

Across Idaho's Snake River Plain runs a trail of dead calderas, older and older to the southwest, the oldest some 16 million years old, because a fixed hotspot deep in the mantle stays put while the North American plate slides southwest over it. Yellowstone is the hotspot's current, living stop. In 1969 Thomas Brock found the microbe Thermus aquaticus thriving in Mushroom Spring, a near-boiling Yellowstone hot spring, and its heat-proof enzyme, Taq polymerase, lets machines copy DNA through repeated heating in the method called PCR. Every modern DNA test depends on it.

yogyakarta-borobudur-and-prambanan.context_blurb:
Yogyakarta, called Jogja, is the cultural heart of the Indonesian island of Java, home of batik, shadow puppets and gamelan, and still the seat of a reigning sultan. On the fertile volcanic plain around it stand two of the greatest temples in Southeast Asia, one Buddhist and one Hindu.

Borobudur is not a tower to enter but a stone mountain to climb, nine stacked terraces about 123 metres to a side yet only some 35 metres tall, and Guinness World Records named it, in 2012, the biggest Buddhist temple on Earth. Under an hour's drive across that plain stands a forest of stone spires, Prambanan, Indonesia's greatest Hindu temple, dedicated in 856 under King Rakai Pikatan and first named Shivagrha, the House of Shiva.

From above, Borobudur's six square and three round terraces form one huge, balanced diagram of the cosmos, a mandala, and pilgrims walk it clockwise, spiralling upward from the world of desire toward enlightenment. Some two million blocks of volcanic stone make up the monument, with no mortar at all, held together by carved knobs, notches and dovetails that interlock like a puzzle. In a restoration from 1975 to 1982, more than a million of them were taken apart and reset. On the three round terraces at the top stand 72 bell-shaped stupas pierced with diamond-shaped holes, and inside each one sits a seated stone Buddha, part of the 504 Buddhas the monument once held.

The two giants are opposites in shape: broad Borobudur is only about 35 metres high, while Prambanan's slender central spire for Shiva soars to about 47 metres, taller than its Buddhist rival some 53 kilometres away. To win Princess Rara Jonggrang, the legend goes, Prince Bandung Bondowoso had to raise a thousand temples before morning, and with an army of spirits he came within one of it, until she tricked the spirits into fleeing. In his rage he turned her to stone as the thousandth temple, and she is said to be the statue of the goddess Durga in the main Shiva temple. Prambanan was a city of shrines, some 240 temples, with 224 small ones in rings around three great towers for Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, and in Southeast Asia only Angkor Wat, in Cambodia, is a larger Hindu temple complex.

At Borobudur's summit stands one great stone dome, the goal of the whole climb, and it holds no statue. The climb passes through three realms: desire at the base, form on the square terraces and the formless on the round summit. By tradition the empty crowning stupa stands for that formless realm, the void of enlightenment itself.

Abandoned around 1000 AD, Borobudur lay hidden for some 800 years under jungle and deep drifts of ash blown from the eruptions of Mount Merapi nearby, though local villagers never forgot it. Clearing began in 1814 under Thomas Stamford Raffles, and in 2010 Merapi dusted the statues again. In 1885 a Dutch engineer found that the builders had walled up the very base of the temple, hiding an entire concealed band of carved panels, the hidden foot, whose 160 scenes show the law of karma through everyday life in 9th-century Java. One corner is left open so visitors can still see them.

One Borobudur panel shows a Javanese outrigger under sail. In 2003 a crew led by the British sailor Philip Beale used the carving as the only plan for a full-sized wooden replica, the Samudra Raksa, and took it all the way to Africa, by way of Madagascar to Ghana. The voyage traced the Cinnamon Route, the old sea road by which Javanese sailors once shipped cargo westward.

zhangye-danxia-rainbow-mountains.context_blurb:
In Gansu province in northwestern China, the Zhangye hills are striped from top to bottom in blue-grey, green, yellow, orange and red, as if a rainbow had been laid across bare stone.

The colours glow most vividly in the low light of dawn and dusk, when every band deepens, and again just after rain, when a wet sheen brightens them. The best season is June to September.

The boldest ridges burn brick red because every sand grain in those ridges is coated with iron oxide, the mineral hematite, the same rust that reddens an old nail and the surface of Mars. Other iron minerals give the yellows and greens.

Long before they were mountains, this was a lowland of streams and shallow lakes, where sand and mud settled in flat sheets that each became a stripe of stone. The oldest beds are about 114 to 106 million years old, laid down in the Cretaceous, when dinosaurs ruled the Earth.

Those layers once lay flat, but about 55 million years ago the Indian plate rammed into the Eurasian plate, the same crash that is still raising the Himalayas, and the push tipped Zhangye's beds steeply onto their edges. That is why the stripes now march up the ridges.

Geologists call this whole family of red sandstone cliffs and towers Danxia, meaning rosy cloud or sunset glow, a name the geologist Feng Jinglan gave in 1928 after Mount Danxia in Guangdong. Zhangye is the most colourful Danxia site of all, and it became a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2020.
